## Abstract

Fractional derivatives have emerged as a powerful mathematical tool for modeling complex physical phenomena exhibiting memory effects and nonlocal interactions, which cannot be adequately captured by classical integer-order models. Fractional differential equations (FDEs) incorporating these derivatives provide a more accurate framework for describing anomalous diffusion, transport in heterogeneous media, and other processes with hereditary dynamics. However, the nonlocal nature that enhances their modeling capability also introduces substantial challenges, particularly in inverse problems where unknown sources, coefficients, or initial conditions must be recovered from indirect and often noisy measurements.

Inverse problems for FDEs are typically ill-posed in the Hadamard sense, necessitating regularization techniques such as the quasi-boundary value method to restore stability and ensure meaningful reconstructions. The numerical solution of these problems relies on discretization techniques that produce large-scale linear systems whose coefficient matrices inherit the nonlocal structure of the fractional operators. Understanding the asymptotic spectral properties of these matrix sequences is essential for designing efficient solvers and preconditioning strategies.

The theory of Generalized Locally Toeplitz (GLT) sequences provides a powerful and unified framework for this purpose, characterizing the spectral distribution of large structured matrices arising from discretizations and offering rigorous guidelines for preconditioner design. This thesis leverages GLT theory to analyze matrix sequences from inverse problems of FDEs, develop structure-preserving preconditioners, and investigate fundamental questions concerning nonlinear operations within the GLT algebra. In particular, it establishes maximal distribution results for geometric means of GLT sequences, proving that when the associated symbols commute, the geometric mean sequence remains GLT without requiring symbol invertibility, thereby resolving a long-standing conjecture while demonstrating that the result is maximal in the noncommuting degenerate case.

Collectively, this thesis contributes to both the theory and numerical solution of inverse problems for FDEs, integrating regularization theory, spectral analysis, and preconditioning into a coherent computational framework. The theoretical advancements concerning GLT sequences and their geometric means further enrich the mathematical foundations of structured matrix analysis, providing practical strategies for solving inverse problems in complex physical systems governed by nonlocal dynamics.

## General notations and acronyms

• N, R, C: Sets of natural, real, and complex numbers, respectively.<tbc>

• R<sup>+</sup>, N<sup>+</sup>: Sets of positive real and natural numbers.<tbc>

• Z: Set of integers.<tbc>

• K: A field, usually R or C.<tbc>

• K_<sup>r</sup>_: Space of vectors of length _r_ with entries in K.<tbc>

• \(\mathbb{K}^{r\times s}\): Space of \(r\times s\) matrices with entries in K.<tbc>

• \(\mathbb{K}^{n\times n}\): Space of square \(n\times n\) matrices over K.<tbc>

• **_x,y_**: Vectors in K_<sup>r</sup>_ (bold letters usually denote vectors).<tbc>

• _A,B_: Matrices in \(\mathbb{K}^{n\times n}\) unless specified otherwise.<tbc>

• I_<sub>n</sub>_ or _I<sub>n</sub>_: \(n\times n\) identity matrix.<tbc>

• **0**_<sub>n</sub>_ or 0_<sub>n</sub>_: \(n\times n\) zero matrix.<tbc>

• \((\cdot)^\top\): denotes the transpose of a vector or matrix.<tbc>

• \((\cdot)^*\): denotes the conjugate transpose of a vector or matrix.<tbc>

• \((\cdot)^\dagger\): denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of a square matrix.<tbc>

• \(\lambda_j(A)\): denotes the _j_-th eigenvalue of \(A\in\mathbb{K}^{n\times n}\), for _j_=1_,...,n_.<tbc>

• \(\sigma_j(A)\): denotes the _j_-th singular value of \(A\in\mathbb{K}^{n\times n}\), for _j_=1_,...,n_.<tbc>

• H: Hilbert space.<tbc>

• \(\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z\): Pauli matrices.<tbc>

• \(\sigma^{(i)}\): Pauli operator acting on the _i_-th spin.<tbc>

• _H_: Hamiltonian operator of the system.<tbc>

• \(\rho(H)\): empirical spectral measure of _H_.<tbc>

• \(\chi\): Magnetic susceptibility.<tbc>

• \(\beta\): Inverse temperature parameter.<tbc>

• _Z_: Partition function.<tbc>

• \(\langle\cdot\rangle\): Expectation with respect to the Gibbs measure.<tbc>

• \(A\ge B\), where \(A,B\in\mathbb{K}^{n\times n}\), means that _A-B_ is positive semidefinite. Likewise, \(A\le B\) means that _A-B_ is negative semidefinite.<tbc>

• _A\>B_, where \(A,B\in\mathbb{K}^{n\times n}\), means that _A-B_ is positive definite. Likewise, _A\<B_ means that _A-B_ is negative definite.<tbc>

• _A∼B_, where \(A,B\in\mathbb{K}^{n\times n}\), denotes that _A_ and _B_ are similar matrices (i.e., there exists an invertible _P_ such that _A=PBP_<sup>-1</sup>).<tbc>

• \(\|\cdot\|_p\): denotes the standard _p_-norm of a vector or matrix, \(1\le p\le\infty\).<tbc>

• \(\|\cdot\|\): denotes the spectral norm (largest singular value), coincides with \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\). If the matrix is normal, the spectral norm coincides with the spectral radius.<tbc>

• \(\otimes\): Kronecker (tensor) product. For \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{p\times q}\), \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times s}\),<tbc>

<tbc>\(A\otimes B=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c }
a_{11}B & \cdots & a_{1q}B \\
\vdots &  & \vdots \\
a_{p1}B & \cdots & a_{pq}B
\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{pr\times qs}\)<tbc>

• _L<sup>p</sup>(D_): Space of _p_-integrable functions on domain _D_.<tbc>

• _C_(\[_a,b_\]): Space of continuous functions on \[_a,b_\].<tbc>

• \(\mathcal{O}(\cdot)\), \(o(\cdot)\): Big-_O_ and little-_o_ notation.<tbc>

• C_<sub>c</sub>_(R), C_<sub>c</sub>_(C): The set of continuous, complex-valued functions with compact support on R or C.<tbc>

• \(\partial D\): boundary of a set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\); in particular, \(\partial\Omega\) denotes the boundary of the spatial domain \(\Omega\).

**Multi-index notation:**

• **_i_** denotes a multi-index \((i_1,\dots,i_d)\in\mathbb{Z}^d\). Its size will be clear from context.<tbc>

• **0,1,2**_,..._ are vectors of all zeros, ones, twos, etc.<tbc>

• **_h_**+**_k_** is the multi-index whose components are _h<sub>r</sub>+k<sub>r</sub>_ for _r_=1_,...,d_. More generally, operations between multi-indices such as subtraction, multiplication, division, and so on, are performed componentwise.<tbc>

• \(h\le k\) means that \(h_r\le k_r\) for all _r_=1_,...,d_. More generally, relations between multi-indices are evaluated componentwise.<tbc>

• **_h_**_,...,**k**_ denotes the multi-index range \(\{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}^d:h\le\ell\le k\}\). With \(\ell=h,\dots,k\) we mean that \(\ell\) varies in this range from **_h_** to **_k_** according to the standard lexicographic ordering:<tbc>

<tbc>\(\left[\cdots\left[[(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_d)]_{\ell_d=h_d,\dots,k_d}\right]_{\ell_{d-1}=h_{d-1},\dots,k_{d-1}}\cdots\right]_{\ell_1=h_1,\dots,k_1}.\)<tbc>

• \(m\rightarrow\infty\) means that \(min(m)=min_{r=1,\dots,d}m_r\rightarrow\infty\), or equivalently, that all the components tend to infinity.<tbc>

• _N_(**_m_**) is the product of all the components of **_m_**, i.e., \(N(m):=\prod_{r=1}^dm_r\).<tbc>

• {_A<sub>n</sub>}<sub>n</sub>_: Sequence of matrices indexed by size/discretization parameter _n_.<tbc>

• _T<sub>n</sub>(f_): Toeplitz matrix of size _n_ generated by symbol _f_.<tbc>

• _C<sub>n</sub>(f_): Circulant matrix of size _n_ generated by symbol _f_.<tbc>

• _H<sub>n</sub>(f_): Hankel matrix of size _n_ generated by symbol _f_.<tbc>

• Symbol (\(\kappa\)): Measurable function associated with a matrix-sequence, e.g., \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\).<tbc>

• Symbol (\(\xi\)): Measurable function associated with a matrix-sequence, e.g., \(\{B_n\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\xi\).<tbc>

• \(D=[0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\): Typical domain for the symbol of a _d_-level GLT sequence.<tbc>

• \(\sim_\sigma\): Singular value distribution.<tbc>

• \(\sim_\lambda\): Eigenvalue distribution.<tbc>

• ∼<sub>GLT</sub>: Matrix-sequence is a GLT sequence with symbol.<tbc>

• ran(_M_): The column space (range) of a matrix _M_.<tbc>

• essRan(_g_): the essential range of a measurable function \(g:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^t\rightarrow Y\) , where _Y_ is C, C_<sup>r</sup>_, \(\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), or the Grassmannian of subspaces of C_<sup>r</sup>_, i.e.<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathrm{essRan}(g)=\big\{y\in Y:\mu_t\big(\{x\in D:g(x)\in B_Y(y,\epsilon)\}\big)>0\forall\epsilon>0\big\},\)<tbc>

<tbc>where \(\mu_t\) is the Lebesgue measure on _D_ and \(B_Y(y,\epsilon)\) is the ball of radius \(\epsilon\) centered at _y_ in _Y_ (with respect to the natural metric on _Y_ ).

**Acronyms and Abbreviations:**

• GLT: Generalized Locally Toeplitz<tbc>

• LT: Locally Toeplitz<tbc>

• HPD: Hermitian positive definite<tbc>

• SPD: Symmetric positive definite<tbc>

• a.c.s.: Approximating class of sequences<tbc>

• FC: Fractional Calculus<tbc>

## Introduction Fractional calculus (FC) provides a natural and powerful extension of classical differential calculus by allowing derivatives and integrals of non-integer order [100, 105]. Although fractional derivatives already appeared in the early development of calculus, for a long time they remained mainly of theoretical interest. In recent decades, however, fractional differential equations (FDEs) have attracted growing attention from both pure and applied mathematics due to their remarkable ability to model complex phenomena that cannot be adequately described by classical integer-order models [74]. The key feature underlying their success is the intrinsic nonlocality of fractional operators, which introduces memory effects in time and long-range interactions in space, allowing a more faithful representation of many real-world processes. FDEs play a central role in the modeling of anomalous diffusion, a class of transport phenomena characterized by deviations from standard Brownian motion [93]. Such deviations arise naturally in heterogeneous and porous media, plasma physics, viscoelastic materials, image reconstruction, finance, and wave propagation in biological tissues [49, 83]. Depending on the physical mechanism involved, fractional derivatives may act in time, space, or both variables. Time-fractional models typically describe non-Markovian dynamics with memory effects, while space- fractional models capture heavy-tailed jump distributions and long-range spatial interactions [75, 84]. Widely used operators include the Riemann–Liouville, Caputo, and Grünwald–Letnikov derivatives, as well as Riesz operators and the fractional Laplacian, together with their tempered variants, which introduce exponential damping to account for finite-range effects [92, 110].
Despite their modeling flexibility and expressive power, FDEs pose significant analytical and computational challenges. Closed-form solutions are rarely available and, when they exist, they are often unsuitable for practical computations. As a consequence, numerical methods play a fundamental role in the study and simulation of fractional models. Many numerical methods have been developed to efficiently solve FDEs, including finite difference methods [132], finite element methods [30], finite volume methods [36], and spectral methods [47]. Although these approaches are capable of producing accurate approximations, achieving high accuracy typically requires very fine spatial and temporal discretizations. As a consequence, the resulting algebraic systems become large and computationally demanding, especially in multi-dimensional settings. A major source of difficulty lies in the intrinsic nonlocal nature of (fractional) differential operators. Unlike classical local operators, their discretization leads to dense coefficient matrices, resulting in high memory requirements and increased computational cost.
In many applications, fractional models arise not only in direct problems, where the governing equations and parameters are known, but also in inverse problems (IPs). Typical IPs include the identification of unknown sources, coefficients, initial conditions, boundary data, or even the fractional order itself from indirect and often noisy measurements [70]. IPs are particularly challenging because they combine the intrinsic ill-posedness of IPs with the nonlocal behavior of fractional operators. From a mathematical standpoint, these problems are often ill-posed in the sense of Hadamard, meaning that solutions may not exist, may not be unique,

or may depend discontinuously on the data. In practice, even small perturbations in the measurements can produce large errors in the reconstructions \[34\]. To address the challenges arising from ill-posed IPs in FDEs, various regularization techniques have been developed to restore stability and ensure meaningful reconstructions. Motivated by their wide-ranging practical applications, IPs for FDEs have been extensively studied using diverse analytical and computational approaches \[58, 59, 129, 60, 61, 62, 63, 70, 111\]. In general, regularization methods incorporate additional information or constraints on the solution in order to control instability and suppress the amplification of noise. Among the most widely used approaches, Tikhonov regularization and its variants, including simplified and generalized formulations, stabilize the solution by introducing penalty terms that control smoothness or enforce _a priori_ assumptions on the unknown solution \[80, 96\]. Another effective approach is the quasi-boundary value method, also known as the nonlocal boundary value method, which has been successfully applied to a variety of ill-posed IPs, particularly for parabolic equations and fractional diffusion models \[29, 48\]. In FDEs, regularization methods must ensure stability and accuracy while accounting for the nonlocal nature of the operators.
The numerical treatment of both direct and IPs for FDEs ultimately leads to the solution of large linear systems of the form \(A_nx_n=b_n,\) where \(A_n\in\mathbb{C}^{d_n\times d_n}\) is a square matrix and the index \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) is related to the fineness of the discretization mesh. As the grid is refined, the dimension _dn_ increases and typically satisfies \(d_n\rightarrow+\infty\) as \(n\rightarrow+\infty\), so that one naturally deals with a _sequence_ of matrices {_An}n_ of growing size rather than a single matrix. The collective spectral behavior of {_An}n_ is therefore a key object of interest, since it reveals important numerical features and potential difficulties, such as severe ill- conditioning and slow convergence of iterative methods \[25, 116, 127\]. In this matrix- sequence setting, the relevant spectral information is not contained in any individual matrix, but rather in the way the spectra of {_An}n_ evolve as the discretization is refined. This naturally leads to the notion of asymptotic eigenvalue and singular value distributions in the Weyl sense, which capture the limiting spectral content of the entire sequence as \(n\rightarrow+\infty\). For a wide class of discretizations, this limiting behavior can be described by a measurable function, referred to as the _symbol_, which reflects the combined influence of the underlying (fractional) differential operator, its coefficients, the computational domain, and the discretization scheme. This symbol- based spectral description plays a central role in numerical analysis, as it explains the observed conditioning of the linear systems and provides a rigorous framework for the design and analysis of effective preconditioners and scalable iterative methods. Structured matrices play a central role in this analysis, because in many relevant settings the discretization of FDEs produces coefficient matrices with Toeplitz or Toeplitz-like patterns that can be exploited to build fast solvers and preconditioners. In particular, when FDEs have constant coefficients and are discretized on uniform grids, the resulting matrices often exhibit a Toeplitz or multilevel Toeplitz structure \[20, 26, 27, 95\]. Such matrices arise from the shift-invariant nature of the underlying operators and possess a rich spectral theory developed over the last century. Moreover, Toeplitz matrices admit fast matrix-vector products and efficient algorithms based on the fast Fourier transform, and their eigenvalue and singular value distribu

tions are directly linked to their generating functions [26]. In more general settings, such as variable coefficients, nonuniform grids, or non-Cartesian domains, the classical Toeplitz structure is typically lost. Nevertheless, many discretization matrices arising in practice belong to the broader class of GLT matrix sequences [124, 41, 42]. The GLT theory provides a unifying framework for describing the asymptotic spectral behavior of large structured and partially structured matrices. GLT sequences form a rich ∗-algebra that includes Toeplitz sequences, diagonal sampling matrices, and zero-distributed sequences as fundamental components. Each GLT sequence is uniquely associated with a symbol, and algebraic operations on matrix sequences correspond, almost everywhere, to pointwise operations on their symbols [41, 42]. This framework supports the design and analysis of numerical solvers, preconditioners, and multigrid methods, since the convergence of Krylov subspace and multigrid schemes depends strongly on conditioning and eigenvalue clustering, which can be predicted and optimized via GLT symbols [41, 27, 95]. Recent developments in symbol-based preconditioning for evolutionary PDEs include the block Toeplitz preconditioner for wave equations introduced by Hon and Serra-Capizzano [51], and the sine transform based preconditioned MINRES method for all-at-once systems developed by Hon, Fung, Dong, and Serra-Capizzano [53]. These works highlight the effectiveness of combining structural properties with fast transforms, and the present thesis extends these ideas to IPs and variable-coefficient FDEs.
A particularly rich connection within the theory of GLT matrix sequences concerns the notion of geometric means of matrices. The geometric mean of Hermitian positive definite matrices was rigorously formalized by Ando, Li, and Mathias and has since become a fundamental concept in matrix analysis and operator theory. Given two Hermitian positive definite matrices _A_ and _B_, their geometric mean is defined by \(G(A,B)=A^{1/2}\big(A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}\big)^{1/2}A^{1/2}=G(B,A),\) a definition that preserves symmetry, positive definiteness, and key variational properties [3, 16]. Geometric means naturally arise in preconditioning strategies, operator interpolation, and the modeling of composite physical systems, where nonlinear matrix operations are unavoidable. When applied to sequences of Hermitian positive definite matrices, the geometric mean interacts in a subtle way with asymptotic spectral properties. Within the GLT framework, this interaction raises fundamental questions concerning symbol calculus, commutativity of matrix-valued symbols, degeneracy, and maximality of distribution results. ## Structure of the thesis This thesis is structured as follows.
**Chapter 1** introduces the analytical foundations required throughout the thesis. We review the main definitions of fractional calculus employed in our work, including the Riemann–Liouville, Caputo, Grünwald–Letnikov, and Riesz fractional operators, together with their relationships under suitable regularity assumptions. Generalized formulations in the form of tempered fractional derivatives are also discussed, due to their relevance in modeling finite-range diffusion processes. The chapter further presents Mittag–Leffler and generalized Mittag–Leffler type functions, along with their key analytical properties used in the study of FDEs and IPs.

In **Chapter 2**, we introduce the foundational concepts related to matrix sequences that are essential for the subsequent spectral analysis. The chapter focuses on singular value and eigenvalue distributions in the asymptotic sense, approximation classes of matrix sequences, and multi-level structures. These topics provide the mathematical background required for understanding the spectral behavior of large structured matrices arising from discretized differential operators.
In **Chapter 3**, we review several classes of classical structured matrices that play a central role in numerical linear algebra. In particular, we discuss Toeplitz, circulant, \(\omega\)-circulant, \(\tau\), and Hankel matrices, presenting their definitions together with their main algebraic and spectral properties. The importance of these matrix classes in both numerical computations and asymptotic linear algebra is highlighted, with particular emphasis on their spectral features and computational advantages.
**Chapter 4** is devoted to the development of the theory of GLT matrix sequences, which constitutes the core theoretical framework for the spectral analysis carried out in this thesis. We introduce the notion of GLT sequences and present the structure of GLT algebras together with their fundamental properties. The chapter establishes the axioms and algebraic rules governing GLT sequences, distinguishing between matrix sequences with explicit and hidden asymptotic structures. Key concepts such as zero-distributed sequences, block Toeplitz and block diagonal sampling matrices, and the construction of _d_-level, _r_-block GLT ∗-algebras are also discussed in detail.
**Chapter 5** is devoted to the study of IPs for a two-dimensional generalized diffusion equation involving memory-dependent time-fractional derivatives. The chapter considers the identification of both a space-dependent source term and a time-dependent coefficient from additional measurement data. The IPs are shown to be ill-posed in the sense of Hadamard, and existence and uniqueness of solutions are established under suitable over-specified and regularity assumptions. Special cases corresponding to particular choices of the memory kernel are analyzed in detail.
In **Chapter 6**, we investigate an IP for a space-time FDE with variable coefficients. The ill-posedness of the problem is addressed through a quasi-boundary value regularization. A finite difference discretization yields large two-by-two block linear system. Its spectral behavior is analyzed within the framework of GLT, which provides guidance for the construction of an effective Krylov subspace preconditioner. Numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy of the reconstruction and the efficiency of the proposed preconditioning strategy.
**Chapter 7** investigates an IP for a two-dimensional space-time FDE involving a tempered time-fractional derivative and Caputo fractional derivatives in space. The ill-posed problem is regularized by a quasi-boundary value method. A finite difference discretization yields large two-by-two block structured linear systems with multilevel Toeplitz-like structure, for which we develop an efficient preconditioning strategy combined with GMRES. A comprehensive GLT analysis of the coefficient matrix sequences guides the construction of the preconditioner. Numerical experiments confirm the stability, accuracy, and computational efficiency of the proposed approach in reconstructing the source term from noisy data.
**Chapter 8** studies the spectral properties and preconditioning of linear systems arising from the finite difference discretization of a time-dependent space-FDE with variable coefficient _a(x_) on \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), _d_=1,2. The equation is discretized by the shifted Grünwald formula in space and the \(\theta\)-method in time, leading to (_d_+1)-level Toeplitz-like all-at-once systems. Using GLT theory, the spectral distribution of the

<tbc>corresponding matrix sequences and of suitable preconditioned systems is analyzed, fully covering the case of nonconstant _a_. Numerical results confirm the theoretical findings.

**Chapter 9** is devoted to the analysis of the spectral distribution of geometric means of Hermitian positive definite GLT matrix sequences to the maximal setting, allowing for degenerate symbols and non-commuting cases. It is shown that, when the associated GLT symbols commute, the geometric mean is again a GLT sequence, with symbol given by the geometric mean of the original symbols, without requiring invertibility almost everywhere. This result completes the proof of a long-standing conjecture in both the scalar and block settings, for arbitrary dimensions. The chapter also presents detailed numerical experiments illustrating that, in the presence of non-commuting symbols and simultaneous degeneracy, the classical relation may fail. These experiments reveal new spectral phenomena and suggest a natural candidate symbol for the geometric mean in such generalized situations.

## Main Contributions of the Thesis

The main contributions of this thesis are theoretical, analytical, and computational, and can be summarized as follows.

1. **Inverse source problems for generalized diffusion equations.** In Chapter 5, we formulate and analyze two ISPs for a two-dimensional generalized diffusion equation involving a Caputo-type time-fractional derivative with a general memory kernel and nonlocal boundary conditions. Using the spectral decomposition of the associated elliptic operator, we derive explicit series representations of the solutions in terms of bi-orthogonal systems of eigenfunctions. We establish rigorous existence and uniqueness results for regular solutions and demonstrate that both ISPs are ill-posed in the Hadamard sense. Several special cases, including tempered, multi-term, mono-term, and classical diffusion models, are obtained as particular choices of the memory kernel, illustrating the unifying nature of the generalized formulation.<tbc>

2. **Krylov preconditioning for inverse problems in space-time fractional diffusion equations.** In Chapter 6, we address an ISP for a space-time FDE involving a tempered fractional derivative in the time variable and a Caputo fractional derivative in the space variable. The ill-posed problem is regularized using the quasi-boundary value method. The considered equation is of great interest in applications, and a finite difference approximation of the resulting regularized problem leads to a two-by-two block linear system of large dimensions. A detailed spectral analysis of the associated matrix sequences is conducted using the GLT framework. Based on this analysis, we develop an efficient block triangular preconditioner for the GMRES method and prove that the preconditioned matrix sequence is weakly clustered at one in the GLT, singular value, and eigenvalue sense.<tbc>

3. **Efficient Krylov solvers for inverse source problems in two-dimensional space- time fractional diffusion equations.** In Chapter 7, we extend the previous work to the two-dimensional setting, developing a fast algorithm to reconstruct the source term in a space-time FDE with variable coefficients. The<tbc>

finite difference discretization of the regularized problem leads to a large-scale all-at-once system with multilevel Toeplitz-like structure. We conduct a comprehensive GLT analysis of the coefficient matrix sequences and construct an effective preconditioner. Numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy of the reconstruction and the efficiency of the proposed preconditioning strategy across various fractional orders and problem sizes. The convergence behavior depends mainly on the spatial discretization, with limited sensitivity to temporal refinement, confirming that the number of outliers depends only on the spatial dimension.<tbc>

4. **Structure-preserving preconditioning for variable-coefficient space-fractional diffusion equations.** In Chapter 8, we study the spectral properties and preconditioning of linear systems arising from the finite difference discretization of time-dependent space-FDEs with variable coefficients. The model involves a one-sided Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative multiplied by a variable coefficient, discretized using the shifted Grünwald formula in space and the \(\theta\)-method in time. The resulting all-at-once systems exhibit a (_d_+1)-level Toeplitz-like matrix structure. Using GLT theory, we provide a detailed analysis of the spectral distribution of both the original and preconditioned matrix sequences and propose structure-preserving preconditioners based on circulant approximations. The main novelty is that the analysis fully covers the nonconstant variable coefficient case, both in one and two spatial dimensions, extending several existing results in the literature which were often restricted to more simplified settings.<tbc>

5. **Maximal results for geometric means of GLT sequences.** In Chapter 9, we address a fundamental open question concerning the spectral distribution of geometric means of Hermitian positive definite (HPD) GLT matrix sequences. We prove that when the GLT symbols commute, the invertibility condition on the symbols can be completely removed, resolving a long-standing conjecture. This result is established both in the scalar setting for any dimension and in the general block setting under the assumption that the symbols commute. We further demonstrate that the result is maximal: when the symbols do not commute and are simultaneously degenerate, the classical relation may fail and the geometric mean sequence may not coincide with the classical geometric mean of the symbols. Numerical experiments reveal new spectral phenomena explained by the theory of momentary GLT symbols, including secondary eigenvalue distributions and extremal spectral behavior connected to the order of vanishing of the associated GLT symbol.

Collectively, these contributions provide a comprehensive framework for addressing ISPs in FDEs, combining analytical regularization techniques, spectral analysis of structured matrix sequences, and advanced preconditioning strategies. The thesis advances both the theoretical understanding of ISPs for fractional models and the development of efficient numerical solvers for large-scale structured linear systems arising from their discretization.

## Chapter 1 ### Fractional operators and Mittag-Leffler type functions This chapter presents the fundamental concepts of FC, encompassing both fractional operators and Mittag-Leffler type functions, which constitute the analytical foundation of this thesis. We review several widely used definitions of fractional integrals and derivatives, which play a central role in the modeling, analysis, and numerical approximation of FDEs.
FC generalizes classical differential calculus by allowing differentiation and integration of non-integer order. Formally, this extension is expressed as \(\frac{\partial^nu}{\partial z^n}\longrightarrow\frac{\partial^\alpha u}{\partial z^\alpha},n\in\mathbb{N},\alpha\in\mathbb{C},\) where the resulting operators exhibit intrinsic nonlocality and memory effects. These properties distinguish fractional derivatives from their integer order counterparts and make them particularly suitable for modeling anomalous transport and diffusion processes in heterogeneous and complex media \[105, 110, 93\].
The origins of FC can be traced back to the seventeenth century, when L’Hôpital raised the question of interpreting derivatives of non-integer order. Subsequent contributions by Euler, Lacroix, Fourier, and Abel gradually clarified the analytical structure of such operators, while the work of Liouville and Riemann in the nineteenth century provided a rigorous integral-based framework. These developments led to the classical Riemann-Liouville formulation and, later, to alternative definitions such as the Caputo, Grünwald-Letnikov, and Riesz derivatives, each tailored to different analytical and modeling requirements \[94, 105, 74\].
In addition to fractional operators, special functions play a fundamental role in the theory of FDEs. In particular, Mittag-Leffler type functions naturally arise in the explicit representation of solutions of FDEs and multi-term FDEs. They generalize the exponential function and govern the temporal behavior, stability, and long-time dynamics of fractional models \[46\]. For this reason, this chapter also introduces Mittag-Leffler function (MLF) and generalized MLF, which provide essential analytical tools for the theoretical and numerical developments presented in the subsequent chapters. ### 1.1 Fractional operators **Definition 1.1** _\[105\] Let_ \(\xi>0\)_, and_ \(u(z)\in L^1([a,b])\)_. Then, the left- and right-sided Riemann-Liouville fractional integrals are defined as_ \(\mathcal{D}_{a+,z}^{-\xi} u(z)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\xi)}\int_a^z\frac{u(\sigma)}{(z-\sigma)^{1-\xi}}d\sigma,\)
\(\mathcal{D}_{b-,z}^{-\xi} u(z)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\xi)}\int_z^b\frac{u(\sigma)}{(\sigma-z)^{1-\xi}}d\sigma.\)

_where_ \(\Gamma(\cdot)\) _is the gamma function._ _Since the development of FC, several definitions of non-integer order derivatives have been proposed, including the Riemann-Liouville, Caputo, and Grünwald-Letnikov formulations \[105, 110\]. These definitions are generally not equivalent on bounded domains, unless additional regularity or boundary conditions are imposed on the function u(z). In the present work, we first focus on the Riemann-Liouville fractional derivatives (R-LFD), which are introduced below._ **Definition 1.2** _\[105\] Let_ \(\xi\in(n-1,n)\), \(n\in\mathbb{N}^+\)_, and let_ \(u(z)\in AC([a,b])\) _be absolutely continuous. Then, the left- and right-sided R-LFD are defined as_ \(\mathcal{D}_{a+,z}^\xi u(z)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(n-\xi)}\frac{d^n}{dz^n}\int_a^z\frac{u(\sigma)}{(z-\sigma)^{\xi-n+1}}d\sigma,\)
\(\mathcal{D}_{b-,z}^\xi u(z)=\frac{(-1)^n}{\Gamma(n-\xi)}\frac{d^n}{dz^n}\int_z^b\frac{u(\sigma)}{(\sigma-z)^{\xi-n+1}}d\sigma.\) If \(\alpha\in\mathbb{N}\), the R-LFDs reduce to the classical integer order derivatives. We now introduce the Riesz fractional derivative, which is closely related to the Riemann- Liouville formulation. **Definition 1.3** _\[110\] For_ \(\xi\in(n-1,n)\), \(n\in\mathbb{N}^+\)_, the Riesz fractional derivative is defined as_ \(\frac{\partial^\xi u(z)}{\partial|z|^\xi}=c(\xi)\left(\mathcal{D}_{a+,z}^\xi u(z)+\mathcal{D}_{b-,z}^\xi u(z)\right),\) (1.1) _where_ \(c(\xi)=-\frac{1}{2\mathrm{cos}\left(\frac{\xi\pi}{2}\right)}>0\) _with_ \(\xi\neq 1\). In the 1D case, the Riesz fractional derivative coincides with the fractional Laplacian, which can also be defined as follows. **Definition 1.4** _Let u(z_) _be in the Schwartz space of rapidly decaying functions and_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\)_. The fractional Laplacian operator_ \((-\Delta)^\xi\) _is defined as_ \((-\Delta)^\xi u(z)=C(\xi)P.V.\int_\mathbb{R}\frac{u(z_1)-u(z_2)}{|z_1-z_2|^{1+2\xi}}d(z_2),\) (1.2) _where_ \(C(\xi)=\frac{\xi 2^{2\xi}\Gamma(\xi+\frac{1}{2})}{\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(1-\xi)}\) _is a normalization constant._ A generalized class of fractional derivatives is obtained by introducing exponential tempering, leading to the so-called tempered fractional derivatives \[108\]. In the Riemann-Liouville framework, these operators are defined as follows. **Definition 1.5** _\[4\] Let_ \(\xi\in(n-1,n)\), \(n\in\mathbb{N}^+\), \(\vartheta\ge 0\) _and let_ \(u(z)\in AC([a,b])\)_. Then, the left- and right-sided Riemann-Liouville tempered fractional derivatives are defined as_ \(\mathcal{D}_{a+,z}^{\xi,\vartheta} u(z)=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\vartheta z}}{\Gamma(n-\xi)}\frac{d^n}{dz^n}\int_a^z\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\vartheta\sigma} u(\sigma)}{(z-\sigma)^{\xi-n+1}}d\sigma,\) (1.3) \(\mathcal{D}_{b-,z}^{\xi,\vartheta} u(z)=\frac{(-1)^n\mathrm{e}^{\vartheta z}}{\Gamma(n-\xi)}\frac{d^n}{dz^n}\int_z^b\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\vartheta\sigma} u(\sigma)}{(\sigma-z)^{\xi-n+1}}d\sigma.\) (1.4)

It is evident that, for \(\vartheta=0\), the exponential tempering disappears and the tempered fractional derivatives reduce to the classical R-LFDs.
Another widely used definition is the Caputo fractional derivative (CFD), introduced by the Italian mathematician Michele Caputo \[105\], which is defined as follows. **Definition 1.6** _\[105\] Let_ \(\xi\in(n-1,n)\), \(n\in\mathbb{N}^+\)_, and assume that the nth derivative of u(z_) _is absolutely integrable, then the left- and right-sided CFDs of order_ \(\xi\) _are defined as_ \(^C\mathcal{D}_{a_{+,z}}^\xi u(z)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(n-\xi)}\int_a^z\frac{1}{(z-\sigma)^{\xi-n+1}}\frac{d^nu(\sigma)}{d\sigma^n}d\sigma,\) (1.5) \(^C\mathcal{D}_{b_{-,z}}^\xi u(z)=\frac{(-1)^n}{\Gamma(n-\xi)}\int_z^b\frac{1}{(\sigma-z)^{\xi-n+1}}\frac{d^nu(\sigma)}{d\sigma^n}d\sigma.\) (1.6) **Remark 1.1** \[74\] If \(\xi\notin\mathbb{N}\) and _u(x_) are such that the Caputo and R-LFDs exist then they are linked through the following relation \(\mathcal{D}_{a_{+,z}}^\xi u(z)=^C\mathcal{D}_{a_{+,z}}^\xi u(z)+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{(z-a)^{i-\xi}}{\Gamma(i-\xi+1)}\frac{d^iu(a)}{dz^i},\)
\(\mathcal{D}_{b_{-,z}}^\xi u(z)=^C\mathcal{D}_{b_{-,z}}^\xi u(z)+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^i(b-z)^{i-\xi}}{\Gamma(i-\xi+1)}\frac{d^iu(b)}{dz^i}.\) In the case where \(\frac{d^iu(a)}{dz^i}=\frac{d^iu(b)}{dz^i}=0\), then the R-LFDs (1.3) and (1.4) coincide with the CFDs (1.5) and (1.6). A tempered extension of the CFD has been introduced to account for finite memory effects through exponential damping. This formulation, known as the Caputo tempered fractional derivative, combines the regularity advantages of the CFD with the flexibility of tempered fractional operators and is defined as follows \[4, 110\]. **Definition 1.7** _\[4, 110\] Let_ \(\xi\in(n-1,n)\), \(n\in\mathbb{N}^+\), \(\vartheta\ge 0\) _and let_ \(u(z)\in AC([a,b])\)_. Then, the left- and right-sided Caputo tempered fractional derivatives are defined as_ \(^C\mathcal{D}_{a_{+,z}}^\xi u(z)=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\vartheta\mathrm{z}}}{\Gamma(n-\xi)}\int_a^z\frac{1}{(z-\sigma)^{\xi-n+1}}\frac{d^n\left(\mathrm{e}^{\vartheta\sigma}\mathrm{u}(\sigma)\right)}{d\sigma^n}d\sigma,\)
\(^C\mathcal{D}_{b_{-,z}}^\xi u(z)=\frac{(-1)^n\mathrm{e}^{\vartheta z}}{\Gamma(n-\xi)}\int_z^b\frac{1}{(\sigma-z)^{\xi-n+1}}\frac{d^n\left(\mathrm{e}^{-\vartheta\sigma}\mathrm{u}(\sigma)\right)}{d\sigma^n}d\sigma.\) ## 1.2 Mittag-Leffler type functions This section is devoted to the introduction of the multinomial MLF and to the presentation of its key analytical properties, which will be used throughout the subsequent analysis. **Definition 1.8** _\[82\] For_ \(\xi_i,\gamma>0,z_i\in\mathbb{C},i=1,2,\dots,n,n\in\mathbb{N}\)_, the multinomial MLF is defined as_ \(E_{(\xi_1,\xi_2,\dots,\xi_n),\gamma}(z_1,z_2,\dots,z_n):=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\sum_{l_1+l_2+\dots+l_n=kl_1\ge 0,\dots,l_n\ge 0}(k;l_1,\dots,l_n)\frac{\prod_{i=1}^nz_i^{l_i}}{\Gamma\left(\gamma+\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_il_i\right)},\)

_where_ \((k;l_1,\dots,l_n)=\frac{k!}{l_1!\times\dots\times l_n!}\). **Remark 1.2** _Notice that the multinomial MLF can be represented as_ \(E_{(\xi_1,\xi_2,\dots,\xi_n),\gamma}(z_1,z_2,\dots,z_n)\)
\(=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\sum_{l_1=0}^k\sum_{l_2=0}^{k-l_1}\dots\sum_{l_{n-1}=0}^{k-l_1-\cdots-l_{n-2}}\frac{k!}{l_1!l_2!\dots(k-l_1-l_2-\dots-l_{n-1})!}\)
\(\times\frac{z_1^{k-l_1-l_2-\dots-l_{n-1}}z_2^{l_1}\dots z_n^{l_{n-1}}}{\Gamma(\gamma+\xi_1(k-l_1-l_2-\dots-l_{n-1})+\xi_2l_1+\dots+\xi_nl_{n-1})}.\) **Remark 1.3** _The parameter of the multinomial MLF commutes, i.e.,_ \(E_{(\xi_1,\xi_2,\dots,\xi_n),\gamma}(z_1,z_2,\dots,z_n)=E_{(\xi_n,\dots,\xi_2,\xi_1),\gamma}(z_n,\dots,z_2,z_1).\) (1.7) **Remark 1.4** _For_ \(z_1\neq 0\), \(z_2\neq 0\), \(z_3=\dots=z_n=0,n\in\mathbb{N}\) _the multinomial MLF takes the following form_ \(E_{(\xi_1,\xi_2),\gamma}(z_1,z_2)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\sum_{l_1+l_2=kl_1\ge 0,l_2\ge 0}\frac{k!}{l_1!l_2!}\frac{z_1^{l_1}z_2^{l_2}}{\Gamma(\gamma+\xi_1l_1+\xi_2l_2)},\)

## Chapter 2 ### Matrix sequences: spectral distributions and asymptotic structures Matrix sequences constitute a fundamental tool in the analysis of numerical methods for differential equations. A matrix sequence is defined as a family of square matrices {_An}n_, where each matrix _An_ has size \(d_n\times d_n\) and the dimension _dn_ increases with _n_, satisfying _d__n_1_\_n_2 whenever _n_1_\2. This increase reflects the refinement of a discretization process and naturally arises in the numerical approximation of continuous problems. Matrix sequences typically originate from the discretization of ordinary differential equation (ODEs), partial differential equations (PDEs), and FDEs. Discretizing a differential equation on a computational grid leads to a linear system whose size depends on the number of degrees of freedom. As the mesh is refined to improve accuracy, the number of unknowns increases and the associated coefficient matrices grow in size, producing a sequence indexed by the discretization parameter. These matrices are not arbitrary, but often inherit structural properties from the underlying differential operator, the equation coefficients, and the geometry of the domain.
The structure of a matrix sequence may be explicit, as in the case of Toeplitz, circulant, \(\tau\), or Hankel matrices, or asymptotic and hidden, as described by the theory of GLT matrix sequences. The study of matrix sequences is primarily motivated by their asymptotic spectral behavior. The limiting distribution of eigenvalues and singular values provides essential insight into stability, conditioning, and convergence of numerical schemes, and plays a key role in the design of efficient algorithms, including preconditioned iterative solvers and multi-level methods.
This chapter introduces the core concepts underlying the study of matrix sequences, which provide the spectral and algebraic foundation for the numerical methods developed in this thesis. We first review eigenvalue and singular value distributions as the main tools for describing the asymptotic spectral behavior of large matrices arising from discretized PDEs and FDEs. We then present the notion of convergence for matrix sequences through approximating classes of sequences, which allows one to capture both explicit and hidden asymptotic structures. Finally, we discuss multi- level matrix structures resulting from multi-dimensional discretizations. These topics form the basis of the GLT framework used throughout the thesis; see [42, Chapter 2] for a comprehensive treatment. ### 2.1 Spectral distributions of matrix sequences In many relevant situations, important asymptotic information about a matrix sequence is captured by its eigenvalue or singular value distribution. In this section, we formally introduce this concept, provide its intuitive interpretation, and outline its role in characterizing the asymptotic spectral behavior of large matrices.

**Definition 2.1** _Let_ {_An}n be a matrix sequence, with An of size dn, and let_ \(\psi:D\subset\mathbb{R}^t\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\) _be a measurable function defined on a set D with_ \(0<\mu_t(D)<\infty\). • _We say that_ {_An}n has an (asymptotic) singular value distribution described by_ \(\psi\)_, and we write_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma\psi\)_, if_ \(\mathrm{lim}_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{d_n}\sum_{i=1}^{d_n}F(\sigma_i(A_n))=\frac{1}{\mu_t(D)}\int_D\frac{1}{r}\sum_{i=1}^rF(\sigma_i(\psi(x)))dx,\forall F\in C_c(\mathbb{R}).\) • _We say that_ {_An}n has an (asymptotic) spectral (or eigenvalue) distribution described by_ \(\psi\)_, and we write_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi\)_, if_ \(\mathrm{lim}_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{d_n}\sum_{i=1}^{d_n}F(\lambda_i(A_n))=\frac{1}{\mu_t(D)}\int_D\frac{1}{r}\sum_{i=1}^rF(\lambda_i(\psi(x)))dx,\forall F\in C_c(\mathbb{C}).\) • _If_ \(\psi\) _describes both the singular value and eigenvalue distribution of_ {_An}n, we write_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_{\sigma,\lambda}\psi\). _In this case, the function_ \(\psi\) _is referred to as the eigenvalue (or spectral) symbol of_ {_An}n.
The same definition holds when the considered matrix sequence shows a multi-level structure. In that case n is replaced by **n** uniformly in An and dn._ From an intuitive viewpoint, when the symbol \(\psi\) is continuous a.e. and the eigenvalues of _An_ can be associated with evaluations of \(\psi\) on an equispaced grid over the domain _D_, the notion of spectral distribution reduces to the classical observation that a Riemann sum of a Riemann-integrable function converges to the corresponding integral. More generally, if \(\psi\) is continuous a.e. and the discretization parameter _n_ is sufficiently large, then the eigenvalues of _An_, after a suitable ordering and possibly up to a negligible number of outliers of order _o(dn_), behave like uniform samples of \(\psi\) over _D_. An analogous interpretation holds for singular value distributions. Within this framework, the following result is therefore natural. **Proposition 2.1** \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi\) _and_ \(\Lambda(A_n)\subseteq S\) _for all_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}\)_, then_ \(\mathrm{essRan}\psi\subseteq\bar{S}\) _a.e., where_ \(S\subseteq\mathbb{C}\) _and_ \(\bar{S}\) _denotes its closure._ In particular \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi\) and _An_ positive definite for all _n_ imply that \(\psi\) is nonnegative definite almost everywhere, simply nonnegative almost everywhere if _r_=1. For singular values, the analogue of positivity is uniform invertibility. Suppose that \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma\psi\) and that there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(\sigma_\mathrm{min}(A_n)\ge\delta\) for all _n_. Then \(\sigma_\mathrm{min}(\psi)>0\) almost everywhere, i.e. \(\mu_t\big(\{x\in D:\sigma_\mathrm{min}(\psi(x))=0\}\big)=0.\) Conversely, if \(\sigma_\mathrm{min}(\psi)=0\) on a set of positive measure, then the sequence {_An}n_ cannot be uniformly invertible. As will become apparent, determining the spectral distribution is generally more straightforward for Hermitian matrix sequences. Nevertheless, several effective techniques are available for treating sequences in which the non-Hermitian component is sufficiently small. In particular, the following proposition shows that perturbations of Hermitian sequences with small norm do not affect the asymptotic spectral distribution.

**Proposition 2.2 (\[12, Corollary 2\])** _Let_ {_A<sub>n</sub>}<sub>n</sub> be a matrix sequence such that A<sub>n</sub>=B<sub>n</sub>+C<sub>n</sub>, where B<sub>n</sub> is Hermitian_ \(\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\)_. Suppose that_

• \(\{B_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi\),<tbc>

• \(\|C_n\|=o(1)\).

_Then_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi\).

An important aspect of spectral distributions for matrix sequences is their intrinsic non-uniqueness. Once a function describing the asymptotic spectral distribution has been identified, it is by no means unique. Indeed, there exist infinitely many alternative representations that encode exactly the same spectral information. In particular, any measurable function that satisfies the same integral identities with respect to all compactly supported continuous test functions yields an equivalent distribution. More precisely, let \(\psi\) be a distribution function defined on a measurable set _D_; then any measurable mapping \(\varphi:E\subset\mathbb{R}^s\rightarrow\mathbb{C}\) such that

\(\frac{1}{\mu_t(D)}\int_DF(\psi(x))dx=\frac{1}{\mu_s(E)}\int_EF(\varphi(x))dx,\forall F\in C_c(\mathbb{C}),\)

represents the same asymptotic distribution. These alternative representations may differ substantially in form, including the dimension of their domain or the number of variables involved. Moreover, by suitably extending the notion of distribution, the associated symbol may take matrix-valued values, provided that the corresponding integral characterization remains valid; see, for example, \[11, 10\].

The notion of clustering can be regarded as a special case of spectral distribution.

**Definition 2.2** _Let_ {_A<sub>n</sub>}<sub>n</sub> be a matrix sequence with_ \(A_n\in\mathbb{C}^{d_n\times d_n}\)_, and let_ \(S\subseteq\mathbb{C}\) _be a nonempty closed set._

• _The sequence_ {_A<sub>n</sub>}<sub>n</sub> is said to be_ strongly clustered at _S_ in the sense of the eigenvalues _if, for any_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _and as_ \(n\rightarrow+\infty\)_, the number of eigenvalues of A<sub>n</sub> lying outside the_ \(\varepsilon\)_-neighborhood of S is bounded independently of n, that is,_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\#\big\{j\in\{1,\dots,d_n\}:\lambda_j(A_n)\notin B(S,\varepsilon)\big\}=O(1),n\rightarrow+\infty.\)<tbc>

• _The sequence_ {_A<sub>n</sub>}<sub>n</sub> is said to be_ weakly clustered at _S_ in the sense of the eigenvalues _if, for any_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _and as_ \(n\rightarrow+\infty\)_, the number of eigenvalues of A<sub>n</sub> lying outside_ \(B(S,\varepsilon)\) _is negligible with respect to the matrix size, namely,_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\#\big\{j\in\{1,\dots,d_n\}:\lambda_j(A_n)\notin B(S,\varepsilon)\big\}=o(d_n),n\rightarrow+\infty.\)<tbc>

<tbc>**Remark 2.1** _Let us clarify the relationship between the concepts of distribution and clustering. We recall that the essential range of a measurable function_ \(g:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^t\rightarrow\mathbb{C}\) _is the set_<tbc>

\(\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mu_t\big(\{g\in B(z,\varepsilon)\}\big)>0\forall\varepsilon>0\}.\)

<tbc>_As reported in \[45, Theorem 4.2\], it holds_<tbc>

\(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi\Longrightarrow\{A_n\}_n\text{\textit{is weakly clustered at the essential range of}}\psi.\)

_Furthermore, if the essential range of_ \(\psi\) _consists of a single number_ \(s\in\mathbb{C}\)_, then_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi\Longleftrightarrow\{A_n\}_n\text{\textit{is weakly clustered at s in the sense of the eigenvalues.}}\) _The latter case is typically of interest in the context of preconditioning. Corresponding statements can be given for the singular values, with the obvious suitable changes._ A corresponding definition can be given for singular values by considering sets \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^+\). When the term clustering is used without further specification, it is implicitly understood in the weak sense. The special case of _single-point clustering_, where _S_={_s_} consists of a single element, plays a particularly important role in the theory of preconditioning. If a matrix sequence admits a continuous spectral distribution, clustering naturally follows. More precisely, if {_An}n_ has eigenvalue distribution described by a function \(\psi\), the eigenvalues can be interpreted as a uniform sampling of \(\psi\), and are therefore clustered around its range. This intuition is formalized in the following result. **Proposition 2.3** _If_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi\)_, then_ {_An}n is weakly clustered at the essential range of_ \(\psi\) _in the sense of the eigenvalues. Moreover, if_ \(\mathrm{essRan}\psi=\{s\}\) _with_ \(s\in\mathbb{C}\) _fixed, then_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi\) _if and only if_ {_An}n is weakly clustered at s in the sense of the eigenvalues._ An analogous statement holds for singular values. **Proposition 2.4** _If_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma\psi\)_, then_ {_An}n is weakly clustered at the essential range of_ \(\psi\) _in the sense of the singular values. Furthermore, if_ \(\mathrm{essRan}\psi=\{s\}\) _with_ \(s\in\mathbb{R}\) _fixed, then_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma\psi\) _if and only if_ {_An}n is weakly clustered at s in the sense of the singular values._ ## 2.2 Approximating classes of sequences We introduce the notion of an approximating class of sequences (a.c.s.), which plays a fundamental role in the modern analysis of matrix sequences. In essence, an a.c.s. associated with a given matrix sequence {_An}n_ consists of a family of matrix sequences that approximate {_An}n_ asymptotically, up to perturbations that are negligible in a precise sense. Such perturbations typically include a component of low rank relative to the matrix dimension and another component whose spectral norm vanishes in the limit. This framework provides a rigorous notion of convergence for matrix sequences and induces a natural topology on their space. The formal definition of a.c.s. and the corresponding convergence results originate from earlier works and are presented in a comprehensive and modern form in \[121, 134, 41, 42\]. **Definition 2.3** _Let_ {_An}n be a matrix sequence and let_ {{_Bn,j}n}j be a class of matrix sequences, with An and Bn,j of size dn. We say that_ {{_Bn,j}n}j is an a.c.s. for_ {_An}n if the following condition is met: for every j, there exists nj such that, for every_ \(n\ge n_j\), \(A_n=B_{n,j}+R_{n,j}+N_{n,j},\)
\(\text{\textit{rank}}(R_{n,j})\le c(j)d_n\text{\textit{and}}\|N_{n,j}\|\le\omega(j),\)

_where nj, c(j), and_ \(\omega(j)\) _depend only on j, and_ \(\mathrm{lim}_{j\rightarrow\infty} c(j)=\mathrm{lim}_{j\rightarrow\infty}\omega(j)=0.\) \(\{\{B_{n,j}\}_n\}_j\longrightarrow^{a.c.s.}\{A_n\}_n\) _denotes that_ {{_Bn,j}n}j is an a.c.s. for_ {_An}n._ In intuitive terms, we say that the family {{_Bn,j}n}j_ forms an a.c.s. for {_An}n_ if, for all sufficiently large values of _j_, the sequence {_Bn,j}n_ provides an accurate asymptotic approximation of {_An}n_. More precisely, each matrix _An_ can be decomposed into the sum of the corresponding matrix _Bn,j_, a perturbation of rank negligible with respect to the dimension of _An_, and a remainder whose norm is arbitrarily small. As _j_ increases, both the rank and the norm of these perturbation terms become increasingly insignificant for large values of _n_.
The following theorem represents the expression of a related convergence theory and it is a powerful tool used, for example, in the construction of the GLT ∗-Algebra. **Theorem 2.1** _Let_ {_An}n,_ {_Bn,j}n, with_ \(j,n\in\mathbb{N}\)_, be matrix sequences and let_ \(\psi,\psi_j:D\subset\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\) _be measurable functions defined on a set D with positive and finite Lebesgue measure. Suppose that:_ 1. \(\{B_{n,j}\}_n\sim_\sigma\psi_j\) _for every j;_ 2. \(\{\{B_{n,j}\}_n\}_j\longrightarrow^{a.c.s.}\{A_n\}_n\); _3._ \(\psi_j\rightarrow\psi\) _in measure._ _Then_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma\psi.\) **Theorem 2.2** _Given a Hermitian matrix sequence_ {_An}n, let_ {_Bn,j}n, be a class of Hermitian matrix sequences and let_ \(\psi,\psi_j:D\subset\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\) _be measurable functions defined on a set D with positive and finite Lebesgue measure. Suppose that:_ 1. \(\{B_{n,j}\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi_j\) _for every j;_ _2._ \(\{\{B_{n,j}\}_n\}_j\longrightarrow^{a.c.s.}\{A_n\}_n\); _3._ \(\psi_j\rightarrow\psi\) _in measure._ _Then_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\psi.\) For clarity, we note that we will occasionally consider so-called _constant_ families of matrix sequences of the form {{_Bn}n}j_, where the underlying sequence {_Bn}n_ is independent of the index _j_. In such cases, the parameter _j_ plays no effective role and serves only as a formal label. As an example, the family {{_In}n}j_ represents the constant identity matrix sequence, since the element associated with each value of _j_ coincides with the same sequence {_In}n_.

## 2.3 Multi-level discretization matrices The discretization of PDEs and FDEs on multi-dimensional domains, such as rectangles, cubes, or higher-dimensional hyperrectangles, inherently results in the formation of multi-level matrices. These matrices are characterized by their hierarchical structure, reflecting the underlying geometry and grid of the computing domain. Multi-level matrices are not simply collections of numbers; they are recursively structured into blocks: each matrix is segmented into larger blocks, which can be further subdivided into smaller sub-blocks, and so on. When a PDE or FDE is discretized on a _d_-dimensional grid comprising _n_1_,n_2_,...,nd_ points in each spatial direction, the resultant matrix is generally of size \(N\times N\), where \(N=n_1n_2\cdots n_d\).
At the highest level, the matrix consists of \(n_1^2\) blocks of size _N/n_1, corresponding to subdivisions along the first coordinate; each block at this level is further broken down into \(n_2^2\) blocks of size _N/(n_1_n_2), according to the second coordinate, and this recursive process continues until, at the final level, we arrive at individual scalar entries. In general, at the _j_-th level, each block is partitioned into \(n_j^2\) blocks of order \(N/(n_1\cdots n_j)\). This multi-level structure is not just a mathematical curiosity: it is vital for the efficient storage, computation, and theoretical analysis of the matrices that arise from multi-dimensional problems.
Using the conventional notation of two scalar indices _i,j_=1_,...,N_ to refer to the entries of a multi-level matrix quickly becomes impractical. To address this, mathematicians use multi-index notation, where each position in the matrix or vector is labeled by a _d_-tuple, or multi-index, **_i_**=(_i_1_,...,id_) in Z_d_, that records its location along every dimension of the grid. This approach not only makes the notation more concise and natural but also aligns perfectly with the recursive construction of multi- level matrices. Using multi-indices, we can systematically and clearly describe the positions of entries in both vectors and matrices: for example, a vector \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})}\) with _N_(**_n_**)=_n_1_,...,nd_ can be indexed as \(\mathbf{x}=[x_\mathbf{i}]_{\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{1}}^\mathbf{n}\), The first component is _x_(1_,...,_1), the second is _x_(1_,...,_1,2), and so on, until _x_(_n_1_,...,nd_). For instance, the component in position _nd_+3 will be _x_(1_,...,_1,2,3). Likewise, a _d_-level matrix \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})\times N(\mathbf{n})}\) can be written as \(A=[a_{\mathbf{ij}}]_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}=1}^\mathbf{n}\), where **_n_**=(_n_1_,...,nd_).
In this setting, a multi-level matrix sequence is understood as a family of matrices {_A_**n**}**_n_**, indexed by a multi-index **_n_** whose components tend to infinity and reflect the refinement of the discretization along each spatial direction, with \(A_\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})\times N(\mathbf{n})}\). This notion captures the intrinsic multi-dimensional structure of matrices arising from high-dimensional problems. With these definitions in place, the next chapter is devoted to the structured matrix classes that will be central to the subsequent analysis.

## Chapter 3 ### Structured matrices Matrices arising from the discretization of differential equations frequently exhibit characteristic structural patterns that reflect the analytical properties of the underlying continuous operators. Identifying and exploiting such structures is a central theme in numerical linear algebra, as it often leads to significant reductions in computational cost and provides insight into the behavior of numerical schemes. Among the most prominent examples are Toeplitz matrices, which are defined by constant entries along each diagonal. This structure naturally emerges from the discretization of constant coefficient PDEs and FDEs, where translation invariance of the operator is preserved at the discrete level. In a one-dimensional setting, the use of uniform grids typically produces standard Toeplitz matrices, while higher-dimensional problems posed on rectangular domains give rise to multi-level Toeplitz structures. In this case, the discretization leads to block Toeplitz matrices whose blocks are themselves Toeplitz, with the number of recursive levels directly linked to the spatial dimension of the problem. Such structured matrices play a fundamental role in both theoretical analysis and algorithmic design, forming the basis for fast matrix- vector products, efficient solvers, and the spectral tools developed in the subsequent sections of this chapter.
Throughout this chapter, all the structures are introduced directly in the _d_-level, _r_- block setting, that is, for \(n\in\mathbb{N}^d\) and \(r\in\mathbb{N}\) the matrices under consideration belong to \(\mathbb{C}^{N(n)r\times N(n)r}\) and their entries are \(r\times r\) matrices rather than scalars. This level of generality is required in the rest of the thesis, where blocks of size _r\>_1 arise from systems of FDEs, from vector-valued unknowns and from all-at-once discretizations. The scalar case treated in the classical literature is recovered by setting _r_=1, in which case all the statements below reduce verbatim to their scalar counterparts.
This chapter is devoted to the systematic study of Toeplitz and related structured matrices. In Section 3.1, we introduce the formal definition of multi-level Toeplitz matrices and review their main algebraic and spectral properties, drawing on the extensive literature developed over the past decades. Unless stated otherwise, these results are collected from [42, Chapter 3]. In addition, we discuss several matrix classes that either arise as special cases of Toeplitz matrices or exhibit strong structural and spectral connections with them, which makes them particularly relevant in numerical applications. Circulant and \(\omega\)-circulant matrices are presented in Sections 3.2 and 3.3, respectively, while Sections 3.4 and 3.5 are devoted to \(\tau\) and Hankel matrices. ### 3.1 Toeplitz matrices Given \(n\in\mathbb{N}^d\) and \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), a matrix of the form \(T_n:=[A_{i-j}]_{i,j=1}^n\in\mathbb{C}^{N(n)r\times N(n)r},\)

with blocks \(A_\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), \(\mathbf{k}\in\{-(\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}),\dots,\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}\}\), where the block in position (**_i_**_,**j**_) depends only on the difference **_i_**-**_j_**, is called a multi-level block Toeplitz matrix, or, more precisely, a _d_-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrix. For _r_=1 the blocks are scalars and one recovers the classical _d_-level (scalar) Toeplitz matrices.
In the simplest case where _d_=1 and **_n_**=_n_, a 1-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrix is just a classical block Toeplitz matrix, whose blocks remain constant along the block diagonals: \(T_n=[A_{i-j}]_{i,j=1}^n=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c } A_0 & A_{-1} & A_{-2} & \cdots & \cdots & A_{1-n} \\ A_1 & A_0 & A_{-1} & A_{-2} & & \vdots \\ A_2 & A_1 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & A_2 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & A_{-2} \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & A_{-1} \\ A_{n-1} & \cdots & \cdots & A_2 & A_1 & A_0 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{nr\times nr}.\) Note that _Tn_ is completely specified by its 2_n_-1 blocks \(A_k\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), _k_=-(_n_-1)_,...,n_-1, or equivalently by its first block row and first block column.
For _d_=2 and **_n_**=(_n_1_,n_2), we have a 2-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrix: \(T_\mathbf{n}=\left[\left[A_{(i_1-j_1,i_2-j_2)}\right]_{i_2,j_2=1}^{n_2}\right]_{i_1,j_1=1}^{n_1}=[\mathcal{A}_{i_1-j_1}]_{i_1,j_1=1}^{n_1}\)
\(=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c } \mathcal{A}_0 & \mathcal{A}_{-1} & \mathcal{A}_{-2} & \cdots & \cdots & \mathcal{A}_{1-n_1} \\ \mathcal{A}_1 & \mathcal{A}_0 & \mathcal{A}_{-1} & \mathcal{A}_{-2} & & \vdots \\ \mathcal{A}_2 & \mathcal{A}_1 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & \mathcal{A}_2 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \mathcal{A}_{-2} \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \mathcal{A}_{-1} \\ \mathcal{A}_{n_1-1} & \cdots & \cdots & \mathcal{A}_2 & \mathcal{A}_1 & \mathcal{A}_0 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{n_1n_2r\times n_1n_2r},\) where each block A_k_ is itself a 1-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrix:
\(\mathcal{A}_k=\left[A_{(k,i_2-j_2)}\right]_{i_2,j_2=1}^{n_2}\)
\(=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c } A_{(k,0)} & A_{(k,-1)} & A_{(k,-2)} & \cdots & \cdots & A_{(k,1-n_2)} \\ A_{(k,1)} & A_{(k,0)} & A_{(k,-1)} & A_{(k,-2)} & & \vdots \\ A_{(k,2)} & A_{(k,1)} & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & A_{(k,2)} & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & A_{(k,-2)} \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & A_{(k,-1)} \\ A_{(k,n_2-1)} & \cdots & \cdots & A_{(k,2)} & A_{(k,1)} & A_{(k,0)} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{n_2r\times n_2r}.\) For _r_=1, this type of matrix is also known as a _block Toeplitz matrix with Toeplitz blocks_ or BTTB matrix; for a general _r_ it is a BTTB matrix whose innermost entries are \(r\times r\) matrices. In the case where _d_=3, a 3-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrix is made up of blocks, and each block has its own 2-level _r_-block Toeplitz structure. A more general way to describe a _d_-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrix is as a block Toeplitz matrix whose blocks

are (_d_-1)-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrices. In this recursive design, the blocks in the first block row and first block column of the matrix tell you everything you need to know about it, just like in the case of a single-level matrix. From the computational perspective, this makes the storage requirement for Toeplitz matrices drop to only _O(N_(**_n_**)_r_2), compared to \(O\big(\big(\)(_N_(**_n_**)_r_)2\(\big)\) for a generic dense matrix.
A compact expression for a multi-level block Toeplitz matrix can be formulated by defining, for \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\), define the matrix \(J_n^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) by \([J_n^{(k)}]_{i,j}:=\delta_{i-j,k}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } 1, & i-j=k, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}, \end{array}\right.i,j=1,\dots,n,\) where \(\delta_{p,q}\) is the Kronecker delta, i.e. \(\delta_{p,q}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } 1, & p=q, \\ 0, & p\neq q. \end{array}\right.\) Equivalently, \(J_n^{(k)}\) is a matrix with all ones on the _k_-th diagonal and zeros elsewhere. The main diagonal is numbered as 0, diagonals above as -1,-2_,...,-n_+1, and those below as 1,2_,...,n_-1. For the multi-level case, where \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\) and \(\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^d\), are both _d_-dimensional vectors (for example, **_n_**=(_n_1_,...,nd_) and **_k_**=(_k_1_,...,kd_)), we define its multi-level version: \(J_\mathbf{n}^{(\mathbf{k})}=J_{n_1}^{(k_1)}\otimes J_{n_2}^{(k_2)}\otimes\cdots\otimes J_{n_d}^{(k_d)}.\) Then, _T_**_n_** admits the following representation: \(T_\mathbf{n}=[A_{\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}}]_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{1}}^\mathbf{n}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{n}}^{\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}}J_\mathbf{n}^{(\mathbf{k})}\otimes A_\mathbf{k}.\) (3.1) It can be proven componentwise by explicitly computing the (**_i_**_,**j**_)-th block on the right-hand side of the equation and applying the properties of the Kronecker product.
Given a matrix-valued function \(f:[-\pi,\pi]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\) belonging to the space of integrable functions \(L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d)\), that is, such that all its entries are in \(L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d)\), it is possible to construct a class of multi-level block Toeplitz matrices associated with _f_. Let \(\hat{f}_\mathbf{k}\) denote the **_k_**-th Fourier coefficient of _f_, defined for any \(\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^d\) as \(\hat{f}_\mathbf{k}:=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^d}\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^d}f(\theta)e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\theta} d\theta\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r},\) where _i_2=-1 and \(\mathbf{k}\cdot\theta=k_1\theta_1+\cdots+k_d\theta_d\), the integral being computed entrywise. For any \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\), the **_n_**-th Toeplitz matrix associated with _f_ is the _d_-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrix, denoted by _T_**_n_**(_f_), whose blocks are the Fourier coefficients of _f_, arranged along the block diagonals according to the following definition: \(T_\mathbf{n}(f):=[\hat{f}_{\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}}]_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{1}}^\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})r\times N(\mathbf{n})r}.\) The family \(\{T_\mathbf{n}(f)\}_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d}\) is called the family of (multi-level block) Toeplitz matrices associated with _f_, which is referred to as the _generating function_. Using Equation (3.1), _T_**_n_**(_f_) can also be represented as \(T_\mathbf{n}(f)=\sum_{\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{n}}^{\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}}J_\mathbf{n}^{(\mathbf{k})}\otimes\hat{f}_\mathbf{k}=\sum_{k_1=1-n_1}^{n_1-1}\cdots\sum_{k_d=1-n_d}^{n_d-1}\big(J_{n_1}^{(k_1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes J_{n_d}^{(k_d)}\big)\otimes\hat{f}_{(k_1,\dots,k_d)}.\)

## 3.1.1 Relationship between the Toeplitz matrix and its generating function By constructing a Toeplitz matrix _Tn(f_) from a given matrix-valued function _f_ in \(L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d)\), we are essentially creating a map that takes functions and produces matrices: \(T_n(\cdot):L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d,\mathbb{C}^{r\times r})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{N(n)r\times N(n)r}\) for any fixed \(n\in\mathbb{N}^d\) and \(r\in\mathbb{N}\). The properties of the function _f_ are closely related to those of the Toeplitz matrix. To start, the operator \(T_n(\cdot)\) is linear. This follows directly from the linearity of the Fourier coefficient operation. **Proposition 3.1** _For any_ \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C}\) _and_ \(f,g\in L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d,\mathbb{C}^{r\times r})\)_, it holds that_ \(T_n(\alpha f+\beta g)=\alpha T_n(f)+\beta T_n(g).\) _Moreover, further results follow from the identities_ \((\widehat{f(-\theta)})_k=\hat{f}_{-k}\text{\textit{and}}\widehat{(f^*)}_k=\big(\hat{f}_{-k}\big)^*,\text{\textit{for all}}k\in\mathbb{Z}^d,\) _where_ \(f^*(\theta):=\overline{f(\theta)^\top}\) _denotes the conjugate transpose of f._ **Proposition 3.2** _For any_ \(f\in L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d,\mathbb{C}^{r\times r})\)_, the following properties hold:_ \(T_n(f(\theta))^\top=T_n\big(f(-\theta)^\top\big),\)
\(T_n(f)^*=T_n(f^*),\) _where Tn(f_)∗ _is the Hermitian (conjugate transpose) of Tn(f)._ In particular, if _f_ is Hermitian a.e., that is, \(f(\theta)=f(\theta)^*\) for almost every \(\theta\), then _Tn(f_) is Hermitian, so that Hermitian matrix-valued generating functions produce block Toeplitz matrices with real eigenvalues. More precisely, the spectrum of _Tn(f_) is contained within the essential infimum of the smallest eigenvalue of _f_ and the essential supremum of its largest eigenvalue. **Theorem 3.1** _Given_ \(f\in L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d,\mathbb{C}^{r\times r})\)_, Hermitian a.e., let_ \(m_f:=\mathrm{essinf}_\theta\lambda_{\mathrm{min}}\big(f(\theta)\big),M_f:=\mathrm{esssup}_\theta\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}\big(f(\theta)\big).\) _Then, for any_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}^d\)_, it holds that_ \(\lambda_j\big(T_n(f)\big)\in[m_f,M_f],\forall j=1,\dots,N(n)r.\) _If, in addition, mf\f, or equivalently f is not constant a.e., then it holds_ \(\lambda_j\big(T_n(f)\big)\in(m_f,M_f),\forall j=1,\dots,N(n)r.\) A valuable addition to this theorem is the following result concerning the extreme eigenvalues of _Tn(f_): for any fixed \(j\ge 1\) and as \(n\rightarrow\infty\), the _j_ smallest eigenvalues of _Tn(f_) converge to _mf_, while the _j_ largest eigenvalues converge to _Mf_.

<tbc>**Theorem 3.2** _Given_ \(f\in L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d,\mathbb{C}^{r\times r})\)_, Hermitian a.e., let m<sub>f</sub> and M<sub>f</sub> be defined as in Theorem 3.1, and let_

\(\lambda_1\big(T_\mathbf{n}(f)\big)\le\lambda_2\big(T_\mathbf{n}(f)\big)\le\cdots\le\lambda_{N(\mathbf{n})r}\big(T_\mathbf{n}(f)\big)\)

_be the eigenvalues of T_**<sub>n</sub>**(_f_) _arranged in increasing order. Then, for any fixed_ \(j\ge 1\)_, it holds that_

\(lim_{\mathbf{n}\rightarrow\infty}\lambda_j\big(T_\mathbf{n}(f)\big)=m_f,lim_{\mathbf{n}\rightarrow\infty}\lambda_{N(\mathbf{n})r-j+1}\big(T_\mathbf{n}(f)\big)=M_f.\)

From Theorem 3.1, we immediately deduce the positivity and monotonicity of the block Toeplitz operator.

**Corollary 3.1** _For any_ \(f,g\in L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d,\mathbb{C}^{r\times r})\)_, Hermitian a.e., the following holds:_<tbc>

\(f\ge O_r\text{\textit{a.e.}}\Longleftrightarrow T_\mathbf{n}(f)\ge O_{N(\mathbf{n})r},\forall\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d,\)

<tbc>_and, consequently,_

\(f\ge g\text{\textit{a.e.}}\Longleftrightarrow T_\mathbf{n}(f)\ge T_\mathbf{n}(g),\forall\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d,\)

_where the inequalities between matrices are understood in the sense of the partial ordering induced by positive semidefiniteness._

These results remain valid even if all of the inequalities are replaced by strict inequalities. In other words, if you consider situations where \(f\ge O_r\) a.e., or \(f\ge g\) a.e., the corresponding conclusions about the block Toeplitz matrices still hold when using the strict inequality signs.

The spectral norm of a block Toeplitz matrix is connected with the \(\infty\)-norm of its generating function through the following inequality, proved in \[122\].

**Proposition 3.3** _For any_ \(f\in L^\infty([-\pi,\pi]^d,\mathbb{C}^{r\times r})\) _and any_ \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\)_, it holds that_

\(\|T_\mathbf{n}(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty,\|f\|_\infty:=\mathrm{ess}\mathrm{sup}_\unknown\|f(\unknown)\|.\)

Finally, we present a useful relation between the separability of the function _f_ and the associated multi-level block Toeplitz matrices.

**Proposition 3.4** _Let_ \(f\in L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d,\mathbb{C}^{r\times r})\)_. If f is separable, i.e.,_<tbc>

\(f=f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_d,\)

<tbc>_with f_<sub>1</sub>_,...,f_<sub>_d_-1</sub> _scalar-valued and f<sub>d</sub> matrix-valued, then, for any_ \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\)_, it holds that_

\(T_\mathbf{n}(f)=T_{n_1}(f_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n_d}(f_d).\)

Now, by allowing \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\) to vary rather than keeping it fixed, we obtain a multi- level block Toeplitz matrix sequence {_T_**<sub>n</sub>**(_f_)}**<sub>n</sub>**. The deep connection between the singular value and eigenvalue distributions of a Toeplitz sequence and its generating function has been established in various forms over the years. We report here the version presented in \[42, Theorem 3.5\], where an elegant proof based on the notion of a.c.s. is provided. For the original formulation in the scalar case, see \[137\], while the case of matrix-valued generating functions considered here can be found in \[134\].

**Theorem 3.3** _With reference to Definition 2.1, if_ \(f\in L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d,\mathbb{C}^{r\times r})\)_, then_ \(\{T_\mathbf{n}(f)\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\sigma f.\) _If, moreover, f is Hermitian a.e., then_ \(\{T_\mathbf{n}(f)\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\lambda f.\) _Here the singular values and the eigenvalues of the matrix-valued symbol_ \(f(\unknown)\) _play the role of the values of the scalar symbol._ ## 3.2 Circulant matrices Given \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\) and \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), a matrix of the form \(C_\mathbf{n}:=[A_{(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})\mathrm{mod}\mathbf{n}}]_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{1}}^\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})r\times N(\mathbf{n})r},\) with blocks \(A_\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), \(\mathbf{k}\in\{\mathbf{0},\dots,\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}\}\), where the block in position (**_i_**_,**j**_) depends only on the difference (**_i_**-**_j_**)mod**_n_**, is called a _multi-level block_ or _d-level r-block circulant matrix_. In particular, since the (**_i_**_,**j**_)-th block depends only on **_i_**-**_j_**, circulant matrices can be regarded as a special subclass of Toeplitz matrices. When _d_=1 and **_n_**=_n_, this reduces to a classic _r_-block circulant matrix, where each block column is a one-position downward shift of the previous one: \(C_n=\big[A_{(i-j)\mathrm{mod}n}\big]_{i,j=1}^n=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c c } A_0 & A_{n-1} & A_{n-2} & \cdots & \cdots & A_1 \\ A_1 & A_0 & A_{n-1} & A_{n-2} & & \vdots \\ A_2 & A_1 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & A_2 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & A_{n-2} \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & A_{n-1} \\ A_{n-1} & \cdots & \cdots & A_2 & A_1 & A_0 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{nr\times nr}.\) _Cn_ is entirely determined by the _n_ blocks in its first block column, \(\{A_k\}_{k=0}^{n-1}\). Similarly, each block row is a one-element rightward shift of the previous block row, so that the matrix is fully specified by its first block row. For _d_=2 and **_n_**=(_n_1_,n_2), we obtain a 2-level _r_-block circulant matrix: \(C_\mathbf{n}=\big[\big[A_{((i_1-j_1)\mathrm{mod}n_1,(i_2-j_2)\mathrm{mod}n_2)}\big]_{i_2,j_2=1}^{n_2}\big]_{i_1,j_1=1}^{n_1}=\big[\mathcal{A}_{(i_1-j_1)\mathrm{mod}n_1}\big]_{i_1,j_1=1}^{n_1}\)
\(=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c } \mathcal{A}_0 & \mathcal{A}_{n_1-1} & \mathcal{A}_{n_1-2} & \cdots & \cdots & \mathcal{A}_1 \\ \mathcal{A}_1 & \mathcal{A}_0 & \mathcal{A}_{n_1-1} & \mathcal{A}_{n_1-2} & & \vdots \\ \mathcal{A}_2 & \mathcal{A}_1 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & \mathcal{A}_2 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \mathcal{A}_{n_1-2} \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \mathcal{A}_{n_1-1} \\ \mathcal{A}_{n_1-1} & \cdots & \cdots & \mathcal{A}_2 & \mathcal{A}_1 & \mathcal{A}_0 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{n_1n_2r\times n_1n_2r},\)

in which each block A_k_ is itself a 1-level _r_-block circulant matrix: \(\mathcal{A}_k=\left[A_{(k,(i_2-j_2)modn_2)}\right]_{i_2,j_2=1}^{n_2}\)
\(=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c } A_{(k,0)} & A_{(k,n_2-1)} & A_{(k,n_2-2)} & \cdots & \cdots & A_{(k,1)} \\ A_{(k,1)} & A_{(k,0)} & A_{(k,n_2-1)} & A_{(k,n_2-2)} & & \vdots \\ A_{(k,2)} & A_{(k,1)} & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & A_{(k,2)} & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & A_{(k,n_2-2)} \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & A_{(k,n_2-1)} \\ A_{(k,n_2-1)} & \cdots & \cdots & A_{(k,2)} & A_{(k,1)} & A_{(k,0)} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{n_2r\times n_2r}.\) For _r_=1 this structure is often called a _block circulant matrix with circulant blocks (BCCB)._
For _d_=3, a 3-level _r_-block circulant matrix is constructed as a block circulant matrix, where each block is itself a 2-level _r_-block circulant matrix. More generally, a _d_-level _r_-block circulant matrix can be defined recursively as a block circulant matrix whose blocks have (_d_-1)-level _r_-block circulant structure. Just as in the classic (uni-level) case, the entire matrix is fully specified by the blocks in its first block column, or, equivalently, by those in its first block row.
A compact expression for a uni-level _r_-block circulant matrix _Cn,r_ can be derived by using \([Z_n]_{i,j}:=\delta_{(i-j-1)modn}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c c } 1 & \text{if}i-j=1modn, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{array}\right.i,j=1,\dots,n,\) where \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(\delta\) is the Dirac delta function. More explicitly, _Zn_ is the matrix that has all ones on the first and (1-_n_)-th diagonals, with zeros elsewhere: \(Z_n=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c } 0 & & & & & 1 \\ 1 & \ddots & & & & \\ \ddots & & \ddots & & & \\ & & \ddots & \ddots & & \\ & & & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & & & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}.\) Raising _Zn_ to the power _k_, for _k_=1_,...,n_-1, cyclically shifts the diagonals by _k_ positions, with entries given by \([Z_n^k]_{i,j}:=\delta_{(i-j-k)modn}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c c c } 1 & \text{if}i-j=kmodn, & & i,j=1,\dots,n. \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{array}\right.\)

More explicitly, \(Z_n^2=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c } 0 & & & & 1 & 0 & \\ 0 & \ddots & & & & & 1 \\ 1 & \ddots & \ddots & & & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & & & \\ & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & & \\ & & & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right],Z_n^3=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c } 0 & & & & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \ddots & & & & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \ddots & \ddots & & & & 1 \\ 1 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right],\cdots\) Hence, any uni-level _r_-block circulant matrix can be expressed as a linear combination of Kronecker products of these powers with the blocks _Ak_: \(C_{n,r}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}Z_n^k\otimes A_k.\) (3.2) Conversely, since \(Z_n^n=I_n\) and, more generally, \(Z_n^k=Z_n^k\mathrm{mod}n\) for any \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\), any finite sum of the form \(\sum_{k\in K}Z_n^k\otimes A_k,A_k\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r},K\subset\mathbb{Z},\) is an _r_-block circulant matrix. For this reason, _Zn_ is commonly referred to as the generator of circulant matrices of order _n_.
The multi-level generalization of circulant matrices is straightforward.
