For \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\) and \(\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^d\), we define \(Z_\mathbf{n}^\mathbf{k}:=Z_{n_1}^{k_1}\otimes Z_{n_2}^{k_2}\otimes\cdots\otimes Z_{n_d}^{k_d}.\) Using this definition, any multi-level block circulant matrix can be written as \(C_{\mathbf{n},r}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0}}^{\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}}Z_\mathbf{n}^\mathbf{k}\otimes A_\mathbf{k}.\) This formula is directly analogous to the uni-level case and demonstrates that, just as for classic circulant matrices, the structure of multi-level block circulant matrices is fully captured by these shift matrices and the set of blocks _Ak_. ## 3.2.1 Spectral structure and fast solvers for circulant matrices Circulant matrices are widely used in numerical analysis due to their deep connection with the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and, consequently, with the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). Recall that the DFT is the linear mapping that associates to a vector \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^n\) its product with the Fourier matrix _Fn_, namely _Fn**x**_. The FFT is an efficient algorithm for computing the DFT in O(_n_log_n_) operations, in contrast to the O(_n_2) operations required by a standard matrix–vector multiplication \[138\]. The fact that block circulant matrices are uniformly block-diagonalizable by the Fourier matrix makes them particularly attractive for practical applications.
We start by introducing the Fourier matrix of order \(n\in\mathbb{N}\): \(F_n:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left[e^{-2\pi i\frac{rs}{n}}\right]_{r,s=0}^{n-1}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n},i=\sqrt{-1}.\) (3.3)

For convenience, this expression involves a slight abuse of notation, as the row and column indices start from 0 rather than 1. It is straightforward to verify that _Fn_ is both symmetric and unitary. Extending this definition, the multi-level Fourier matrix for \(n\in\mathbb{N}^d\) is given by \(F_n:=F_{n_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes F_{n_d},\) and its _r_-block counterpart is defined as \(F_{n,r}:=F_n\otimes I_r.\) The matrix _Fn_ preserves the symmetry and unitarity of its constituent matrices _Fni_, _i_=1_,...,d_, as a direct consequence of the structural properties of the Kronecker product; the same holds for _Fn,r_, which is unitary as well.
_Fn_ inherits its symmetry and unitarity from its components _Fni_, _i_=1_,...,d_, by virtue of the properties of the Kronecker product.
For any multi-level block circulant matrix, we have the following block-diagonalization. **Theorem 3.4** _For all_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}^d\) _and_ \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), \(C_{n,r}=\left[A_{(i-j)modn}\right]_{i,j=1}^n=F_{n,r}\Lambda_{n,r}F_{n,r}^*,\) (3.4) _where_ \(\Lambda_{n,r}\) _is the block diagonal matrix_ \(\Lambda_{n,r}:=\mathrm{diag}_{j=0,\dots,n-1}\left(p\left(\frac{2\pi j}{n}\right)\right),\) _whose_ \(r\times r\) _diagonal blocks are the values of_ \(p(\theta):=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}A_ke^{ik\cdot\theta}\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r},k\cdot\theta=k_1\theta_1+\cdots+k_d\theta_d.\) The proof of this theorem relies on finding a diagonalization of the uni-level generator _Zn_, which can be obtained explicitly by computing its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The block-diagonalization for _Cn,r_ then follows directly from equation (3.2), and the extension to the multi-level case is achieved by exploiting the properties of the Kronecker product.
Theorem 3.4 offers numerous significant discoveries. Every multi-level _r_-block circulant matrix is unitarily similar to the block diagonal matrix \(\Lambda_{n,r}\); in particular, it is normal if and only if each \(r\times r\) block \(p(2\pi j/n)\) is normal, which for _r_=1 is always the case. Secondly, the spectrum of _Cn,r_ is the union of the spectra of these blocks, \(\Lambda\big(C_{n,r}\big)=\bigcup_{j=0}^{n-1}\Lambda\big(p(\theta_j)\big),p(\theta_j)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}A_ke^{ik\cdot\theta_j},\theta_j:=\frac{2\pi j}{n},j=0,\dots,n-1,\) which means that the blocks \(p(\theta_j)\) can be computed by performing the DFT of the first block column of _Cn,r_. The corresponding invariant subspaces are spanned by the columns of _Fn,r_. Moreover, for _r_=1 circulant matrices form an algebra that is closed under inversion, and every matrix in this algebra is uniformly diagonalized by _Fn_; for _r\>_1 the block circulant matrices are simultaneously block-diagonalized by _Fn,r_, and the algebraic operations are inherited from those of the blocks.

Last but not least, many computations involving block circulant matrices can be significantly accelerated by using the FFT. The computational cost of the matrix-vector product _C_<sub>**_n_**_,r_</sub>**_x_**, where \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})r}\), is reduced from the conventional \(O\big((N(\mathbf{n})r)^2\big)\) operations necessary for dense matrices to only \(O\big(rN(\mathbf{n})logN(\mathbf{n})+r^2N(\mathbf{n})\big)\) operations, by using the following approach:

1. Compute \(\mathbf{y}=F_{\mathbf{n},r}^*\mathbf{x}\) via the FFT applied to each of the _r_ components, in _O(rN_(**_n_**)log_N_(**_n_**)) flops;<tbc>

2. Compute \(\mathbf{z}=\Lambda_{\mathbf{n},r}\mathbf{y}\), that is, _N_(**_n_**) products of size _r_, in _O(r_<sup>2</sup>_N_(**_n_**)) flops;<tbc>

3. Compute _F_<sub>**_n_**_,r_</sub>**_z_** via the FFT, in _O(rN_(**_n_**)log_N_(**_n_**)) flops.

In the same way, \(C_{\mathbf{n},r}^{-1}\mathbf{x}\) can be computed as \(F_{\mathbf{n},r}\Lambda_{\mathbf{n},r}^{-1}F_{\mathbf{n},r}^*\mathbf{x}\), where the inversion of \(\Lambda_{\mathbf{n},r}\) amounts to solving _N_(**_n_**) independent linear systems of size _r_. Similar techniques apply to the most relevant matrix operations, such as matrix-matrix products, matrix inversion, the solution of linear systems, and the computation of the spectrum, which makes block circulant matrices exceptionally efficient and powerful in practical applications. For a fixed _r_, all the above costs reduce to _O(N_(**_n_**)log_N_(**_n_**)), with a hidden constant depending on _r_.

**Remark 3.1** _This algorithm can be adapted to accommodate general multi-level block Toeplitz matrices through the use of an immersion (or embedding) technique. The central idea is to embed the original Toeplitz matrix into a larger block circulant matrix, and then perform the matrix-vector multiplication using the circulant structure as described above. The required result is then obtained by appropriately extracting the relevant portion from the output. By adopting this strategy, the computational complexity of the block Toeplitz matrix-vector product is also reduced to O(rN_(**_n_**)log_N_(**_n_**)+_r_<sup>2</sup>_N_(**_n_**)).

**Remark 3.2** _Finally, it is important to note that each step of the process is fully parallelizable. Therefore, in a parallel model of computation, the theoretical computational cost of all the aforementioned algorithms can be further reduced to O_(log_N_(**_n_**))_, for a fixed block size r._

## 3.3 \(\omega\)-circulant matrices

By introducing a parameter \(\omega\in\mathbb{C}\backslash\{0\}\), the class of uni-level circulant matrices can be extended to the so-called \(\omega\)_-circulant matrices_. In this thesis, we restrict our attention to the uni-level case and do not consider multi-level \(\omega\)-circulant matrices. These matrices have the following structure:

\([C_n^{\omega]}_{i,j}:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
a_{(i-j)modn} & \text{if}i>j, \\
\omega a_{(i-j)modn} & \text{if}i\le j,
\end{array}\right.i,j=1,\dots,n.\)

where \(a_k\in\mathbb{C}\) for _k_=0_,...,n_-1. Here, the parameter \(\omega\) acts as a scaling factor for certain matrix entries, setting these matrices apart from the standard circulant case.

Essentially, all entries above and on the main diagonal are multiplied by the factor \(\omega\), resulting in the following structure:<tbc>

\(C_n^\omega=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c }
a_0 & \omega a_{n-1} & \omega a_{n-2} & \cdots & \cdots & \omega a_1 \\
a_1 & a_0 & \omega a_{n-1} & \omega a_{n-2} &  &  & \vdots \\
a_2 & a_1 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\vdots & a_2 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots &  &  \\
\vdots &  & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \omega a_{n-2} \\
a_{n-1} & \cdots & \cdots & a_2 & a_1 & a_0
\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}.\)

<tbc>Note that \(C_n^\omega\) still retains a Toeplitz structure, and that for \(\omega=1\) it reduces to the standard circulant matrix. To generalize equation (3.2), we define the \(\omega\)-circulant generator as<tbc>

\([Z_n^\omega]_{i,j}:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\delta_{(i-j-1)modn} & \text{if}i>j, \\
\omega\delta_{(i-j-1)modn} & \text{if}i\le j,
\end{array}\right.i,j=1,\dots,n.\)

<tbc>Equivalently,<tbc>

\([Z_n^\omega]_{i,j}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
1 & \text{if}i-j=1, \\
\omega & \text{if}i=1\wedge j=n, \\
0 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{array}\right.i,j=1,\dots,n.\)

<tbc>In other words, \(Z_n^\omega\) has all ones on the first superdiagonal and \(\omega\) in the top-right corner:<tbc>

\(Z_n^\omega=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c }
0 &  &  &  &  & \omega \\
1 & \ddots &  &  &  &  &  \\
\ddots &  & \ddots &  &  &  &  \\
 &  & \ddots & \ddots &  &  &  \\
 &  &  & \ddots & \ddots &  &  \\
 &  &  &  & 1 & 0
\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}.\)

<tbc>In this framework, \(C_n^\omega\) can be expressed as a linear combination of powers of \(Z_n^\omega\):<tbc>

\(C_n^\omega=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k(Z_n^\omega)^k.\)

<tbc>A diagonalization formula, paralleling equation (3.4), naturally extends to the case of \(\omega\)-circulant matrices:<tbc>

\(C_n^\omega=F_n^\omega\Lambda_n^\omega(F_n^\omega)^{-1},\)

<tbc>where the diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of \(C_n^\omega\) is given by<tbc>

\(\Lambda_n^\omega:=\mathrm{diag}_{j=0,\dots,n-1}\left(p\left(\frac{2\pi j}{n}\right)\right)\)

with \(p(\theta):=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\omega^\frac{k}{n}a_ke^{ik\theta},\) and the adapted Fourier matrix containing the eigenvectors is defined as \(F_n^\omega:=D_n^\omega F_n,D_n^\omega:=\mathrm{diag}_{k=0,\dots,n-1}\left(\omega^{-\frac{k}{n}}\right).\) Observe that the eigenvalues of \(C_n^\omega\) are obtained by computing the matrix-vector product \(F_n^\omega\mathbf{c}\), where **c** denotes the first column of \(C_n^\omega\).
Extending the computation of the matrix-vector product to \(\omega\)-circulant matrices, as well as adapting all the algorithms discussed in the previous subsection, is immediate and requires only minor modifications: 1. Compute \(\mathbf{y}=(D_n^\omega F_n)^{-1}\mathbf{x}=F_n^*(D_n^\omega)^{-1}\mathbf{x}\) using the FFT, which requires _O(n_log_n_) flops; 2. Compute \(\mathbf{z}=\Lambda_n^\omega\mathbf{y}\), in _O(n_) flops; 3. Compute \(D_n^\omega F_n\mathbf{z}\) via the FFT, again in _O(n_log_n_) flops. Overall, this sequence of operations leads to a computational cost of _O(n_log_n_) in a sequential implementation, while in a parallel environment it requires _O_(log_n_) steps. Nevertheless, the presence of the parameter \(\omega\) may affect numerical stability. Since _Fn_ is unitary, the conditioning of the transformation \(D_n^\omega F_n\) depends exclusively on the diagonal scaling \(D_n^\omega\). More precisely, as \(n\rightarrow+\infty\), the condition number of \(D_n^\omega\) approaches \(\mathrm{max}\{|\omega|,|\omega|^{-1}\}\), and therefore becomes unbounded whenever \(\omega\rightarrow 0\) or \(|\omega|\rightarrow\infty\). Recent developments have extended the use of \(\omega\)-circulant preconditioners to more complex applications. For instance, Fung and Hon \[40\] introduced block \(\omega\)-circulant preconditioners for parabolic optimal control problems, demonstrating their effectiveness in accelerating the convergence of iterative solvers for large-scale all-at-once systems. More recently, Hon, Fung, and Lin \[55\] developed an optimal diagonalization- based preconditioner for parabolic optimal control problems, further showcasing the versatility of circulant-based approaches. These works highlight the continued relevance of \(\omega\)-circulant structures in modern numerical linear algebra. **Remark 3.3** _In the standard circulant case of Theorem 3.4, the Fourier matrix Fn is unitary, so_ \(F_n^*=F_n^{-1}\) _and the two notations_ \(F_n\Lambda_nF_n^*\) _and_ \(F_n\Lambda_nF_n^{-1}\) _coincide. For the_ \(\omega\)_-circulant case, the adapted Fourier matrix_ \(F_n^\omega=D_n^\omega F_n\) _is not unitary unless_ \(|\omega|=1\)_, since_ \(D_n^\omega\) _is a non-trivial diagonal scaling. Hence_ \((F_n^\omega)^*\neq(F_n^\omega)^{-1}\) _in general, and the diagonalization must be written as_ \(C_n^\omega=F_n^\omega\Lambda_n^\omega(F_n^\omega)^{-1}.\) ## 3.3.1 Block \(\omega\)-circulant matrices To set the stage for certain practical applications to the solution of linear systems, we briefly extend the definition and diagonalization of \(\omega\)-circulant matrices to the

block case. For \(n,r\in\mathbb{N}\), we define an _r_-block \(\omega\)-circulant matrix \(C_{n,r}^\omega\in\mathbb{C}^{nr\times nr}\) as follows:<tbc>

\(\left[C_{n,r}^\omega\right]_{i,j}:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
A_{(i-j)\mathrm{mod}n} & \text{if}i>j, \\
\omega A_{(i-j)\mathrm{mod}n} & \text{if}i\le j,
\end{array}\right.i,j=1,\dots,n,\)

<tbc>where \(A_k\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\) for _k_=0_,...,n_-1 are _n_ general (not necessarily structured) matrices. Explicitly:<tbc>

\(C_{n,r}^\omega=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c }
A_0 & \omega A_{n-1} & \omega A_{n-2} & \cdots & \cdots & \omega A_1 \\
A_1 & A_0 & \omega A_{n-1} & \omega A_{n-2} & & \vdots \\
A_2 & A_1 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\vdots & A_2 & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \omega A_{n-2} \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \omega A_{n-1} \\
A_{n-1} & \cdots & \cdots & A_2 & A_1 & A_0
\end{array}\right].\)

<tbc>A compact representation for \(C_{n,r}^\omega\) is given by<tbc>

\(C_{n,r}^\omega=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(Z_n^\omega)^j\otimes A_j.\)

<tbc>Moreover, \(C_{n,r}^\omega\) can be block-diagonalized as<tbc>

\(C_{n,r}^\omega=F_{n,r}^\omega\Lambda_{n,r}^\omega(F_{n,r}^\omega)^{-1},\)

<tbc>where<tbc>

\(F_{n,r}^\omega:=F_n^\omega\otimes I_r,\)

<tbc>and<tbc>

\(\Lambda_{n,r}^\omega:=\mathrm{diag}_{j=0,\dots,n-1}\left(p\left(\frac{2\pi j}{n}\right)\right)\)

<tbc>with

\(p(\theta):=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\omega^\frac{k}{n}A_ke^{ik\theta}\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}.\)

Note that \(C_{n,r}^\omega\) is not a two-level \(\omega\)-circulant matrix, since the matrices _A<sub>k</sub>_ do not necessarily possess a specific structure and the function \(p(\theta)\) is an \(r\times r\) matrix rather than a scalar. Nevertheless, when _r_ is a fixed integer, the matrix-vector product can still be computed in O(_n_log_n_) floating-point operations in a sequential setting, or in O(log_n_) steps in a parallel computational model, where the hidden constant in the O-notation depends on _r_. If _r_ varies and tends to infinity and each inner matrix _A<sub>k</sub>_ admits a diagonalization with cost O(_r_log_r_), then the overall computational cost becomes O(_nr_log(_nr_)) flops in the sequential case, or O(log(_nr_)) parallel steps. For a review on recent applications concerning _r_-block \(\omega\)-circulant structures, refer to \[31\] and references therein.

## 3.4 \(\tau\) matrices A uni-level _r_-block \(\tau\) matrix is defined as a square matrix \(S_{n,r}\in\mathbb{R}^{nr\times nr}\), partitioned into \(r\times r\) blocks _Si,j_, whose blocks satisfy the so-called _cross-sum condition_ \(S_{i-1,j}+S_{i+1,j}=S_{i,j-1}+S_{i,j+1},i,j=1,\dots,n,\) where we assume the boundary conditions \(S_{n+1,j}=S_{i,n+1}=S_{0,j}=S_{i,0}=O_r.\) For _r_=1 the blocks reduce to the scalar entries _si,j_ and the classical definition is recovered. This relation implies the block-centrosymmetry of _Sn,r_, that is, symmetry with respect to the center of the matrix at the block level. As a consequence, _Sn,r_ is both symmetric and persymmetric, namely symmetric with respect to the main anti- diagonal, whenever the generating blocks are symmetric. Furthermore, all the blocks of _Sn,r_ are uniquely determined by the blocks in its first block row or, equivalently, in its first block column. Additional details on this definition and the resulting properties can be found in \[19\].
Much like circulant matrices, there is a generator for the set of \(\tau\) matrices, defined by \([W_n]_{i,j}:=\delta_{|i-j|-1}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } 1 & \text{if}i-j=\pm 1, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{array}\right.i,j=1,\dots,n,\) or, in explicit matrix form \(W_n=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c c } 0 & 1 & & & & & & \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & & & & & \\ & 1 & \ddots & & \ddots & & & \\ & & \ddots & & \ddots & & \ddots & \\ & & & & \ddots & & \ddots & 1 \\ & & & & & & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.\) The _r_-block \(\tau\) algebra is defined as the set of matrices generated by _Wn_ in the block sense, meaning that every _r_-block \(\tau\) matrix can be represented as \(S_{n,r}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}W_n^k\otimes A_k,A_k\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},\) that is, as a linear combination, with matrix coefficients, of the powers \(W_n^0=I_n\), _Wn_, \(W_n^2\), _..._, \(W_n^{n-1}\). This representation is equivalent to the cross-sum condition stated above, since the latter acts independently on each of the _r_2 entry positions inside the blocks. As is characteristic of matrix algebras, for _r_=1 this set is closed under inversion, a property that follows from the Hamilton-Cayley theorem \[17\]. Furthermore, for any \(n,k\in\mathbb{N}\), the matrix \(W_n^k\) is symmetric and is invertible if and only if _n_ is even.

This construction can be extended to the multi-level setting by defining the multi- level generators for \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\) as

\(W_\mathbf{n}^{(1)}=W_{n_1}\otimes\left(\otimes_{l=2}^dI_{n_l}\right),W_\mathbf{n}^{(2)}=I_{n_1}\otimes W_{n_2}\otimes\left(\otimes_{l=3}^dI_{n_l}\right),\vdots W_\mathbf{n}^{(d)}=\left(\otimes_{l=1}^{d-1}I_{n_l}\right)\otimes W_{n_d}.\text{(3.5)}\)

Accordingly, a multi-level _r_-block \(\tau\) matrix admits the representation

\(S_{\mathbf{n},r}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0}}^{\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}}\left(W_{n_1}^{k_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes W_{n_d}^{k_d}\right)\otimes A_\mathbf{k},A_\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}.\)

Matrices _S_<sub>**_n_**_,r_</sub> that belong to the multi-level _r_-block \(\tau\) algebra are referred to as multi-level block \(\tau\) matrices.

## 3.4.1 Spectral properties and the discrete sine transform

In close analogy with the diagonalization theory for circulant matrices, \(\tau\) matrices can also be diagonalized by means of a related fast transform. More precisely, the Discrete Sine Transform (DST) is the linear mapping that associates with each vector \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^n\) the vector _Q<sub>n</sub>**x**_, where the matrix _Q<sub>n</sub>_, known as the sine transform matrix, is defined as

\(Q_n:=\sqrt{\frac{2}{n+1}}\left[sin\left(\frac{rs\pi}{n+1}\right)\right]_{r,s=1}^n.\)

It is closely connected to the Fast Sine Transform, which enables the DST to be computed in O(_n_log_n_) real arithmetic operations, requiring roughly half the computational cost of the well-known FFT \[138\]. The matrix _Q<sub>n</sub>_ is real, symmetric, and orthogonal. Its multilevel extension, for \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\), is defined as

\(Q_\mathbf{n}:=Q_{n_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_{n_d},\)

and the _d_-level DST is given by the matrix-vector product _Q_**_<sub>n</sub>x_**, with \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})}\). By exploiting the properties of the Kronecker product, it follows that _Q_**_<sub>n</sub>_** is a real, symmetric, and orthogonal matrix, and therefore \(Q_\mathbf{n}=Q_\mathbf{n}^T=Q_\mathbf{n}^{-1}\). Its _r_-block counterpart is defined as

\(Q_{\mathbf{n},r}:=Q_\mathbf{n}\otimes I_r,\)

which inherits the same properties, so that \(Q_{\mathbf{n},r}=Q_{\mathbf{n},r}^T=Q_{\mathbf{n},r}^{-1}\). As a consequence, we obtain the following spectral decomposition for multi-level block \(\tau\) matrices.

**Theorem 3.5** _For all_ \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\) _and_ \(r\in\mathbb{N}\)_, it holds that_

\(S_{\mathbf{n},r}=Q_{\mathbf{n},r}\Lambda_{\mathbf{n},r}Q_{\mathbf{n},r},\)

_where_ \(\Lambda_{\mathbf{n},r}\) _is block diagonal and its_ \(r\times r\) _diagonal blocks are given by the d-level DST of the first block column (or, equivalently, the first block row) of S<sub>**n**,r</sub>._

All the properties established after Theorem 3.4 for block circulant matrices extend to the multi-level block \(\tau\) setting, once the necessary adaptations are made. In particular, any multi-level block \(\tau\) matrix is real and, when the generating blocks _A<sub>**k**</sub>_ are symmetric, its spectrum is the union of the spectra of the \(r\times r\) diagonal blocks of \(\Lambda_{\mathbf{n},r}\), which are obtained in explicit form by applying the DST to its first block column, while the corresponding invariant subspaces are spanned by the columns of _Q<sub>**n**,r</sub>_. Moreover, the fundamental matrix operations, including matrix-vector multiplication, inversion, the solution of linear systems, and spectral computation, can be performed with a sequential computational cost of _O(N_(**_n_**)log_N_(**_n_**)), or in _O_(log_N_(**_n_**)) steps within a parallel computational framework, with hidden constants depending on the block size _r_.

Recently, \(\tau\) preconditioners have gained renewed attention for solving FDEs. Li and Hon \[77\] developed multilevel tau preconditioners for symmetrized multilevel Toeplitz systems arising from space-FDEs, providing a comprehensive GLT-based analysis of their spectral properties. Building on this work, Hon, Li, Sormani, Krause, and Serra-Capizzano \[54\] introduced symbol-based multilevel block \(\tau\) preconditioners for general multilevel block Toeplitz systems, establishing a rigorous GLT framework for analyzing their asymptotic spectral behavior. These developments demonstrate that \(\tau\)-preconditioners remain a powerful tool for structured linear systems, particularly in the fractional diffusion setting.

## 3.5 Hankel matrices

Given \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\) and \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), a matrix of the form

\(H_\mathbf{n}:=[A_{\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}}]_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{1}}^\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})r\times N(\mathbf{n})r},\)

with blocks \(A_\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), where the block in position (**_i_**_,**j**_) depends only on the sum **_i_**+**_j_**, is known as a multi-level block (or _d_-level _r_-block) Hankel matrix.

In practice, it can be interpreted as a mirrored Toeplitz structure. In the one- dimensional case, i.e., for _d_=1 and **_n_**=_n_, a one-level (uni-level) _r_-block Hankel matrix is defined by the property that its blocks are constant along the block anti- diagonals:

\(H_n=\left[A_{i+j}\right]_{i,j=1}^n=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c }
A_2 & A_3 & A_4 & \cdots & A_{n+1} \\
A_3 & A_4 & & \ddots & \vdots \\
A_4 & & \ddots & & A_{2n-2} \\
\vdots & \ddots & & A_{2n-2} & A_{2n-1} \\
A_{n+1} & \cdots & A_{2n-2} & A_{2n-1} & A_{2n}
\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{nr\times nr}.\)

Just like Toeplitz matrices, _Hn_ is completely determined by its 2_n_-1 blocks _Ak_ for _k_=2_,...,_2_n_, or, equivalently, by its first block row and last block column. For _d_=2 and **_n_**=(_n_1_,n_2), a 2-level _r_-block Hankel matrix takes the form \(H_n=\left[A_{i+j}\right]_{i,j=1}^n=\left[\left[A_{(i_1+j_1,i_2+j_2)}\right]_{i_2,j_2=1}^{n_2}\right]_{i_1,j_1=1}^{n_1}=\left[\mathcal{A}_{i_1+j_1}\right]_{i_1,j_1=1}^{n_1}\)
\(=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c } \mathcal{A}_2 & \mathcal{A}_3 & \mathcal{A}_4 & \cdots & \mathcal{A}_{n_1+1} \\ \mathcal{A}_3 & \mathcal{A}_4 & & \ddots & \vdots \\ \mathcal{A}_4 & & \ddots & & \mathcal{A}_{2n_1-2} \\ \vdots & \ddots & & \mathcal{A}_{2n_1-2} & \mathcal{A}_{2n_1-1} \\ \mathcal{A}_{n_1+1} & \cdots & \mathcal{A}_{2n_1-2} & \mathcal{A}_{2n_1-1} & \mathcal{A}_{2n_1} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{n_1n_2r\times n_1n_2r},\) where each block A_k_ is itself a 1-level _r_-block Hankel matrix, \(\mathcal{A}_k=\left[A_{(k,i_2+j_2)}\right]_{i_2,j_2=1}^{n_2}\)
\(=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c } A_{(k,2)} & A_{(k,3)} & A_{(k,4)} & \cdots & A_{(k,n_2+1)} \\ A_{(k,3)} & A_{(k,4)} & & \ddots & \vdots \\ A_{(k,4)} & & \ddots & & A_{(k,2n_2-2)} \\ \vdots & \ddots & & & A_{(k,2n_2-2)} & A_{(k,2n_2-1)} \\ A_{(k,n_2+1)} & \cdots & A_{(k,2n_2-2)} & A_{(k,2n_2-1)} & A_{(k,2n_2)} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{n_2r\times n_2r}.\) In the multi-level setting, a _d_-level _r_-block Hankel matrix admits a recursive block structure, in the sense that it can be interpreted as a block Hankel matrix whose blocks are (_d_-1)-level _r_-block Hankel matrices. As in the one-level case, the entire matrix is uniquely specified by the blocks in its first block row and last block column. To obtain a compact representation of _Hn_, we introduce, for \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\), the matrix \(\left[K_n^{(k)}\right]_{i,j}:=\delta_{i+j-k}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } 1 & \text{if}i+j=k, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{array}\right.i,j=1,\dots,n,\) which places ones on the (_k_-1)-th anti-diagonal and zeros elsewhere. The multi-level generalization for \(n\in\mathbb{N}^d\) and \(k\in\mathbb{Z}^d\) is given by \(K_n^{(k)}:=K_{n_1}^{(k_1)}\otimes K_{n_2}^{(k_2)}\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n_d}^{(k_d)}.\) This leads to the following compact expression for _Hn_: \(H_n=\left[A_{i+j}\right]_{i,j=1}^n=\sum_{k=2}^{2n}K_n^{(k)}\otimes A_k.\) (3.6) In analogy with the Toeplitz and circulant cases, the above representation follows from a direct verification of the individual matrix blocks. Block Hankel matrices are closely related to block Toeplitz matrices through the anti-identity matrix; see \[37\] for spectral properties and applications.

## Chapter 4 ### GLT matrix sequences and their algebraic structure We are now in a position to introduce the theory of GLT matrix sequences, which provides the central spectral framework for the analysis carried out in this thesis. The GLT machinery offers a unified language for describing the asymptotic behavior of large structured matrices generated by the discretization of differential and nonlocal operators and, at the same time, supplies the theoretical tools required for the design of efficient numerical solvers.
In the present setting we consider the multi-level block case, corresponding to _d_- level GLT matrix sequences with \(r\times r\) matrix-valued symbols, where \(d\ge 1\) denotes the number of structural levels and \(r\ge 1\) is the block size. For fixed _d_ and _r_, the associated GLT class is characterized by symbols given by measurable functions \(\kappa:[0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r},\) which encode the asymptotic spectral distribution of the matrix sequence. While the scalar case is thoroughly treated in the monographs [41, 42], the matrix-valued framework adopted here follows the more general and flexible approach developed in [11, 10]. This setting is essential for the study of block discretizations and coupled systems arising in PDEs and FDEs. Moreover, the theory continues to evolve, as witnessed by recent developments on reduced and rectangular GLT sequences [8, 9]. Rather than presenting the full constructive definition of the multi-level GLT class, we focus on the fundamental operative properties that uniquely characterize it and that are most relevant for numerical applications. These properties, commonly referred to as the _GLT axioms_, provide a complete algebraic and spectral description of the class and will be systematically used in the subsequent analysis. They are introduced and discussed in Section 4.6. In addition, we highlight how the GLT framework naturally guides the construction of effective preconditioning strategies, thereby establishing the link between asymptotic spectral theory and fast iterative solvers. ### 4.1 The GLT class Let us first review some basic aspects to better understand GLT sequences. The theory of LT sequences provides a powerful framework for analyzing the asymptotic singular value and eigenvalue distributions of structured matrix sequences that arise in numerical analysis. In the context of PDE discretization, the matrices resulting from numerical approximations often fail to retain the classical Toeplitz structure due to the presence of variable coefficients. Traditionally, Toeplitz matrices have played a central role in problems involving translation-invariant differential operators, where constant coefficients ensure a globally repeating structure. Instead, the

resulting matrices exhibit a Toeplitz-like structure that varies smoothly along the diagonals as the matrix size increases, leading to the broader class of LT sequences \[134, 136\].
A classical Toeplitz matrix generated by a function \(f:[-\pi,\pi]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\) belonging to \(L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d)\), where the constant diagonal entries correspond to the Fourier coefficients of _f_. However, for differential operators with non-constant coefficients, the resulting matrices do not maintain this global Toeplitz structure but instead belong to the LT class. Specifically, an LT matrix _An_ is obtained by modulating the entries of a Toeplitz matrix using an almost everywhere (a.e.) continuous function \(a(x):[0,1]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), scaling the entries along the same diagonal \(a\left(\frac{i}{n}\right)\) for **_i_**=**1**_,...,n_**. As \(n\rightarrow\infty\), the differences between consecutive diagonal elements vanish due to continuity, making the structure asymptotically Toeplitz-like. More precisely, this structure can be represented as the product of a Toeplitz matrix and a diagonal matrix, where the diagonal entries correspond to evaluations of the function _a(x_), such that _An=Dn(a)Tn_, where _Dn(a_) is a diagonal matrix whose entries are given by \(D_n(a)=\mathrm{diag}\left(a\left(\frac{i}{n}\right)\right)_{i=1}^n\). This formulation allows LT sequences to accurately capture local variations in variable-coefficient differential operators while preserving the structural properties of Toeplitz matrices. Formally, a LT sequence {_A_**n**}**n** can be expressed through the product of the weight function _a(x_) and the generating function \(f(\theta)\), leading to the LT symbol \(a\otimes f:[0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r},\) where \((a\otimes f)(x,\theta):=a(x)f(\theta),(x,\theta)\in[0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d.\) Here the symbol "\(\otimes\)" in \(a\otimes f\) denotes the pointwise matrix product of the two matrix-valued functions, not the Kronecker product of the two matrices. Since \(a(x),f(\theta)\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), the product is well defined and belongs to \(\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), in accordance with the target space of the LT symbol. This is consistent with the use of "\(\otimes\)" in GLT 7, where at the matrix level "\(\otimes\)" denotes the Kronecker product, while at the symbol level it denotes the pointwise product of the symbols.
Building on this concept, a GLT matrix sequence is defined as the limit, in the sense of the a.c.s., as described in Definition 2.3, of a finite sum of LT sequences. The construction of GLT sequences was formalized through a.c.s. limits in \[124\] and refined to a **d-level** ∗**-algebra of structured matrix sequences** satisfying specific axioms, listed in \[42, Chapter 6, pp. 118-120\]. The theory of GLT sequences provides a fundamental framework for analyzing structured matrix sequences arising from discretizations of differential equations.
A particularly relevant development in the spectral analysis of structured matrix sequences concerns symmetrized Toeplitz structures. Hon, Mursaleen, and Serra- Capizzano \[50\] provided a note on the spectral distribution of symmetrized Toeplitz sequences, establishing precise distribution results for this important class of matrices. Building on this work, Ferrari, Furci, Hon, Mursaleen, and Serra-Capizzano \[38\] studied the eigenvalue distribution of special \(2\times 2\) block matrix sequences, with applications to symmetrized Toeplitz structures. These results are particularly relevant for understanding the spectral behavior of preconditioned matrix sequences and for analyzing the convergence of iterative methods applied to non-Hermitian Toeplitz systems. The analysis presented in later chapters of this thesis, particularly concerning nonsymmetric Toeplitz systems, draws upon this theoretical framework.

## 4.2 Matrix sequences with explicit or hidden (asymptotic) structure In this section, we introduce three types of matrix structures that serve as the fundamental building blocks of the GLT ∗-algebras. Specifically, for any positive integers _d_ and _r_, we consider the set of _d_-level _r_-block GLT matrix sequences. This set forms a ∗-algebra of matrix sequences, which is both maximal and isometrically equivalent to the maximal ∗-algebra of 2_d_-variate \(r\times r\) matrix-valued measurable functions (with respect to the Lebesgue measure) that are naturally defined over \([0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\); see \[11, 10, 41, 42\] and references therein.
The reduced version of this structure plays a crucial role in approximating integro- differential operators, including their fractional versions, particularly when defined over general (non-Cartesian) domains. This concept was initially introduced in \[124, 125\] and later extensively developed in \[8\], where GLT symbols are again defined as measurable functions over \(\Omega\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\), with \(\Omega\) being Peano-Jordan measurable and contained within \[0,1\]_d_. Additionally, the reduced versions also form maximal ∗- algebras that are isometrically equivalent to their corresponding maximal ∗-algebras of measurable functions.
These GLT ∗-algebras provide a rich framework of hidden (asymptotic) structures, built upon three fundamental classes of explicit algebraic structures: _d_-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrix sequences and sampling diagonal matrix sequences (discussed in Sections 4.4 and 4.5), along with asymptotic structures described by zero-distributed matrix-sequences (see Section 4.3). Notably, the latter class serves an analogous role to compact operators in relation to bounded linear operators, forming a two-sided ideal of matrix sequences within any of the GLT ∗-algebras. ## 4.3 Zero-distributed sequences Zero-distributed sequences are defined as matrix sequences {_An}n_ such that \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma 0\). Note that, for any \(r\ge 1\), \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma 0\) is equivalent to \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma O_r\), where _Or_ is the \(r\times r\) zero matrix. The following theorem, taken from \[121, 41\], provides a useful characterization for detecting this type of sequence. **Theorem 4.1** _Let_ {_An}n be a matrix sequence, with An of size dn, and let_ \(p\in[1,\infty]\)_, with_ \(\|X\|_p\) _being the Schatten p-norm of X, that is, the_ \(\ell^p\) _norm of the vector of its singular values. Let_ \(\|\cdot\|=\|\cdot\|_\infty\) _be the spectral norm. With the natural convention_ \(1/\infty=0\)_, we have:_ • \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma 0\) _if and only if An=Rn+Nn with_ \(rank(R_n)/d_n\rightarrow 0\) _and_ \(\|N_n\|\rightarrow 0\) _as_ \(n\rightarrow\infty\); • \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma 0\) _if there exists_ \(p\in[1,\infty]\) _such that_ \(\frac{\|A_n\|_p}{(d_n)^{1/p}}\rightarrow 0\text{\textit{as}}n\rightarrow\infty.\) As in Section 2.2, the same definition can be given and the corresponding result (with obvious changes) holds when the involved matrix sequences show a multi-level structure. In that case, _n_ is replaced by **_n_** uniformly in _An_, _Nn_, _Rn_, _dn_.

Further results connecting Schatten _p_-norms, unitarily invariant norms (see \[16\]), variational characterization, and Toeplitz/Hankel structures can be found in \[128\]. ## 4.4 Multi-level block Toeplitz matrices Given \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\), a matrix of the form \([A_{\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}}]_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{1}}^\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})r\times N(\mathbf{n})r},\) with blocks \(A_\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), \(\mathbf{k}\in\{-(\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}),\dots,\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}\}\), is called a _multi-level block Toeplitz matrix_, or, more precisely, a _d_-level _r_-block Toeplitz matrix.
Given a matrix-valued function \(f:[-\pi,\pi]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\) belonging to \(L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d)\), the **_n_**-th Toeplitz matrix associated with _f_ is defined as \(T_\mathbf{n}(f):=[\hat{f}_{\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}}]_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{1}}^\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})r\times N(\mathbf{n})r},\) where \(\hat{f}_\mathbf{k}=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^d}\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^d}f(\theta)e^{-i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\unknown)}d\unknown\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times r},\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^d,\) are the Fourier coefficients of _f_.
The family \(\{T_\mathbf{n}(f)\}_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d}\) is called the family of (multi-level block) Toeplitz matrices associated with _f_, which is referred to as the _generating function_. ## 4.5 Block diagonal sampling matrices Given \(d\ge 1\), \(\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}^d\) and a function \(a:[0,1]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), we define the multi-level block diagonal sampling matrix _D**n**(a_) as the block diagonal matrix \(D_\mathbf{n}(a)=\mathrm{diag}_{\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{1},\dots,\mathbf{n}}\left(a\left(\frac{\mathbf{i}}{\mathbf{n}}\right)\right)\in\mathbb{C}^{N(\mathbf{n})r\times N(\mathbf{n})r}.\) (4.1) Essentially, _D**n**(a_) is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the evaluations of _a(x_) at the points of a uniform mesh over the domain \[0,1\]_d_, with the points arranged in lexicographical order. ## 4.6 The ∗-algebra of _d_-level _r_-block GLT matrix sequences Let \(r\ge 1\) be a fixed integer. A multi-level _r_-block GLT sequence, or simply a GLT sequence if _r_ does not need to be specified, is a special multi-level _r_-block matrix sequence equipped with a measurable function \(\kappa:[0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\), \(d\ge 1\), called the _symbol_. We write \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\) to denote that {_An}n_ is a GLT sequence with symbol \(\kappa\). A fundamental property of the GLT symbol is that it is unique: if two symbols are associated with the same matrix sequence, then they must coincide almost everywhere. **Proposition 4.1** _If_ \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\) _and_ \(\{B_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\xi\)_, then_ \(\kappa=\xi\) _a.e._

The symbol plays a central role in determining the singular value distribution and, in the Hermitian setting, the eigenvalue distribution of GLT matrix sequences.
It can be proven that the set of multilevel block GLT sequences is the ∗-algebra generated by the three classes of sequences defined in Sections 4.3, 4.4, 4.5: zero- distributed sequences, multi-level block Toeplitz sequences, and block diagonal sampling matrix sequences. The GLT class satisfies several algebraic and topological properties, which are discussed in detail in \[11, 10, 41, 42\]. Here, we focus on the main operative properties listed below, which provide a complete characterization of GLT sequences, equivalent to the full constructive definition. **GLT 1** _If_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\)_, then_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\sigma\kappa\) _in the sense of Definition 2.1, with t_=2_d and_ \(D=[0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\)_. If moreover each An is Hermitian, then_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\kappa\)_, again in the sense of Definition 2.1, with t_=2_d._ **GLT 2** _It holds_ • \(\{T_\mathbf{n}(f)\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa(\mathbf{x},\theta)=f(\theta)\) _for any_ \(f:[-\pi,\pi]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\) _with_ \(f\in L^1([-\pi,\pi]^d)\); • \(\{D_\mathbf{n}(a)\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa(\mathbf{x},\theta)=a(\mathbf{x})\) _for any Riemann-integrable_ \(a:[0,1]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r}\); • \(\{Z_n\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa(\mathbf{x},\theta)=O_r\) _if and only if_ \(\{Z_n\}_n\sim_\sigma 0\)_, i.e.,_ {_Zn}n is zero- distributed._ **GLT 3** _If_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\) _and_ \(\{B_n\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\varsigma\)_, then_ • \(\{A_n^*\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\bar{\kappa}\)_, where_ \(A_n^*\) _denotes the conjugate transpose of An and_ \(\bar{\kappa}\) _the complex conjugate of_ \(\kappa\); • \(\{\alpha A_n+\beta B_n\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\alpha\kappa+\beta\varsigma\) _for any_ \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C}\); • \(\{A_nB_n\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\varsigma\); • \(\{A_n^\dagger\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa^{-1}\) _for any_ \(\kappa\) _invertible a.e., where_ \(A_n^\dagger\) _denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of An._ **GLT 4** \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\) _if and only if there exist_ \(\{B_{\mathbf{n},j}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa_j\) _such that_ \(\{\{B_{\mathbf{n},j}\}_\mathbf{n}\}_j\longrightarrow^{a.c.s.wrt j}\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\) _and_ \(\kappa_j\rightarrow\kappa\) _in measure._ **GLT 5** _If_ \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\) _and A**n**=X**n**+Y**n**, where_ • _every X**n** is Hermitian,_ • ||_X**n_||, \(||Y_\mathbf{n}||\le C\) _for some constant C independent of n,_ • \(N(\mathbf{n})^{-1}\|Y_\mathbf{n}\|_1\rightarrow 0\), _then_ \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_n\sim_\lambda\kappa\). **GLT 6** _If_ \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\) _and each A**n** is Hermitian, then_ \(\{f(A_\mathbf{n})\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}f(\kappa)\) _for every continuous function_ \(f:\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}\).

**GLT 7** _Let_ \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\) _and_ \(\{B_\mathbf{m}\}_\mathbf{m}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\xi\) _with_ \(\kappa(x_1,\theta_1):[0,1]^{d_1}\times[-\pi,\pi]^{d_1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C},\)
\(\xi(x_2,\theta_2):[0,1]^{d_2}\times[-\pi,\pi]^{d_2}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}.\) _Then, it holds_ \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\otimes\{B_\mathbf{m}\}_\mathbf{m}=\{A_\mathbf{n}\otimes B_\mathbf{m}\}_\mathbf{nm}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\otimes\xi,\) _where_ \((\kappa\otimes\xi):[0,1]^{d_1+d_2}\times[-\pi,\pi]^{d_1+d_2}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}\) _is given by_ \((\kappa\otimes\xi)(x_1,x_2,\theta_1,\theta_2):=\kappa(x_1,\theta_1)\xi(x_2,\theta_2),\) _i.e., the tensor product is a_ (_d_1+_d_2)_-level GLT matrix sequence with scalar symbol. In particular, when d_1=_d_2=1_, the tensor product is a two-level GLT matrix sequence._ Note that, by **GLT 1**, it is always possible to obtain the singular value distribution from the GLT symbol, while the eigenvalue distribution can only be deduced either if the involved matrices are Hermitian or the related matrix-sequence is quasi- Hermitian in the sense of **GLT 5**. ## 4.6.1 GLT theory and preconditioning: a practical perspective Before proceeding to the numerical applications in Part II, it is useful to clarify how the abstract GLT framework directly informs preconditioner design. The central idea is as follows: if a preconditioned matrix sequence has GLT symbol equal to the constant function 1, then, by GLT 1, its singular values are asymptotically distributed as 1. In other words, the singular values cluster at 1 in the weak sense. If, in addition, the matrices are Hermitian, the eigenvalues also cluster at 1. For non- Hermitian matrices, eigenvalue clustering at 1 may still be obtained under suitable additional assumptions, such as normality or the existence of a low-rank perturbation structure that allows the application of perturbation arguments \[12, 45\]. Such clustering is of significant practical importance: when the eigenvalues or singular values of the preconditioned matrix are clustered around 1, Krylov subspace methods such as GMRES or MINRES typically exhibit fast convergence. Thus, the GLT symbol serves as a powerful predictive tool: it not only describes the asymptotic spectral behavior of the coefficient matrices but also guides the construction of preconditioners whose symbols match those of the original matrices, thereby ensuring favorable convergence properties. Throughout the following chapters, this principle will be applied systematically to design and analyze preconditioners for ISPs of the FDEs.

## Chapter 5

### Inverse source problems for a 2D generalized diffusion equation

Having introduced in the previous chapters the analytical foundations of fractional operators, the spectral framework of matrix sequences, the main classes of structured matrices, and the GLT theory, we now turn to the study of inverse source problems (ISPs) for a two-dimensional generalized diffusion equation. This chapter is based on the work [64], with additional details, examples, and reformulations included for completeness of the thesis presentation. This chapter is devoted to the identification of unknown source coefficients in diffusion equation governed by generalized time- fractional derivative of Caputo-type and nonlocal boundary conditions. Such models arise naturally in the description of anomalous transport processes in heterogeneous and complex media, where memory and spatial nonlocality play a dominant role [93, 114, 76].

We investigate two ISPs based on the given final time and integral observational data and derive explicit series representations of the solutions using a bi-orthogonal system of functions. [71, 72, 13, 59]. Rigorous existence and uniqueness results are established, and both ISPs are shown to be ill-posed in the sense of Hadamard, since small perturbations in the measured data may lead to unbounded reconstruction errors [106]. Special cases of the diffusion equation are obtained by appropriate choices of the memory kernel in the time-fractional derivative, allowing the proposed framework to encompass tempered, multi-term, mono-term, and classical diffusion models within a unified setting [113, 105]. The results presented in this chapter provide a rigorous mathematical foundation for ISPs in generalized FDEs and contribute to a deeper understanding of anomalous transport processes governed by memory dependent and nonlocal dynamics.

The remainder of this chapter is organized as follows. Section 5.2 presents the spectral problem associated with the system (5.5)-(5.8), which forms the analytical foundation for the subsequent inverse analysis. Section 5.3 is devoted to the first inverse source problem, where the existence and uniqueness of the regular solution are established and its ill-posed nature is rigorously demonstrated. Section 5.4 investigates the second inverse source problem, proving the existence and uniqueness of a regular solution and analyzing its inherent instability. Section 5.5 provides several numerical examples that illustrate and validate the theoretical results.

### 5.1 Mathematical formulation and preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the generalized time-fractional derivative of Caputo- type and recall its main analytical properties. We then formulate the two dimensional generalized diffusion equation under consideration, discuss several important special cases of this equation, and define the mathematical formulation of the ISPs.

## 5.1.1 Generalized Caputo-type fractional derivative In this study, we utilize the generalized time-fractional derivative of Caputo-type as formulated by Kochubei \[76\], presented in the following form \(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}u(x,y,t):=\int_0^t\varrho(t-\tau)\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}u(x,y,\tau)d\tau,\) (5.1) where \(\varrho(t)\in L_{loc}^1(\mathbb{R}_+)\) represents a locally integrable, non-negative function commonly referred to as the memory kernel. The Laplace transform of \(\varrho(t)\), denoted \(\widehat{\varrho}(s)\), exists for all _s\>_0 and satisfies \(\widehat{\varrho}(s)\in\mathbb{SF},\text{and}lim_{s\rightarrow\infty} s\widehat{\varrho}(s)=+\infty,\) (5.2) where SF denotes the class of Stieltjes functions, as discussed in \[13\]. The class of SF includes all functions on R+ that have the following representation \(\widehat{\phi}(s)=\frac{a}{s}+b+\int_0^\infty\mathrm{e}^{-s\tau}\varphi(\tau)d\tau,s>0,\) (5.3) where \(a,b\ge 0\), \(\varphi\) is the completely monotone function and the Laplace transform of \(\varphi\) exists for any _s\>_0. A function \(\phi\) defined on R+ is said to be a complete Bernstein function (CBF) if and only if \(\frac{\widehat{\phi}(s)}{s}\in\mathbb{SF},s>0.\) (5.4) Assuming \(\widehat{\varrho}(s)\in\mathbb{SF}\) implies that \(\widehat{\varrho}(s)\) can be represented in the specific form given by Eq. (5.3). Therefore, the kernel \(\varrho(t)\) is completely monotone for _t\>_0 and can have an additional term \(b\delta(t)\), where \(b\ge 0\), and \(\delta(\cdot)\) denotes the Dirac delta function. Moreover, the condition \(\widehat{\varrho}(s)\in\mathbb{SF}\) is equivalent to the condition \(s\widehat{\varrho}(s)\in\mathbb{CBF}\), see Eq. (5.4). ## 5.1.2 Statement of the problem In this work, we investigate a two-dimensional generalized diffusion equation with memory kernel of the form \(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}u(x,y,t)=u_{xx}(x,y,t)+u_{yy}(x,y,t)+F(x,y,t),(x,y,t)\in\Omega,\) (5.5) within the domain \(\Omega:=(0,1)\times(0,1)\times(0,T],\) alongside the following boundary conditions \(u(0,y,t)=0,u_x(1,y,t)-d\big(u_{xx}(1,y,t)+u_{yy}(1,y,t)\big)=0,\) (5.6) \(y\in[0,1],t\in[0,T],d=const>0,\)
\(u(x,0,t)=0,u_y(x,1,t)=0,x\in[0,1],t\in[0,T],\) (5.7) and the initial condition \(u(x,y,0)=\psi(x,y),y\in[0,1],x\in[0,1],\) (5.8) where \(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}\) is given by Eq. (5.1).

## 5.1.3 Special cases

We examine specific cases of Eq. (5.5) based on the properties of \(\varrho(t)\).

_n_**-Tempered FDE:** Assume the following power-law memory kernel

\(\varrho(t)=\sum_{\xi=1}^n\frac{P_\xi}{\Gamma(1-\beta_\xi)}e^{-pt}t^{-\beta_\xi},\)

where \(0<\beta_n<\dots<\beta_2<\beta_1<1,D_\xi>0,\xi=1,2,\dots n\), and _p\>_0 represents the truncation parameter. Applying this kernel in (5.5), we derive the corresponding _n_-tempered FDE

\(\sum_{\xi=1}^nP_\xi\mathcal{D}_t^{\beta_{\xi,p}}u(x,y,t)=u_{xx}(x,y,t)+u_{yy}(x,y,t)+F(x,y,t),\) (5.9)

where \(\mathcal{D}_t^{\beta_{\xi,p}}\) denotes the tempered fractional derivative of order \(\beta_\xi\in(0,1)\) and _p\>_0.

Now, we present few special cases of Eq. (5.9) and Eq. (5.5):

**Case-I:** Setting _p_=0 in Eq. (5.9), we obtain the following multi-term FDE

\(\sum_{\xi=1}^nP_\xi_C\mathcal{D}_t^{\beta_\xi} u(x,y,t)=u_{xx}(x,y,t)+u_{yy}(x,y,t)+F(x,y,t),\) (5.10)

where \(0<\beta_n<\dots<\beta_2<\beta_1<1,P_\xi>0,\xi=1,2,\dots n\). \(_C\mathcal{D}_t^{\beta_\xi}\) represents the CFD of order \(\beta_\xi\in(0,1)\).

**Case-II:** Take _P_<sub>1</sub>=1_,P_<sub>2</sub>=_P_<sub>3</sub>=_...=P<sub>n</sub>_=0, and _p_=0 in Eq. (5.9), the following mono-FDE is obtained

\(_C\mathcal{D}_t^{\beta_1}u(x,y,t)=u_{xx}(x,y,t)+u_{yy}(x,y,t)+F(x,y,t),\) (5.11)

where \(0<\beta_1<1\).

**Case-III:** By choosing \(\beta_1=1,P_1=1,P_2=P_3=\dots=P_n=0,\) and _p_=0 in Eq. (5.9), we derive the SDE as follows

\(u_t(x,y,t)=u_{xx}(x,y,t)+u_{yy}(x,y,t)+F(x,y,t).\) (5.12)

## 5.1.4 Mathematical formulation of the ISPs

In connection with the system (5.5)-(5.8), we explore two ISPs, defining each and addressing their solutions.

**In the first-ISP**, the source term in Eq. (5.5) depends only on spatial variables, denoted as _F(x,y,t_)=_f(x,y_). The first-ISP is to determine both _f(x,y_) and _u(x,y,t_) simultaneously for the system (5.5)-(5.8), given an additional condition

\(u(x,y,T)=g(x,y),x\in[0,1]y\in[0,1].\) (5.13)

The additional condition in the first-ISP denotes the concentration of diffusive particles at time _T_ in a diffusion process and the final temperature distribution at time _T_ in heat conduction. The solution of first-ISP, expressed as {_u(x,y,t),f(x,y_)}, is termed regular if it satisfies the system (5.5)-(5.8) and the additional condition (5.13), with the requirements: \(f(x,y)\in C([0,1]\times[0,1]);u(x,y,t)\in C(\overline{\Omega});\overline{\Omega}=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,T];\)
\(u_{xx}(\cdot,y,t)\in C^2([0,1]);u_{yy}(x,\cdot,t)\in C^2([0,1]);_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}u(x,y,\cdot)\in C([0,T]).\) **In the second-ISP**, we consider the source term in the form _F(x,y,t_)=_w(t)f(x,y,t_), where _f(x,y,t_) is given. The objective of the second-ISP is to identify both _w(t_) and _u(x,y,t_) for the system defined by Eqs. (5.5)-(5.8). To ascertain _w(t_), we impose the following integral condition \(\int_0^1\int_0^1u(x,y,t)dxdy=\mathcal{E}(t),t\in[0,T],\) (5.14) where \(\mathcal{E}(t)\in AC([0,T])\) and AC denotes the space of absolutely continuous functions. The integral-type condition serves as essential information for recovering the source term. For instance, in diffusion processes, Eq. (5.5) describes the anomalous diffusion of particles in turbulent plasma, where E(_t_) represents the total concentration of particles. Similarly, in the case of heat conduction, E(_t_) corresponds to the total heat energy in a heated plate. The regular solution of second-ISP, represented as {_u(x,y,t),w(t_)}, meets the conditions: \(u(x,y,t)\in C(\overline{\Omega});w(t)\in C([0,T]);u_{xx}(\cdot,y,t)\in C^2([0,1]);\)
\(u_{yy}(x,\cdot,t)\in C^2([0,1]);_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}u(x,y,\cdot)\in C([0,T]).\) ## 5.2 Spectral problem This section recalls the spectral analysis of the problem outlined in (5.5)-(5.8), as explored in \[71\]. Let us consider the spectral problem corresponding to (5.5)-(5.8) \(\begin{array}{ c c c } X_{xx}(x,y)+X_{yy}(x,y)+\lambda X(x,y)=0, & \\ X(0,y)=X(1,y), & \end{array}\begin{array}{ c } y\in[0,1] \\ X_x(1,y)-d\left(X_{xx}(1,y)+X_{yy}(1,y)\right)=0, & \end{array}\begin{array}{ c } y\in[0,1],d>0, \\ X(x,0)=0, & \end{array}\right\}\) (5.15) The eigenfunctions associated with this spectral problem are given by \(X_{j,k}(x,y)=2sin\left(\sqrt{\nu_j^k}x\right)sin(\mu_ky),j=0,1,2,\dots,;k=1,2,\dots,\) (5.16) with corresponding eigenvalues given by \(\lambda_{j,k}=\nu_j^k+\mu_k^2,\) where \(\mu_k=\frac{\pi}{2}(2k-1)\), and \(\nu_j^k\) denotes the roots of the characteristic equation \(tan\left(\sqrt{s}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{s}}{d(s+\mu_k^2)},\) (5.17)

listed in ascending order. The square root branch is taken on the right half-plane, ensuring \(\nu_j^k>0\) for \(j\ge 1\), with further behavior outlined as \(\mathrm{lim}_{j\rightarrow\infty}\left(\sqrt{\nu_j^k}-\pi j\right)=0\), \(\nu_j^k>0\) if \(d\mu_k^2<1\), \(\nu_0^k<0\) if \(d\mu_k^2>1\), and \(\nu_0^k=0\) if \(d\mu_k^2=1\). In the latter case, the eigenfunction takes the form \(X_{0,k}(x,y)=2x\mathrm{sin}(\mu_ky).\) It is verified that the system _Yj,k(x,y),j_=1,2_,...;k_=1,2_,..._, defined as \(Y_{j,k}(x,y)=\frac{2}{\chi_{j,k}}\left[\mathrm{sin}\left(\sqrt{\nu_j^k}x\right)-\frac{\mathrm{sin}\left(\sqrt{\nu_j^k}\right)}{\mathrm{sin}\left(\sqrt{\nu_0^k}\right)}\mathrm{sin}\left(\sqrt{\nu_0^k}x\right)\right]\mathrm{sin}(\mu_ky),\) is bi-orthogonal in \(L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))\) to the system _Xj,k(x,y),j,k_=1,2_,..._. The denominator \(\chi_{j,k}\) for _Yj,k(x,y_) is given by \(\chi_{j,k}=1+\frac{d\mathrm{sin}^2\left(\sqrt{\nu_j^k}\right)}{\sqrt{\nu_j^k}}\left(\sqrt{\nu_j^k}-\frac{\mu_k^2}{\sqrt{\nu_j^k}}\right)\)
\(=d\mathrm{sin}^2\left(\sqrt{\nu_j^k}\right)+\int_0^1\mathrm{sin}^2\left(\sqrt{\nu_j^k}x\right)dx.\) (5.18) After performing the integral and using Eq. (5.17), we get \(\sqrt{\nu_j^k}=\pi j+\frac{\pi k}{d\gamma_{j,k}}+\sigma_j^k,\) (5.19) where \(\gamma_{j,k}=(\pi j)^2+\mu_k^2\), and \(|\sigma_k^j|\le A\gamma_{j,k}^{-\frac{3}{2}}\), for a constant _A\>_0.
The following theorem applies to the basis property of the eigenfunctions. **Theorem 5.1** _\[71\] The system of functions_ {_Xj,k(x,y_)}_, with j_=1,2_,...;k_=1,2_,..., form a Riesz basis in_ \(L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))\). **Lemma 5.1** _Consider_ \(\phi(x,y)\in C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])\) _that meets the following conditions_ \(\begin{array}{ c c c c c } \phi(x,0)=0, & \phi(0,y)=0, & \phi(1,y)=0 & \phi_y(x,1)=0, & \phi_x(0,y)=0, \\ \phi_x(1,y)=0, & \phi_{xx}(x,0)=0, & \phi_{xx}(0,y)=0, & \phi_{xx}(1,y)=0, \\ \phi_{xyx}(1,y)=0, & \int_0^1\phi(x,y)\mathrm{sin}\left(\sqrt{\nu_0^j}x\right)dx=0, & y\in[0,1], & j=1,2,\cdots \end{array}\right.\) (5.20) _then the following inequalities_ \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty\lambda_{j,k}|\phi_{j,k}|\le C\|\phi^{(iv)}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])},\) (5.21) \(|\phi_{j,k}|\le\frac{1}{\nu_k^j\mu_j^2}\|\phi_{xyxy}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}\) (5.22) _hold, where_ \(\phi_{j,k}:=\frac{2}{\chi_{j,k}}\int_0^1\int_0^1\phi(x,y)Y_{j,k}(x,y)dydx.\)

**Proof:** The inequality (5.21) is proved in \[69\]. To prove the inequality (5.22), consider<tbc>

\(\phi_{j,k}=\langle\phi(x,y),Y_{j,k}(x,y)\rangle=\frac{2}{\chi_{j,k}}\int_0^1\int_0^1\phi(x,y)Y_{j,k}(x,y)dxdy.\)

<tbc>Using integration by parts w.r.t _x_ followed by _y_, we obtain<tbc>

\(|\phi_{j,k}|\le\frac{2}{\chi_{j,k}\sqrt{\nu_j^k}\mu_k}\int_0^1\int_0^1\phi_{xy}(x,y)Y_{j,k}(x,y)dydx.\)

<tbc>Similarly, by integrating by parts twice w.r.t _x_ and once w.r.t _y_, we find<tbc>

\(|\phi_{j,k}|\le\frac{2}{\chi_{j,k}\nu_j^k\mu_k^2}\int_0^1\int_0^1\phi_{xyxy}(x,y)Y_{j,k}(x,y)dydx.\)

<tbc>Using Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we deduce

\(|\phi_{j,k}|\le\frac{1}{\nu_j^k\mu_k^2}\|\phi_{xyxy}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])},\)

where \(\|Y_{j,k}(x,y)\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}\le 1\).

## 5.3 First-ISP

The aim of this section is to recover a space-dependent source term, namely _F(x,y,t_)=_f(x,y_) and _u(x,y,t_), from the systems (5.5)-(5.8) and (5.13).

### 5.3.1 Series solution construction for first-ISP

The series solution for first-ISP in relation to the system defined by Eqs. (5.5)-(5.8) and (5.13) can be written as follows

\(u(x,y,t)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty U_{j,k}(t)X_{j,k}(x,y),\) (5.23)

and

\(f(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty f_{j,k}X_{j,k}(x,y),\) (5.24)

where _U<sub>j,k</sub>(t_) and _f<sub>j,k</sub>_, for \(j,k=1,2,\cdots\) , are the unknowns, governed by the differential equation system

\(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}U_{j,k}(t)=-\lambda_{j,k}U_{j,k}(t)+f_{j,k}.\) (5.25)

Taking into account the Laplace transform of (5.25) and using the initial condition in (5.8), we obtain

\(U_{j,k}(t)=\psi_{j,k}\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(t)+f_{j,k}\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t),\) (5.26)

where \(\psi_{j,k}=\left\langle\psi(x,y),Y_{j,k}(x,y)\right\rangle:=\int_0^1\int_0^1\psi(x,y)Y_{j,k}(x,y)dxdy.\) The functions **W**_j,k(t_) and **Z**_j,k(t_) are defined as follows \(\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(t)=1-\lambda_{j,k}\int_0^t\mathbf{V}_{j,k}(\tau)d\tau\text{and}\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t)=\int_0^t\mathbf{V}_{j,k}(\tau)d\tau,\) (5.27) where \(\mathbf{V}_{j,k}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{s\widehat{\varrho}(s)+\lambda_{j,k}}\right),\) (5.28) and **V**_j,k(t_) is the impulse-response function. From Lemma 4.1 in \[13\], we establish that **V**_j,k(t_) is a completely monotone function, meaning that its Laplace transform \(\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{j,k}(s)\) is a Stieltjes function.
In the Laplace domain, the representations of **W**_j,k(t_) and **Z**_j,k(t_) are given as follows \(\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{j,k}(s)=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{\lambda_{j,k}}{s(s\widehat{\varrho}(s)+\lambda_{j,k})},\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{j,k}(s)=\frac{1}{s(s\widehat{\varrho}(s)+\lambda_{j,k})}.\big\}\) (5.29) The additional condition (5.13) provides the following expression for _fj,k_ \(f_{j,k}=\frac{1}{\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(T)}\left(g_{j,k}-\psi_{j,k}\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(T)\right),\) (5.30) where \(g_{j,k}=\left\langle g(x,y),Y_{j,k}(x,y)\right\rangle\).
By plugging the value of _fj,k_ in Eq. (5.26), we obtain \(U_{j,k}(t)=\psi_{j,k}\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(t)+\frac{\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t)}{\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(T)}\big(g_{j,k}-\psi_{j,k}\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(T)\big).\) (5.31) Now, we examine specific cases of Eqs. (5.26) and (5.30) based on the behavior of \(\varrho(t)\).
To analyze the Laplace transform of the power-law memory kernel, given by \(\widehat{\varrho}(s)=\sum_{\xi=1}^n\frac{P_\xi}{(s+p)^{1-\beta_\xi}}\) and apply it in Eq. (5.29), we obtain the following estimates \(\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(t)=\frac{1}{P_1}-\frac{\lambda_{j,k}}{D_1}\int_0^te^{-p\tau}\tau^{\beta_1-1}E_{\bar{\beta},\beta_1}(\cdots\lambda\tau\cdots)d\tau\left.\begin{array}{ c } =\frac{1}{P_1}e^{-pt}E_{\bar{\beta},1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{t}\cdots), \\ \mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t)=\frac{1}{P_1}\int_0^te^{-p\tau}\tau^{\beta_1-1}E_{\bar{\beta},\beta_1}(\cdots\lambda\tau\cdots)d\tau \\ =\frac{1}{P_1}e^{-pt}t^{\beta_1}E_{\bar{\beta},\beta_1+1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{t}\cdots), \end{array}\right\},\) (5.32) where \(E_{\bar{\beta},\beta_1}(\cdot)\) denotes the multinomial (generalized) Mittag–Leffler function, with parameters \(\bar{\beta}=(\beta_1-\beta_n,\dots,\beta_1-\beta_2,\beta_1),\)

and argument vector<tbc>

\((\cdots\lambda\mathbf{t}\cdots)=\left(-\frac{P_n}{P_1}t^{\beta_1-\beta_n},\dots,-\frac{P_2}{P_1}t^{\beta_1-\beta_2},-\frac{\lambda_{j,k}}{P_1}t^{\beta_1}\right).\)

<tbc>Plugging the values of Eq. (5.32) into Eq. (5.26), we infer the expression of _U<sub>j,k</sub>(t_) for the _n_-tempered FDE (5.9). Its precise formulation is given by

\(U_{j,k}(t)=\frac{1}{P_1}\left(\psi_{j,k}e^{-pt}E_{\bar{\beta},1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{t}\cdots)+f_{j,k}e^{-pt}t^{\beta_1}E_{\bar{\beta},\beta_1+1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{t}\cdots)\right),\) (5.33)

where<tbc>

\(f_{j,k}=\frac{P_1g_{j,k}-\psi_{j,k}e^{-pt}E_{\bar{\beta},1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{T}\cdots)}{e^{-pt}T^{\beta_1}E_{\bar{\beta},\beta_1+1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{T}\cdots)}.\) (5.34)

<tbc>\(\bullet\) Substituting _p_=0 in Eqs. (5.33) and (5.34), the following expression of _U<sub>j,k</sub>(t_) for the solution of multi-term FDE (5.10) is obtained<tbc>

\(U_{j,k}(t)=\frac{1}{P_1}\big(\psi_{j,k}E_{\bar{\beta},1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{t}\cdots)+f_{j,k}t^{\beta_1}E_{\bar{\beta},\beta_1+1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{t}\cdots)\big),\)

<tbc>where<tbc>

\(f_{j,k}=\frac{P_1g_{j,k}-\psi_{j,k}E_{\bar{\beta},1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{T}\cdots)}{T^{\beta_1}E_{\bar{\beta},\beta_1+1}(\cdots\lambda\mathbf{T}\cdots)}.\)

<tbc>\(\bullet\) By setting _p_=0_,P_<sub>1</sub>=1, and _P_<sub>2</sub>=_P_<sub>3</sub>=_...=P<sub>n</sub>_=0 in Eqs. (5.33) and (5.34), we get the following expression for _U<sub>j,k</sub>(t_), which provides a solution for a mono-FDE (5.11)<tbc>

\(U_{j,k}(t)=\psi_{j,k}E_{\beta_1,1}(-\lambda_{j,k}t^{\beta_1})+f_{j,k}t^{\beta_1}E_{\beta_1,\beta_1+1}(-\lambda_{j,k}t^{\beta_1}),\)

<tbc>where<tbc>

\(f_{j,k}=\frac{1}{T^{\beta_1}E_{\beta_1,\beta_1+1}(-\lambda_{j,k}T^{\beta_1})}\left(g_{j,k}-\psi_{j,k}E_{\beta_1,1}(-\lambda_{j,k}T^{\beta_1})\right).\)

<tbc>\(\bullet\) Taking \(\beta_1=1,p=0,P_1=1\), and _P_<sub>2</sub>=_P_<sub>3</sub>=_...=P<sub>n</sub>_=0 in Eqs. (5.33) and (5.34), the expression for _U<sub>j,k</sub>(t_) in the solution of the SDE (5.12) is given by

\(U_{j,k}(t)=\psi_{j,k}\big(1-\lambda_{j,k}\int_0^te^{-\lambda_{j,k}\zeta} d\zeta\big)+f_{j,k}\int_0^te^{-\lambda_{j,k}\zeta} d\zeta,\)

where

\(f_{j,k}=\frac{g_{j,k}-\psi_{j,k}\big(1-\lambda_{j,k}\int_0^te^{-\lambda_{j,k}\zeta} d\zeta\big)}{\int_0^te^{-\lambda_{j,k}\zeta} d\zeta}.\)

## 5.3.2 Ill-posedness of first-ISP

In this subsection, we see the ill-posedness of first-ISP. Reviewing some relevant results will be the first step before moving forward.

**Lemma 5.2** _\[60\] Given that_ \(\lambda_{j,k}>0\)_, the following holds:_

\(\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(t)=-\lambda_{j,k}\mathbf{V}_{j,k}(t).\) (5.35)

_Moreover, for T\>_0_, we have the following bound:_

\(\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t)=\int_0^T\mathbf{V}_{j,k}(\zeta)d\zeta\le\frac{1}{\lambda_{j,k}}.\) (5.36)

Consider the following example as a way to demonstrate the ill-posedness of first-ISP. The final and initial data are set as follows

\(\tilde{g}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{j,k}}}Y_{j,k}(x,y),\text{and}\tilde{\psi}(x,y)=0,\)

where \(j,k\in\mathbb{N}\). With these choices, the source term becomes

\(\tilde{f}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{j,k}}\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(T)}X_{j,k}(x,y).\) (5.37)

Now, by taking an alternative final data and the initial data

\(g(x,y)=0,\text{and}\psi(x,y)=0,\)

then, the source term becomes _f(x,y_)=0. We then calculate the _L_<sup>2</sup>-norm between the two final data \(\tilde{g}\) and _g_

\(\|\tilde{g}-g\|_{L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))}=\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{j,k}}}X_{j,k}(x,y)\right\|_{L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))}.\)

Due to (5.19), the equality

\(\|\tilde{g}-g\|_{L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{j,k}}}\)

is obtained, leading to the limit relation

\(lim_{j,k\rightarrow+\infty}\|\tilde{g}-g\|_{L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))}=lim_{j,k\rightarrow+\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{j,k}}}=0.\) (5.38)

To compute the error in the _L_<sup>2</sup>-norm between the two source terms \(\tilde{f}\) and _f_, we have

\(\|\tilde{f}-f\|_{L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))}=\left\|\frac{X_{j,k}(x,y)}{\sqrt{\lambda_{j,k}}\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(T)}\right\|_{L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{j,k}}\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(T)}.\)

Using the estimate from Lemma 5.2, we arrive at

\(\|\tilde{f}-f\|_{L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))}\ge\sqrt{\lambda_{j,k}}.\)

This leads to

\(lim_{j,k\rightarrow+\infty}\|\tilde{f}-f\|_{L^2((0,1)\times(0,1))}>lim_{j,k\rightarrow+\infty}\sqrt{\lambda_{j,k}}=+\infty.\) (5.39)

From Eqs. (5.38) and (5.39), we conclude that first-ISP is ill-posed.

## 5.3.3 The main results of first-ISP

In this subsection, we outline the existence and the uniqueness of the solution of the first-ISP. To demonstrate the regularity of solutions for both first-ISP and second- ISP, we present the following lemma:

**Lemma 5.3** _[13] Consider_ **Z**_<sub>j,k</sub>(t_) _as defined by Eq. (5.27), which is continuous on_ \([0,\infty)\)_, vanish at t_=0_, positive, and nondecreasing on_ R<sub>+</sub>_. For any t,T\>_0_, the following inequalities_

(_a)_ \(\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t)\le\frac{1}{\lambda_{j,k}}\),<tbc>

_(b)_ \(\frac{1}{\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t)}\le C_0\lambda_{j,k}\),<tbc>

<tbc>_hold. where C_<sub>0</sub>=_C_<sub>0</sub>(_T)\>_0.

\(\bullet\) From the expression for **W**_<sub>j,k</sub>(t_) in Eq. (5.27), we can written as<tbc>

\(\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(t)=1-\lambda_{j,k}\int_0^t\mathbf{V}_{j,k}(\zeta)d\zeta.\)

<tbc>The form of **V**_<sub>j,k</sub>(t_) here aligns with the expression provided in [13] (Lemma 4.1, Eq. (42)). Given this, the estimate for **V**_<sub>j,k</sub>(t_) can be written as

\(0<c_0\le\lambda_{j,k}\int_0^t\mathbf{V}_{j,k}(\zeta)d\zeta<1,\) (5.40)

based on the inequalities in (5.40), we deduce that

\(\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(t)\le C_1,\) (5.41)

where _c_<sub>0</sub> and _C_<sub>1</sub> are positive constants.

**Theorem 5.2** _Suppose that_ \(\psi(y,x)\) _and g(y,x_) _are given functions in_ \(C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])\) _and meet the conditions given in_ (5.20)_. Then, a regular solution exists for first-ISP associated with the system_ (5.5)-(5.8) _and_ (5.13).

**Proof:** This theorem is proved in two parts.

**Part-I:** To establish the existence of a solution for first-ISP, we need to demonstrate the continuity of the associated series<tbc>

\(f(x,y),u(x,y,t),u_{xx}(x,y,t),u_{yy}(x,y,t),\text{and}_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}u(x,y,t).\)

<tbc>First, we focus on verifying the continuity of _f(x,y_). Using Lemma 5.3, along with estimate (5.41) and Eq. (5.30), we obtain<tbc>

\(|f_{j,k}|\le C_0\lambda_{j,k}(|g_{j,k}|-C_1|\psi_{j,k}|).\)

<tbc>By invoking Lemma 5.1, we deduce

\(|f_{j,k}|\le C_0C\big(\|g^{(iv)}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}-C_1\|\psi^{(iv)}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}\big)\) (5.42)

From inequality (5.42), we deduce that the series of _f(x,y_) as given by Eq. (5.24) is bounded. Thus, the continuity of _f(x,y_) is established by the WMT.
Now, our goal is to establish the continuity of _u(x,y,t_). By applying Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.1, and Eq. (5.31), we find that \(|U_{j,k}(t)|\le\frac{C}{\lambda_{j,k}}\big(K\|\psi^{(iv)}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}+C_0\|g^{(iv)}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}\big),\) (5.43) where _K=C_1(1-_C_0) is a positive constant. Based on Eq. (5.43), we deduce that the series of _u(x,y,t_) in Eq. (5.23) is bounded above. Hence, the continuity of _u(x,y,t_) follows by applying the WMT.
Our next task is to demonstrate the continuity of _uxx(x,y,t_). To achieve this, we differentiate each term of the series solution provided in Eq. (5.23) w.r.t _x_ \(u_{xx}(x,y,t)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty U_{j,k}(t)X_{xx,j,k}(x,y),\) (5.44) where \(X_{xx,j,k}(x,y)=-\nu_j^kX_{j,k}(x,y).\) Indeed, we can have \(|X_{j,k}(x,y)|<1,\) which implies \(\big|X_{xx,j,k}(x,y)\big|\le\nu_j^k.\) (5.45) Based on Lemma 5.1, Eq. (5.43), and inequality (5.45), we derive the following expression \(u_{xx}(x,y,t)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{C}{\mu_k^2\lambda_{j,k}}\big(K\|\psi^{(iv)}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}+C_0\|g^{(iv)}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}\big).\) (5.46) Eq. (5.46) demonstrates that the series form of _uxx(x,y,t_) is bounded above. Consequently, by WMT, _uxx(x,y,t_) is continuous.
Next, we establish the continuity of _uyy(x,y,t_). By applying term-by-term differentiation w.r.t _y_ on the series solution from Eq. (5.23), we obtain \(u_{yy}(x,y,t)=-\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty\mu_k^2U_{j,k}(t)X_{j,k}(x,y).\) (5.47) Using Lemma 5.1 and Eq. (5.43), we obtain \(u_{yy}(x,y,t)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{C}{\nu_j^k\lambda_{j,k}}\big(K\|\psi^{(iv)}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}+C_0\|g^{(iv)}\|_{C^4([0,1]\times[0,1])}\big).\) (5.48) Thus, _uyy(x,y,t_), as given in Eq. (5.48), is also bounded above, ensuring its continuity by WMT.

In the similar way, we establish the continuity of \(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}u(x,y,t)\). For the continuity of \(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}u(x,y,t)\), using Eq. (5.23), we have \(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}u(x,y,t)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty_G\mathcal{D}_{0+,t}^{(\varrho)}U_{j,k}(t)X_{j,k}(x,y).\) By virtue of Eq. (5.25), we obtain \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}U_{j,k}(t)X_{j,k}(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty\big(-\lambda_{j,k}U_{j,k}(t)+f_{j,k}\big)X_{j,k}(x,y)\)
\(=-\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty\lambda_{j,k}U_{j,k}(t)X_{j,k}(x,y)+f(x,y).\) Using Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.1 and Eq. (5.43), we can prove the continuity of the series, i.e., \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty\lambda_{j,k}U_{j,k}(t)X_{j,k}(x,y).\) Furthermore, we have discussed already the continuity of _f(x,y_). Hence, we can say that \(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}u(x,y,t)\) is a continuous function due to WMT. **Part-II:** Assume \(\{_{(1)}u(x,y,t),_{(1)}f(x,y)\}\text{and}\{_{(2)}u(x,y,t),_{(2)}f(x,y)\}\) are two regular solution sets of first-ISP. Suppose that for some \(x_0,y_0\in(0,1)\times(0,1)\), we have (1)_u(x_0_,y_0_,t_)=(2)_u(x_0_,y_0_,t_). Then, it follows that \(_{(1)}u(x,y,t)=_{(2)}u(x,y,t),(x,y,t)\in\Omega,\) and similarly \(_{(1)}f(x,y)=_{(2)}f(x,y),\forall x,y\in(0,1)\times(0,1).\) To prove the uniqueness for the solution of first-ISP, let’s consider the following expressions for (1)_Uj,k(t_) and (2)_Uj,k(t_) \(_{(1)}U_{j,k}(t)=\int_0^1\int_0^1_{(1)}u(x,y,t)X_{j,k}(x,y)dxdy,\) (5.49) \(_{(2)}U_{j,k}(t)=\int_0^1\int_0^1_{(2)}u(x,y,t)X_{j,k}(x,y)dxdy.\) (5.50) Applying \(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}\) to both sides of Eq. (5.50) and using Eq. (5.5), along with the initial condition (5.8), yields \(_{(2)}U_{j,k}(t)=\psi_{j,k}\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(t)+_{(2)}f_{j,k}\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t).\) Similarly, an expression for (2)_Uj,k(t_) is obtained. \(_{(1)}U_{j,k}(t)=\psi_{j,k}\mathbf{W}_{j,k}(t)+_{(1)}f_{j,k}\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t).\)

Since <sub>(1)</sub>_u(x_<sub>0</sub>_,y_<sub>0</sub>_,t_)=<sub>(2)</sub>_u(x_<sub>0</sub>_,y_<sub>0</sub>_,t_) for some \(x_0,y_0\in(0,1)\times(0,1)\), it follows that<tbc>

\(_{(1)}U_{j,k}(t)=_{(2)}U_{j,k}(t),\)

<tbc>and therefore<tbc>

\(_{(1)}f_{j,k}\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t)=_{(2)}f_{j,k}\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t),\Rightarrow(_{(1)}f_{j,k}-_{(2)}f_{j,k})\mathbf{Z}_{j,k}(t)=0.\)

<tbc>Applying the Laplace transform, we get

\(\frac{_{(1)}f_{j,k}-_{(2)}f_{j,k}}{s(s\widehat{\varrho}(s)+\lambda_{j,k})}=0,Res>0,\Rightarrow\frac{_{(1)}f_{j,k}-_{(2)}f_{j,k}}{\Delta+\lambda_{j,k}}=0,\) (5.51)

where \(\Delta=s\widehat{\varrho}(s)\).

By selecting the disk for _j_=1_,k_=1 such that \(\lambda_{1,1}\) lies within it, and applying the Cauchy Integral Theorem to Eq. (5.51), we obtain<tbc>

\(_{(1)}f_{1,1}=_{(2)}f_{1,1}.\)

<tbc>Similarly, by considering different disks for \(j,k=2,3,\cdots\) , we find that<tbc>

\(_{(1)}f_{j,k}=_{(2)}f_{j,k}.\)

<tbc>Therefore, we conclude that

\(_{(1)}f(x,y)=_{(2)}f(x,y).\)

## 5.4 Second-ISP

This section examines the second-ISP for the system described by Eqs. (5.5)-(5.8) and (5.14), incorporating the source term _F(x,y,t_)=_w(t)f(x,y,t_). We will discuss how to recover _w(t_) along with _u(x,y,t_), given the additional condition specified by (5.14).

### 5.4.1 Series solution construction for second-ISP

The solution to second-ISP for the system given by Eqs. (5.5)-(5.8) and (5.14) can be expressed as

\(u(x,y,t)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty U_{j,k}(t)X_{j,k}(x,y),\) (5.52)

Here, _U<sub>j,k</sub>(t_) for \(j,k\in\mathbf{N}\) are unknown that satisfy the following differential equation

\(_G\mathcal{D}_t^{(\varrho)}U_{j,k}(t)=-\lambda_{j,k}U_{j,k}(t)+w(t)f_{j,k}(t),\) (5.53)

Taking the Laplace transform of Eq. (5.53) and Applying the initial condition provided in (5.8), we derive<tbc>
