\(u(x,y,t)=2tsin\left(\sqrt{\nu_1^1}x\right)sin(\mu_1y),\) with \(w(t)=t^{(1-\beta_1)}.\) The analytical results presented in this chapter establish a rigorous foundation for ISPs in a two-dimensional generalized diffusion equation. We have shown that these problems are severely ill-posed in the Hadamard sense, requiring regularization to restore stability. The series representations derived here, based on bi-orthogonal systems of eigenfunctions, provide explicit formulas for the solutions and highlight the challenges that arise when attempting to reconstruct unknown source coefficients from noisy observational data. In the following chapters, we shift our focus from the analytical treatment of ISPs to their numerical solution. The regularized formulations of these ISPs will be discretized using finite difference schemes, leading to large structured linear systems of the all-at-once type. The GLT framework, developed in Part I, will then become essential for understanding the spectral behavior of these systems and for designing efficient preconditioners that accelerate the convergence of Krylov subspace methods. In particular, Chapters 6 and 7 address the numerical solution of ISPs for space-time FDEs, building upon the regularization and analytical techniques introduced in this chapter.

## Chapter 6 ### Krylov preconditioning for inverse problems in space-time fractional diffusion equations Having introduced in the previous chapters the analytical foundations of fractional operators, the spectral framework of matrix sequences, and the theory of GLT sequences, we now turn to the numerical solution of an IP for a space-time FDE. This chapter is based on the work \[66\], with additional details, numerical experiments, and reformulations included for completeness of the thesis presentation. This chapter investigates the reconstruction of a space-dependent source term in a model that incorporates a tempered fractional derivative in time and a Caputo fractional derivative in space, both of order in (0,1). Such equations are particularly valuable for modeling complex transport phenomena where diffusion transitions from anomalous to normal behavior over time, a feature that cannot be captured by standard fractional or classical models \[110, 112\].
The inverse problem is inherently ill-posed in the Hadamard sense, as small perturbations in the final-time data can lead to large errors in the recovered source term. To address this instability, we apply a quasi-boundary value regularization method, which reformulates the problem into a well-posed form \[29, 48\]. The finite difference discretization of the regularized system leads to a large two-by-two block linear system. We conduct a detailed spectral analysis of the associated matrix sequences using the GLT framework, which provides a rigorous description of their asymptotic spectral behavior despite the presence of the variable coefficient that spoils the pure Toeplitz structure \[41, 42\]. Based on this analysis, we design an efficient preconditioner for the GMRES method. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of the proposed preconditioning strategy in reducing iteration counts and computational cost.
The aim of this work is to numerically solve the IP of identifying the source term _f(x_) in the space-time FDE \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } ^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho} u(x,t)+a(x)^C\mathcal{D}_x^\eta u(x,t)=q(t)f(x), & x\in(0,1),t\in(0,T), \\ u(0,t)=u(1,t)=0, & t\in(0,T), \\ u(x,0)=\varphi(x), & x\in(0,1), \\ u(x,T)=\phi(x), & x\in(0,1), \end{array}\right.\) (6.1) where _T\>_0 is the final time, _a(x_) is a continuous a.e. variable coefficient such that \(a(x)\neq 0\), _q(t_) is a given function, \(\varphi(x)\) is the initial condition, and \(\phi(x)\) is the final time data. Moreover, \(^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho}\) represents the tempered fractional derivative in the time variable of order \(\xi\in(0,1)\), defined for \(\rho>0\) as follows \(^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho} u(x,t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\xi)}\int_0^te^{-\rho(t-\tau)}(t-\tau)^{-\xi}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}u(x,\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau,\) while \(^C\mathcal{D}_x^\eta\) denotes the Caputo fractional derivative in the space variable of order

\(\eta\in(0,1)\), defined as \(^C\mathcal{D}_x^\eta u(x,t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\eta)}\int_0^x(x-\zeta)^{-\eta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\zeta}u(\zeta,t)\mathrm{d}\zeta.\) To address the ill-posedness in the sense of Hadamard of the inverse problem (6.1), we apply the so-called nonlocal or quasi-boundary value method, transforming it into a well-posed formulation. First, we observe that the measurement of the final time data is inevitably contaminated by noise, therefore we denote the noisy data as \(\phi_\varepsilon(x)\), where \(\varepsilon>0\) is the noise level, and assume that \(\|\phi-\phi_\varepsilon\|_{L^2}\le\varepsilon,\) where \(\|\cdot\|_{L^2}\) is the _L_2 norm on (0,1). Applying the quasi-boundary value method leads to the following well-posed regularized problem \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } ^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho} u(x,t)+a(x)^C\mathcal{D}_x^\eta u(x,t)=q(t)f_{\varepsilon,\lambda}(x), & x\in(0,1),t\in(0,T), \\ u(0,t)=u(1,t)=0, & t\in(0,T), \\ u(x,0)=\varphi(x), & x\in(0,1), \\ u(x,T)=\phi_\varepsilon(x)-\lambda a(x)^C\mathcal{D}_x^\eta f_{\varepsilon,\lambda}(x), & x\in(0,1), \end{array}\right.\) (6.2) where \(\lambda>0\) is a regularization parameter, \(f_{\varepsilon,\lambda}\) approximates _f(x_) and the solution _u(x,t_) represents an approximation of the solution of the original problem (6.1). The remainder of this chapter is organized as follows. Section 6.1 provides the discretization of the regularized problem by using a finite difference scheme in space and time and presents the resulting linear system, emphasizing the structural features of the resulting matrices. In Section 6.2 the coefficient matrix sequence is studied via GLT tools, while in Section 6.3 the same type of analysis is performed for the preconditioned matrix sequences. In Section 6.4, numerical experiments are conducted to assess the effectiveness of the proposed preconditioner. ## 6.1 Discretization and matrix structures We now present the discretization of the regularized problem (6.2), using a finite difference scheme [130]. Then we describe with care the global structure of the arising coefficient matrix. Let _n_ and _m_ be positive integers and denote the corresponding spatial and temporal meshes as \(x_i=i\Delta x,\Delta x=\frac{1}{n+1},i=0,1,\dots,n,\) (6.3) \(t_j=j\Delta t,\Delta t=\frac{T}{m},j=0,1,\dots,m.\) (6.4) To deal with the tempered fractional derivative, we use the _L_1 formula: \(^T\mathcal{D}_{L1}^{\xi,\rho} u(x,t_j)=\frac{(\Delta t)^{-\xi}}{\Gamma(2-\xi)}\big[b_0u(x,t_j)-\sum_{l=1}^{j-1}\left(b_{j-l-1}-b_{j-l}\right)e^{\rho(t_l-t_j)}u(x,t_l)\)
\(-b_{j-1}e^{\rho(t_0-t_j)}u(x,t_0)\big],\)

in which \(b_l=(l+1)^{1-\xi}-l^{1-\xi},l=0,1,\dots\) Denoting \(\alpha_m:=(\Delta t)^\xi\Gamma(2-\xi)=\left(\frac{T}{m}\right)^\xi\Gamma(2-\xi)\) and \(\gamma_0:=b_0,\gamma_l:=b_l-b_{l-1}=(l+1)^{1-\xi}-2l^{1-\xi}+(l-1)^{1-\xi},l=1,\dots,m-1,\) (6.5) and using \(t_j=j\Delta t\), the _L_1 approximation of the tempered fractional derivative is expressed as \(^T\mathcal{D}_{L1}^{\xi,\rho} u(x,t_j)=\frac{1}{\alpha_m}\left[\gamma_0u(x,t_j)+\sum_{l=1}^{j-1}\gamma_{j-l}e^{-(j-l)\rho\Delta t}u(x,t_l)-b_{j-1}e^{-j\rho\Delta t}u(x,t_0)\right].\) (6.6) The following error estimate holds, see \[140, page 10\]. Assuming that \(u(\cdot,t)\in C^2(0,T)\). For \(t_j\in(0,T)\), we have \(\left|^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho} u(x,t)|_{t=t_j}-^T\mathcal{D}_{L1}^{\xi,\rho} u(x,t_j)\right|\le\chi_\xi\big[\rho^2max_{t_0\le t\le t_j}|u(x,t)|+2\rho max_{t_0\le t\le t_j}|u_t(x,t)|\)
\(+\Delta t^{2-\xi} max_{t_0\le t\le t_j}|u_{tt}(x,t)|\big],\) where _ut_ and _utt_ denote the first and second partial derivative of _u_ with respect to _t_, and \(\chi_\xi:=\frac{1}{2\Gamma(1-\xi)}\left[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\xi}{(1-\xi)(2-\xi)}\right].\) To discretize the CFD, we exploit the spatial counterpart of the _L_1 formula: \(^C\mathcal{D}_{L1}^\eta u(x_i,t)=\frac{1}{\beta_n}\left[\delta_0u(x_i,t)+\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}\delta_{i-k}u(x_k,t)-d_{i-1}u(x_0,t)\right],\) (6.7) where \(\beta_n:=(\Delta x)^\eta\Gamma(2-\eta)=\left(\frac{1}{n+1}\right)^\eta\Gamma(2-\eta)\) and \(d_k:=(k+1)^{1-\eta}-k^{1-\eta},k=0,1,\dots\delta_0:=d_0,\delta_k:=d_k-d_{k-1}=(k+1)^{1-\eta}-2k^{1-\eta}+(k-1)^{1-\eta},k=1,\dots,n-1.\) (6.8) The corresponding error estimate takes the form, see \[130, page 32\]. Assume that \(u(x,\cdot)\in C^2(0,1)\). For \(x_i\in(0,1)\), we have \(\left|^C\mathcal{D}_x^\eta u(x,t)|_{x=x_i}-^C\mathcal{D}_{L1}^\eta u(x_i,t)\right|\le\chi_\eta\Delta x^{2-\eta} max_{0\le x\le x_i}|u_{xx}(x,t)|,\)

where _uxx_ denote the second partial derivative of _u_ with respect to _x_ and \(\chi_\eta:=\frac{1}{2\Gamma(1-\eta)}\left[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\eta}{(1-\eta)(2-\eta)}\right].\) Substituting the fractional derivatives in problem (6.2) with their respective _L_1 approximations (6.6) and (6.7), and omitting the truncation errors, the finite difference scheme is constructed as follows: in (_xi,tj_) for _i_=1_,...,n_ and _j_=1_,...,m_ we have \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c } \frac{1}{\alpha_m}\left[\gamma_0u_i^{(j)}+\sum_{l=1}^{j-1}\gamma_{j-l}e^{-(j-l)\rho\Delta t}u_i^{(l)}-b_{j-1}e^{-j\rho\Delta t}u_i^{(0)}\right] \\ +\frac{a_i}{\beta_n}\left[\delta_0u_i^{(j)}+\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}\delta_{i-k}u_k^{(j)}-d_{i-1}u_0^{(j)}\right]=q^{(j)}f_i, \\ u_0^{(j)}=u_{n+1}^{(j)}=0, \\ u_i^{(0)}=\varphi_i, \\ u_i^{(m)}=\phi_{\varepsilon,i}-\lambda\frac{a_i}{\beta_n}\left[\delta_0f_i+\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}\delta_{i-k}f_k-d_{i-1}f_0\right], \end{array}\right.\) where \(u_i^{(j)}:=u(x_i,t_j),a_i:=a(x_i),f_i:=f_{\varepsilon,\lambda}(x_i),\)

**Remark 6.1** _We remark that the tempered fractional derivative is discretized by the L_1 _finite difference scheme. Under the regularity assumption_ \(u(\cdot,t)\in C^2(0,T)\)_, the L_1 _approximation satisfies an error estimate of order_ \(O(\Delta t^{2-\xi})\)_, while the spatial L_1_- type discretization of the CFD yields an error of order_ \(O(\Delta x^{2-\eta})\)_. ## 6.2 GLT analysis This section is devoted to the spectral analysis of the coefficient matrix sequence via the GLT theory, in order to gather information on the asymptotic behavior of the matrices. We start with the sequence associated with the space block _Gn_, then proceed to the time block _Um_, and conclude with the overall coefficient matrix sequence. **Theorem 6.1** _There exists a continuous_ \(2\pi\)_-periodic function_ \(g_\eta\) _such that_ \(\{B_n\}_n\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} g_\eta(\theta),\theta\in[-\pi,\pi].\) _Moreover,_ \(\{B_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\delta_0.\) **Proof:** To demonstrate that {_Bn}n_ is a GLT sequence, we claim that _Bn_ is a Toeplitz matrix generated by a measurable function, i.e., there exists \(g_\eta\) such that \(B_n=T_n(g_\eta)\) for all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). The idea is simple: we prove that the series \(g_\eta(\theta):=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\delta_ke^{\mathrm{i}k\theta},\) where the coefficients \(\delta_k\) are given by (6.8), belongs to the Wiener class, so that \(g_\eta\) is well defined, continuous and \(2\pi\)-periodic, and the corresponding Toeplitz matrix sequence is precisely {_Bn}n_ by definition. Let us consider the auxiliary function \(\psi_\eta(x):=x^{1-\eta}\). From (6.3), for any index _k_ we have _k_=(_n_+1)_xk_. Hence, \(\delta_k=(k+1)^{1-\eta}-2k^{1-\eta}+(k-1)^{1-\eta}\)
\(=(n+1)^{1-\eta}\big[x_{k+1}^{1-\eta}-2x_k^{1-\eta}+x_{k-1}^{1-\eta}\big]\)
\(=(n+1)^{1-\eta}\big[\psi_\eta(x_{k+1})-2\psi_\eta(x_k)+\psi_\eta(x_{k-1})\big]\)
\(=(n+1)^{1-\eta}\left[\frac{\psi_\eta(x_{k+1})-2\psi_\eta(x_k)+\psi_\eta(x_{k-1})}{\Delta x^2}\right]\Delta x^2\)
\(=\frac{1}{(n+1)^{1+\eta}}\big[\psi''_\eta(x_k)+O(\Delta x^2)\big]\text{as}\Delta x\rightarrow 0,\) where we used a standard second order central finite difference scheme and the fact that \(\Delta x=\frac{1}{n+1}\). From \(\psi''_\eta(x)=\eta(\eta-1)\frac{1}{x^{1+\eta}},\) we have \(\delta_k=\frac{\eta(\eta-1)}{(n+1)^{1+\eta}}\cdot\frac{1}{x_k^{1+\eta}}+\Delta x^{1+\eta} O(\Delta x^2)\)
\(=\frac{\eta(\eta-1)}{(n+1)^{1+\eta}}\cdot\frac{(n+1)^{1+\eta}}{k^{1+\eta}}+O(\Delta x^{3+\eta})\)
\(=\eta(\eta-1)\frac{1}{k^{1+\eta}}+O(\Delta x^{3+\eta}).\)

Since \(\eta\in(0,1)\), we deduce that the series<tbc>

\(\sum_{k=0}^\infty|\delta_k|\)

<tbc>is convergent, and consequently \(g_\eta\) belongs to the Wiener class. Therefore, since \(g_\eta\) belongs to the Wiener class, it is a continuous and hence Lebesgue integrable function, so that \(B_n=T_n(g_\eta)\) and Axiom GLT 2 and Axiom GLT 1 imply<tbc>

\(\{B_n\}_n\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} g_\eta(\theta).\)

<tbc>Finally, all the eigenvalues of _B<sub>n</sub>_ are trivially equal to \(\delta_0\) because of the triangular structure, so that

\(\{B_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\delta_0\)

follows immediately from the definition of distribution.

**Theorem 6.2** _There exists a continuous_ \(2\pi\)_-periodic function_ \(h_\xi\) _such that_<tbc>

\(\{U_m\}_m\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} h_\xi(\theta),\theta\in[-\pi,\pi].\)

**Proof:** We follow the proof of Theorem 6.1, showing that there exists \(h_\xi\) such that \(U_m=T_m(h_\xi)\) for all \(m\in\mathbb{N}\). We prove that the series \(h_\xi(\theta):=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\gamma_ke^{-\rho k\Delta t}e^{\mathrm{i}k\theta},\) with \(\gamma_k\) defined by (6.5), belongs to the Wiener class. Considering \(\psi_\xi(t):=t^{1-\xi}\) and using (6.4), we have \(\gamma_k=(k+1)^{1-\xi}-2k^{1-\xi}+(k-1)^{1-\xi}\)
\(=\left(\frac{m}{T}\right)^{1-\xi}\left[t_{k+1}^{1-\xi}-2t_k^{1-\xi}+t_{k-1}^{1-\xi}\right]\)
\(=\left(\frac{m}{T}\right)^{1-\xi}\left[\psi_\xi(t_{k+1})-2\psi_\xi(t_k)+\psi_\xi(t_{k-1})\right]\)
\(=\left(\frac{m}{T}\right)^{1-\xi}\left[\frac{\psi_\xi(t_{k+1})-2\psi_\xi(t_k)+\psi_\xi(t_{k-1})}{\Delta t^2}\right]\Delta t^2\)
\(=\left(\frac{T}{m}\right)^{1+\xi}\left[\psi''_\xi(t_k)+O(\Delta t^2)\right]\text{as}k\rightarrow\infty,\) using \(\Delta t=\frac{T}{m}\) and a standard central finite difference scheme. From \(\psi''_\xi(x)=\xi(\xi-1)\frac{1}{t^{1+\xi}},\) we have \(\gamma_k=\left(\frac{T}{m}\right)^{1+\xi}\xi(\xi-1)\frac{1}{t_k^{1+\xi}}+\Delta t^{1+\xi} O(\Delta t^2)\)
\(=\left(\frac{T}{m}\right)^{1+\xi}\frac{\xi(\xi-1)}{k^{1+\xi}}\left(\frac{m}{T}\right)^{1+\xi}+O(\Delta t^{3+\xi})\)
\(=\frac{\xi(\xi-1)}{k^{1+\xi}}+O(\Delta t^{3+\xi}).\) Since \(\xi\in(0,1)\) and \(\rho>0\), the series \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\left|\gamma_ke^{-\rho k\Delta t}\right|\) is convergent, and \(h_\xi\) belongs to the Wiener class by definition. Since \(h_\xi\) belongs to the Wiener class, it is a continuous and hence Lebesgue integrable function, so that \(U_m=T_m(h_\xi)\). As a consequence of Axiom GLT 2 and of Axiom GLT 1 we conclude \(\{U_m\}_m\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} h_\xi(\theta),\) while the eigenvalue distribution is obvious from the triangular structure. **Remark 6.3** _As it is evident from the final part of the proofs of Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 6.2, the fact that the involved generating functions belong to the Wiener class is not a goal, but it is instrumental in applying the GLT axioms for deducing in a fast way the distribution in the sense of the singular values._

We are now ready to compute the GLT symbol of the sequence associated with the full coefficient matrix. To provide meaningful results, we introduce a mild assumption regarding the rate at which the discretization parameters tend to zero with respect to one another.

**Theorem 6.3** _With A<sub>N</sub> defined in_ (6.11)_, assume that_<tbc>

\(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}\rightarrow\nu,\text{\textit{as}}m,n\rightarrow\infty,\)

<tbc>_with_ \(\nu\neq 0\)_. Then, it holds_

\(\{A_N\}_N\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} h_\xi(\theta_1)+\nu a(x)g_\eta(\theta_2),(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in[-\pi,\pi]^2,x\in[0,1],\)

_where_ \(h_\xi\) _and_ \(g_\eta\) _are given in Theorems 6.1-6.2._

**Proof:** We begin by decomposing (6.11) as<tbc>

\(A_N=\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
U_m\otimes I_n & \mathrm{O}_{mn\times n} \\
\mathrm{O}_{n\times mn} & \mathrm{O}_n
\end{array}\right]}_{=:C_N^{(1)}}+\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
I_m\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n & \mathrm{O}_{mn\times n} \\
\mathrm{O}_{n\times mn} & \frac{\lambda}{\beta_n}G_n
\end{array}\right]}_{=:C_N^{(2)}}+\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{O}_{mn} & -\alpha_m\mathbf{q}\otimes I_n \\
\mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_n & \mathrm{O}_n
\end{array}\right]}_{=:C_N^{(3)}},\)

<tbc>so we can focus on each component individually. For the first one, we have<tbc>

\(C_N^{(1)}=U_{m+1}\otimes I_n-\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{O}_{mn} & \mathrm{O}_{mn\times n} \\
\gamma_me^{-\rho m\Delta t}I_n & \cdots \\
\gamma_1e^{-\rho\Delta t}I_n & \gamma_0I_n
\end{array}\right]}_{=:R_N^{(1)}},\)

<tbc>where \(\mathrm{rank}R_N^{(1)}\le n=o(N)\) as \(m,n\rightarrow\infty\). By Lemma 4.1, \(\{R_N^{(1)}\}_N\) is zero- distributed, hence by GLT 2<tbc>

\(\{R_N^{(1)}\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}0.\)

<tbc>Moreover, we have \(U_{m+1}\otimes I_n=T_{m+1}(h_\xi)\otimes T_n(1)\), therefore applying GLT 2-7 leads to

\(\left\{C_N^{(1)}\right\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}h_\xi(\theta_1).\) (6.12)

Concerning \(C_N^{(2)}\), we notice that<tbc>

\(C_N^{(2)}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
I_m\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n & \mathrm{O}_{mn\times n} \\
\mathrm{O}_{n\times mn} & \frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n+\frac{\lambda-\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n
\end{array}\right]=I_{m+1}\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n+\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{O}_{mn} & \mathrm{O}_{mn\times n} \\
\mathrm{O}_{n\times mn} & \frac{\lambda-\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n
\end{array}\right]}_{=:R_N^{(2)}},\)

<tbc>in which once again \(\mathrm{rank}R_N^{(2)}=n=o(N)\) as \(m,n\rightarrow\infty\), so that<tbc>

\(\{R_N^{(2)}\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}0.\)

<tbc>On the other hand, with the assumption that \(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}\rightarrow\nu\), by GLT 2 and GLT 7 we have<tbc>

\(\left\{I_{m+1}\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n\right\}_N=\left\{T_{m+1}(1)\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}D_n(a)T_n(g_\eta)\right\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\nu a(x)g_\eta(\theta_2).\)

We conclude by GLT 3 that

\(\big\{C_N^{(2)}\big\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\nu a(x)g_\eta(\theta_2).\) (6.13)

Finally, we have

\(C_N^{(3)}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{O}_{mn} & -\alpha_m\mathbf{q}\otimes I_n \\
\mathrm{O}_{n\times mn} & \mathrm{O}_n
\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{O}_{mn} & \mathrm{O}_{mn\times n} \\
\mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_n & \mathrm{O}_n
\end{array}\right],\)

where each of these components has rank at most _m=o(N_). Therefore,

\(\big\{C_N^{(3)}\big\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}0.\) (6.14)

By summing the contributions in (6.12), (6.13) and (6.14), we find the GLT symbol of the overall coefficient matrix sequence {_A<sub>N</sub>}<sub>N</sub>_ via GLT 3, and then the singular value distribution via GLT 1.

Since the matrices _A<sub>N</sub>_ are non-Hermitian, the GLT symbol obtained in Theorem 6.3 directly implies the singular value distribution via GLT 1. However, the GLT theory alone does not guarantee the eigenvalue distribution. In the present setting, the eigenvalue distribution can be established because the preconditioned matrix sequence is weakly clustered at one, as shown in Theorem 6.5. This clustering result relies on the fact that the perturbation between the preconditioner and the coefficient matrix is of low rank relative to the matrix size, which is sufficient to characterize the eigenvalue behavior in the sense of weak clustering. In general, for non-Hermitian matrix sequences, eigenvalue distributions require additional assumptions, such as Hermitian structure, normality, or suitable perturbation arguments; see \[12, 45\] and references therein.

## 6.3 GLT preconditioning

In the present section, we propose preconditioners _P<sub>N</sub>_ for the linear system (6.9), with the aim of clustering at 1 the eigenvalues of \(\{P_N^{-1}A_N\}_N\). Let us define

\(P_N:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
U_m\otimes I_n+I_m\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n & \mathrm{O}_{nm\times n} \\
\mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_n & \frac{\lambda}{\beta_n}G_n
\end{array}\right].\) (6.15)

Note that both _U<sub>m</sub>_ and _G<sub>n</sub>_ are invertible, in consequence of their lower triangular structure with non-zero diagonal elements, and the same is true for \(U_m\otimes I_n+I_m\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n\), which is also lower triangular. Because of the block triangular structure, the eigenvalues of _P<sub>N</sub>_ are the eigenvalues of the diagonal blocks, therefore _P<sub>N</sub>_ is invertible.

The following theorem proves that {_P<sub>N</sub>}<sub>N</sub>_ has the same GLT symbol, and hence the same singular value distribution, as the coefficient matrix sequence.

**Theorem 6.4** _With P<sub>N</sub> defined in_ (6.15)_, assume that_

\(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}\rightarrow\nu,\text{\textit{as}}m,n\rightarrow\infty,\)

_with_ \(\nu\neq 0\)_. Then, it holds_

\(\{P_N\}_N\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} h_\xi(\theta_1)+\nu a(x)g_\eta(\theta_2),(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in[-\pi,\pi]^2,x\in[0,1],\)

_where_ \(h_\xi\) _and_ \(g_\eta\) _are given in Theorems 6.1-6.2._

**Proof:** Immediate by following the same reasoning as in the proof of Theorem 6.3. \(\square\)

The GLT symbol and singular value distribution of the preconditioned matrix sequence can be derived as a corollary of Theorems 6.3 and 6.4, simply by exploiting the algebra properties in GLT 3. However, it can also be computed more in general avoiding the assumption on the discretization parameters, as we show in the following theorem. Moreover, we can derive the distribution of the eigenvalues.

**Theorem 6.5** _With A<sub>N</sub> as in_ (6.11) _and P<sub>N</sub> as in_ (6.15)_, it holds_<tbc>

\(\{P_N^{-1}A_N\}_N\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} 1.\)

<tbc>_Moreover,_<tbc>

\(\{P_N^{-1}A_N\}_N\sim_\lambda 1.\)

<tbc>**Proof:** Setting _R<sub>N</sub>_:=_A<sub>N</sub>-P<sub>N</sub>_, we have<tbc>

\(P_N^{-1}A_N=I_N+P_N^{-1}R_N.\)

<tbc>From the fact that \(\mathrm{rank}R_N\le n\), it follows \(\mathrm{rank}(P_N^{-1}R_N)\le n=o(N)\), therefore<tbc>

\(\{P_N^{-1}R_N\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT} 0\)

<tbc>by Lemma 4.1. Hence, by GLT 3 and the fact that {_I<sub>N</sub>}<sub>N</sub>_∼<sub>GLT</sub>1,<tbc>

\(\{P_N^{-1}A_N\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT} 1.\)

<tbc>The singular value distribution follows immediately from GLT 1. Concerning the eigenvalue distribution, it is obvious that<tbc>

\(\lambda_j(P_N^{-1}A_N)=1+\lambda_j(P_N^{-1}R_N),j=1,\dots,N,\)

<tbc>therefore

\(\#\left\{j=1,\dots,N:\lambda_j(P_N^{-1}A_N)\neq 1\right\}\le n=o(N).\)

In other words, the eigenvalues of \(\{P_N^{-1}A_N\}_N\) are weakly clustered at 1, in the sense of Definition 2.2. Recalling Remark 2.1, this is equivalent to the fact that the sequence is spectrally distributed as 1.

Recent developments in preconditioning for all-at-once systems and inverse problems for FDEs are closely related to the present work. Li, Lin, Hon, and Wu [78] developed a preconditioned MINRES method for block lower triangular Toeplitz systems, which are ubiquitous in evolutionary PDE discretizations. More recently, Lin, Ke, Hon, and Ng [81] proposed a matching Schur complement preconditioning technique specifically designed for discrete time fractional diffusion ISPs, demonstrating its effectiveness in accelerating the convergence of Krylov methods. These works highlight the growing interest in structure-preserving preconditioners for all-at-once formulations, and the block triangular preconditioner proposed in this chapter builds upon this foundation.

**Remark 6.4** _In the special case where a(x_)=_a is constant, so that D<sub>n</sub>(a_)=_aI<sub>n</sub> and G<sub>n</sub>=aB<sub>n</sub>, a more efficient preconditioner can be constructed by approximating each Toeplitz matrix appearing in P<sub>N</sub> with the corresponding Strang preconditioner, as follows:_

\(S_N:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
S(U_m)\otimes I_n+I_m\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}aS(B_n) & \mathrm{O}_{nm\times n} \\
\mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_n & \frac{\lambda}{\beta_n}aS(B_n)
\end{array}\right],\)

_where S(U<sub>m</sub>), S(B<sub>n</sub>_) _are the standard Strang preconditioners of U<sub>m</sub> and B<sub>n</sub>, respectively. Since circulant matrices are uniformly diagonalizable through the Fourier matrix F<sub>m</sub>, we can write_

\(S(U_m)=F_m\Lambda_m^{(1)}F_m^*,S(B_n)=F_n\Lambda_n^{(2)}F_n^*,\)

_where_ \(\Lambda_m^{(i)}\)_, i_=1,2_, are the diagonal matrices containing the eigenvalues and can be computed starting from the coefficients of U<sub>m</sub>, B<sub>n</sub> via the FFT. Then, S<sub>N</sub> becomes_

\(S_N:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
(F_m\otimes F_n)\big[\Lambda_m^{(1)}\otimes I_n+I_m\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}a\Lambda_n^{(2)}\big](F_m\otimes F_n)^* & \mathrm{O}_{nm\times n} \\
\mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_n & \frac{\lambda}{\beta_n}aF_n\Lambda_n^{(2)}F_n^*
\end{array}\right].\)

_With this approach, the computational cost of inverting S<sub>N</sub> is of_ \(O\big(nm\mathrm{log}(nm)\big)\) _arithmetic operations, since all the necessary computations can be performed via the FFT. The same reasoning can be carried out using any suitable preconditioner for Toeplitz matrices, drawn from a matrix algebra which is uniformly diagonalizable through a fast transform._

**Remark 6.5** _From an implementation viewpoint, we can define a custom function that inverts P<sub>N</sub> through a forward substitution method, thanks to the block triangular structure of the matrix and the triangular structure of the blocks themselves. The computational cost amounts to O(n_<sup>2</sup>_m_<sup>2</sup>) _arithmetic operations. However, a linear system with coefficient matrix_ \(\frac{\lambda}{\beta_n}D_n(a)B_n=\frac{\lambda}{\beta_n}G_n\) _and variable coefficient a can be still solved within_ \(O\big(n\mathrm{log}n\big)\) _arithmetic operations as in Remark 6.4, while the more difficult additive structure in the other diagonal blocks_ \(\gamma_0I_n+\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}G_n\) _can be treated e.g. via preconditioned GMRES and Strang preconditioner_ \(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_n}\bar{a}S(B_n)\)_, with_ \(\bar{a}\) _being an average of a(x), again within_ \(O\big(n\mathrm{log}n\big)\) _arithmetic operations._

## Chapter 7

### Efficient Krylov solvers for inverse source problem in 2D space-time fractional diffusion equation

The motivation for this work stems from the increasing importance of space-time FDEs, which offer a versatile framework for modeling complex, multiscale phenomena in a rich variety of scientific disciplines. By incorporating fractional derivatives, FDEs can capture essential features such as memory effects, non-local interactions, and anomalous diffusion behaviors. These characteristics make FDEs ideal for modeling processes that involve complex transport phenomena, including anomalous diffusion, subdiffusion, and superdiffusion in heterogeneous media. In particular, the Caputo fractional derivative is widely used for modeling spatial heterogeneities, as it incorporates physically meaningful initial conditions and avoids singularities at the boundaries. Meanwhile, tempered fractional derivatives are effective in describing transient anomalous diffusion, where the diffusion initially follows a fractional power law and later transitions to normal diffusion [112].

In this chapter, based on the results presented in [68], we develop a fast algorithm to reconstruct the source term _f(x,y_) in the context of a two-dimensional space-time FDE, generalizing the work in [66] devoted to the uni-dimensional space version. Additional details, numerical experiments, and reformulations are included for completeness of the thesis presentation. Since IPs are often ill-posed in the sense of Hadamard, small perturbations in the input data can lead to significant errors in the solution [60, 70, 135, 61, 67]. To address this, we apply the quasi-boundary value method, a nonlocal regularization technique that has been successfully utilized to handle similar ill-posed problems in both parabolic and FDEs [29, 48]. The finite difference discretization of the regularized problem leads to a two-by-two block linear system. We design symbol-based approximations [66, 54] to the resulting coefficient matrices and construct an effective preconditioner for the GMRES method [107]. A detailed spectral analysis of the associated matrix sequences is carried out using the GLT theory, which provides a rigorous description of their asymptotic spectral behavior despite the presence of the variable coefficient _a(x,y_) that spoils the pure Toeplitz structure [41, 42, 10, 11]. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of the proposed preconditioning strategy in reducing iteration counts and computational cost.

## Problem tion

We consider the inverse source problem of identifying the source term _f(x,y_) from the space-time fractional diffusion equation

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho} u(x,y,t)+a(x,y)\left(^C\mathcal{D}_x^{\eta_1}+^C\mathcal{D}_y^{\eta_2}\right)u(x,y,t)=q(t)f(x,y),(x,y,t)\in\Omega_T, \\
u(0,y,t)=0=u(1,y,t),y\in(0,1),t\in(0,T), \\
u(x,0,t)=0=u(x,1,t),x\in(0,1),t\in(0,T), \\
u(x,y,0)=\varphi(x,y),x\in(0,1),y\in(0,1), \\
u(x,y,T)=\phi(x,y),x\in(0,1),y\in(0,1),
\end{array}\right.\) (7.1)

where \(\Omega_T:=(0,1)\times(0,1)\times(0,T)\), \(^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho}\) denotes the tempered fractional derivative of order \(\xi\in(0,1)\) and \(\rho>0\) is the truncation parameter, _a(x,y_) is a continuous variable coefficient such that \(a(x,y)\neq 0\), \(^C\mathcal{D}_x^{\eta_1}\) and \(^C\mathcal{D}_y^{\eta_2}\) denote the Caputo fractional derivatives of orders \(\eta_1,\eta_2\in(0,1)\), _q(t_) is a given function, \(\varphi(x,y)\) is the initial condition, and \(\phi(x,y)\) is the final time datum.

The tempered fractional derivative in time variable of order \(\xi\in(0,1)\) is defined as follows<tbc>

\(^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho} u(x,y,t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\xi)}\int_0^te^{-\rho(t-\tau)}(t-\tau)^{-\xi}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}u(x,y,\tau)d\tau.\)

<tbc>The Caputo fractional derivative in the space variable of orders \(\eta\in(0,1)\) is defined as follows<tbc>

\(^C\mathcal{D}_x^\eta u(x,y,t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\eta)}\int_0^x(x-\zeta)^{-\eta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\zeta}u(x,y,\zeta)d\zeta,x>0,\)

<tbc>In practice, the measurement of the final time datum is inevitably affected by noise. Let us denote the noisy datum by \(\phi_\varepsilon(x,y)\), where \(\varepsilon>0\) represents the noise level. Assuming the noise is sufficiently small, we impose the condition<tbc>

\(\|\phi-\phi_\varepsilon\|_{L^2}\le\varepsilon,\)

<tbc>where \(\|\cdot\|_{L^2}\) is the _L_<sup>2</sup> norm on \((0,1)\times(0,1)\). Applying the quasi-boundary value method yields a class of parameter-dependent well-posed regularized problems

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho} u(x,y,t)+a(x,y)\left(^C\mathcal{D}_x^{\eta_1}+^C\mathcal{D}_y^{\eta_2}\right)u(x,y,t)=q(t)f_{\varepsilon,\lambda}(x,y),(x,y,t)\in\Omega_T, \\
u(0,y,t)=0=u(1,y,t),y\in(0,1),t\in(0,T), \\
u(x,0,t)=0=u(x,1,t),x\in(0,1),t\in(0,T), \\
u(x,y,0)=\varphi(x,y),x\in(0,1),y\in(0,1), \\
u(x,y,T)=\phi_\varepsilon(x,y)-\lambda a(x,y)\left(^C\mathcal{D}_x^{\eta_1}+^C\mathcal{D}_y^{\eta_2}\right)f_{\varepsilon,\lambda}(x,y),x\in(0,1),y\in(0,1),
\end{array}\right.\) (7.2)

which approximate the original FDE in (7.1). Here, \(\lambda>0\) is a regularization parameter, \(f_{\varepsilon,\lambda}\) represents the regularized approximation of the source term _f(x,y_), and the solution \(u(x,y,t)\equiv u_{\varepsilon,\lambda}(x,y,t)\) provides an approximation to the original solution of problem (7.1). The regularization term \(\lambda a(x,y)\left(^C\mathcal{D}_x^{\eta_1}+^C\mathcal{D}_y^{\eta_2}\right)\) ensures that the reconstructed source term is stable and well-behaved, even in the presence of noise.

We then carefully discuss the global structure of the resulting coefficient matrix.
Let _n_1, _n_2 and _m_ be positive integers and denote the corresponding spatial and temporal meshes as \(x_i=i\Delta x,\Delta x=\frac{1}{n_1+1},i=0,1,\dots,n_1,\) (7.3) \(y_j=j\Delta y,\Delta y=\frac{1}{n_2+1},j=0,1,\dots,n_2,\) (7.4) \(t_s=s\Delta t,\Delta t=\frac{T}{m},s=0,1,\dots,m.\) (7.5) The approximate values of the functions at the grid points are denoted as follows \(u_{i,j}^s:=u(x_i,y_j,t_s),a_{i,j}:=a(x_i,y_j),f_{i,j}:=f_{\varepsilon,\lambda}(x_i,y_j),\)
\(\varphi_{i,j}:=\varphi(x_i,y_j),\phi_{i,j}:=\phi_\varepsilon(x_i,y_j),q^s:=q(t_s).\) To deal with the tempered fractional derivative, we use the _L_1 formula: \(^T\mathcal{D}_{L1}^{\xi,\rho} u(x_i,y_j,t_s)=\frac{(\Delta t)^{-\xi}}{\Gamma(2-\xi)}\left[b_0u_{i,j}^s-\sum_{l=1}^{s-1}(b_{s-l-1}-b_{s-l})e^{\rho(t_l-t_s)}u_{i,j}^l-b_{s-1}e^{\rho(t_0-t_s)}u_{i,j}^0\right],\) in which \(b_l=(l+1)^{1-\xi}-l^{1-\xi},l=0,1,\dots\) Denoting \(\alpha_m:=(\Delta t)^\xi\Gamma(2-\xi)=\left(\frac{T}{m}\right)^\xi\Gamma(2-\xi)\) and \(\gamma_0:=b_0,\gamma_l:=b_l-b_{l-1}=(l+1)^{1-\xi}-2l^{1-\xi}+(l-1)^{1-\xi},l=1,\dots,m-1,\) (7.6) and using \(t_s=s\Delta t\), the _L_1 approximation of the tempered fractional derivative is expressed as \(^T\mathcal{D}_{L1}^{\xi,\rho} u(x_i,y_j,t_s)=\frac{1}{\alpha_m}\left[\gamma_0u_{i,j}^s+\sum_{l=1}^{s-1}\gamma_{s-l}e^{-(s-l)\rho\Delta t}u_{i,j}^l-b_{s-1}e^{-s\rho\Delta t}u_{i,j}^0\right].\) (7.7)

To discretize the Caputo fractional derivative with respect to _x_, we exploit the _L_1 formula: \(^c\mathcal{D}_{L1}^{\eta_1}u(x_i,y_j,t_s)=\frac{1}{\beta_{n_1}}\left[\delta_0u_{i,j}^s+\sum_{k_1=1}^{i-1}\delta_{i-k_1}u_{k_1,j}^s-d_{i-1}u_{0,j}^s\right],\) (7.8) where \(\beta_{n_1}:=(\Delta x)^{\eta_1}\Gamma(2-\eta_1)=\left(\frac{1}{n_1+1}\right)^{\eta_1}\Gamma(2-\eta_1)\) (7.9) and \(d_{k_1}:=(k_1+1)^{1-\eta_1}-k_1^{1-\eta_1},k_1=0,1,\dots\)
\(\delta_0:=d_0,\)
\(\delta_{k_1}:=d_{k_1}-d_{k_1-1}=(k_1+1)^{1-\eta_1}-2k_1^{1-\eta_1}+(k_1-1)^{1-\eta_1},k_1=1,\dots,n_1-1.\) (7.10) Now, we proceed to discretize the Caputo fractional derivative with respect to _y_ by employing the _L_1 approximation formula \(^c\mathcal{D}_{L1}^{\eta_2}u(x_i,y_j,t_s)=\frac{1}{\beta_{n_2}}\left[\sigma_0u_{i,j}^s+\sum_{k_2=1}^{j-1}\sigma_{j-k_2}u_{i,k_2}^s-c_{j-1}u_{i,0}^s\right],\) (7.11) where \(\beta_{n_2}:=(\Delta x)^{\eta_2}\Gamma(2-\eta_2)=\left(\frac{1}{n_2+1}\right)^{\eta_2}\Gamma(2-\eta_2)\) (7.12) and \(c_{k_2}:=(k_2+1)^{1-\eta_2}-k_2^{1-\eta_2},k_2=0,1,\dots\)
\(\sigma_0:=c_0,\)
\(\sigma_{k_2}:=c_{k_2}-c_{k_2-1}=(k_2+1)^{1-\eta_2}-2k_2^{1-\eta_2}+(k_2-1)^{1-\eta_2},k_2=1,\dots,n_2-1.\) (7.13) Substituting the fractional derivatives in problem (7.2) with their respective _L_1 approximations (7.7) and (7.8) and (7.11), and omitting the truncation errors, the finite difference scheme is constructed as follows: \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c } \frac{1}{\alpha_m}\left[\gamma_0u_{i,j}^s+\sum_{l=1}^{s-1}\gamma_{s-l}e^{-(n-l)\rho\Delta t}u_{i,j}^l-b_{s-1}e^{-s\rho\Delta t}u_{i,j}^0\right]+\frac{a_{i,j}}{\beta_{n_1}}\left[\delta_0u_{i,j}^s+\sum_{k_1=1}^{i-1}\delta_{i-k_1}u_{k_1,j}^s \\ -d_{i-1}u_{0,j}^s\right]+\frac{a_{i,j}}{\beta_{n_2}}\left[\sigma_0u_{i,j}^s+\sum_{k_2=1}^{j-1}\sigma_{j-k_2}u_{i,k_2}^s-c_{j-1}u_{j,0}^s\right]=q^sf_{i,j}, \\ u_{0,j}^s=u_{n_1+1,j}^s=0,u_{i,0}^s=u_{i,n_2+1}^s=0, \\ u_{i,j}^0=\varphi_{i,j}, \\ u_{i,j}^m=\phi_{i,j}-\lambda\frac{a_{i,j}}{\beta_{n_1}}\left[\delta_0f_{i,j}+\sum_{k_1=1}^{i-1}\delta_{i-k_1}f_{k_1,j}-d_{i-1}f_{0,j}\right]-\lambda\frac{a_{i,j}}{\beta_{n_2}}\left[\sigma_0f_{i,j}+\sum_{k_2=1}^{j-1}\sigma_{j-k_2}f_{i,k_2} \\ -c_{j-1}f_{i,0}\right]. \end{array}\right.\)

By defining the corresponding vectors \(\mathbf{u}^s:=\left[u_{i,j}^s\right]_{i=1,\dots,n_1,j=1,\dots,n_2},\mathbf{a}:=\left[a_{i,j}\right]_{i=1,\dots,n_1,j=1,\dots,n_2},\mathbf{f}:=\left[f_{i,j}\right]_{i=1,\dots,n_1,j=1,\dots,n_2},\)
\(\varphi:=\left[\varphi_{i,j}\right]_{i=1,\dots,n_1,j=1,\dots,n_2},\varphi:=\left[\phi_{i,j}\right]_{i=1,\dots,n_1,j=1,\dots,n_2},\) Now, let **n**=_n_1_n_2, then we can write the numerical scheme in matrix form as \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c } \gamma_0\mathbf{u}^s+\sum_{l=1}^{s-1}\gamma_{s-l}e^{-(s-l)\rho\Delta t}\mathbf{u}^l+D_\mathbf{n}(a)\left(B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y\right)\mathbf{u}^s-\alpha_mq^s\mathbf{f}=b_{s-1}e^{-s\rho\Delta t}\varphi, \\ s=1,\dots,m, \\ \mathbf{u}^m+\lambda D_\mathbf{n}(a)\left(B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y\right)\mathbf{f}=\varphi, \end{array}\right.\) where _D_**n**(_a_) is the diagonal sampling matrix of size _M_ associated to _a(x,y_), while \(B_M^x\) are \(B_M^y\) are defined as follows \(B_\mathbf{n}^x=I_{n_2}\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_1}}B_{n_1}^x,\) (7.14) and \(B_\mathbf{n}^y=\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_2}}B_{n_2}^y\otimes I_{n_1}.\) (7.15) Here _B__n_1 are _B__n_2 are the following lower triangular Toeplitz matrices \(B_{n_1}^x:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c c } \delta_0 & 0 & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & 0 \\ \delta_1 & \delta_0 & 0 & & & \vdots \\ \delta_2 & \delta_1 & \delta_0 & \ddots & & \vdots \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\ \delta_{n_1-1} & \cdots & \delta_2 & \delta_1 & \delta_0 \end{array}\right],\) and \(B_{n_2}^y:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c } \sigma_0 & 0 & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots & 0 \\ \sigma_1 & \delta_0 & 0 & & & \vdots \\ \sigma_2 & \delta_1 & \delta_0 & \ddots & & \vdots \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\ \sigma_{n_2-1} & \cdots & \delta_2 & \sigma_1 & \sigma_0 \end{array}\right].\) By gathering the equations for all the time levels and the regularization equation, we obtain the all-at-once linear system \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\mathbf{v}_\lambda=\mathbf{z}_\lambda,\) (7.16)

where \(\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}=\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}(m,\mathbf{n}):=(m+1)\nu(\mathbf{n})\) and \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c } \gamma_0I_\mathbf{n}+G_\mathbf{n} & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} & \cdots & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} & -\alpha_mq^1I_\mathbf{n} \\ \gamma_1e^{-\rho\Delta t}I_\mathbf{n} & \gamma_0I_\mathbf{n}+G_\mathbf{n} & \ddots & \vdots & -\alpha_mq^2I_\mathbf{n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} & \vdots \\ \gamma_{m-1}e^{-(m-1)\rho\Delta t}I_\mathbf{n} & \cdots & \gamma_1e^{-\rho\Delta t}I_\mathbf{n} & \gamma_0I_\mathbf{n}+G_\mathbf{n} & -\alpha_mq^mI_\mathbf{n} \\ \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} & \cdots & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} & I_\mathbf{n} & \frac{\lambda}{\alpha_m}G_\mathbf{n} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\times\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}},\)
\(\mathbf{v}_\lambda:=\left[\begin{array}{ c } \mathbf{u}^1 \\ \mathbf{u}^2 \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\mathbf{u}^m}{\mathbf{f}} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^\widetilde{\mathbf{N}},\mathbf{z}_\lambda:=\left[\begin{array}{ c } b_0e^{-\rho\Delta t}\varphi \\ b_1e^{-2\rho\Delta t}\varphi \\ \vdots \\ \frac{b_{m-1}e^{-m\rho\Delta t}\varphi}{\phi} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^\widetilde{\mathbf{N}},\) in which _I_**n** is the \(\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{n}\) identity matrix, O**n** is the \(\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{n}\) zero matrix, and \(G_\mathbf{n}:=D_\mathbf{n}(a)\left(B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y\right).\) (7.17) Moreover, setting \(U_m:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c } \gamma_0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \gamma_1e^{-\rho\Delta t} & \gamma_0 & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\ \gamma_{m-1}e^{-\rho(m-1)\Delta t} & \cdots & \gamma_1e^{-\rho\Delta t} & \gamma_0 \end{array}\right],\) the coefficient matrix can be expressed into the compact form \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}=\left[\frac{U_m\otimes I_\mathbf{n}+I_m\otimes G_\mathbf{n}}{\mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_\mathbf{n}}\right|\frac{-\alpha_m\mathbf{q}\otimes I_\mathbf{n}}{\frac{\lambda}{\alpha_m}G_\mathbf{n}}\right],\) (7.18) in which \(\mathbf{e}_m:=\left[\begin{array}{ c } 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbf{q}:=\left[\begin{array}{ c } q^1 \\ q^1 \\ \vdots \\ q^m \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^m.\) ## 7.2 GLT analysis This section presents the spectral analysis of the coefficient matrix sequence via GLT theory to describe its asymptotic behavior. We first report the symbols of \(\{B_n^x\}_n\) and the time block {_Um}m_ given in Chapter 6, then analyze the space block {_G_**n**}**n**, and finally consider the full coefficient matrix sequence.

**Theorem 7.1** _\[66\] There exist continuous_ \(2\pi\)_-periodic functions_ \(g_{\eta_1}\) _and_ \(g_{\eta_2}\) _such that_ \(\{B_{n_1}^x\}_{n_1}\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} g_{\eta_1}(\theta_1),\theta_1\in[-\pi,\pi],\)
\(\{B_{n_2}^y\}_{n_2}\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} g_{\eta_2}(\theta_2),\theta_2\in[-\pi,\pi].\) _Moreover,_ \(\{B_{n_1}^x\}_{n_1}\sim_\lambda\delta_0,\)
\(\{B_{n_2}^y\}_{n_2}\sim_\lambda\sigma_0.\) **Theorem 7.2** _\[66\] There exists a continuous_ \(2\pi\)_-periodic function_ \(h_\xi\) _such that_ \(\{U_m\}_m\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} h_\xi(\theta),\theta\in[-\pi,\pi].\) _Moreover,_ \(\{U_m\}_m\sim_\lambda\gamma_0.\) **Corollary 7.1** _If_ \(a:[0,1]^2\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) _is continuous a.e. and if_ \(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_1}}\rightarrow\nu_1,\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_2}}\rightarrow\nu_2,\text{\textit{as}}m,n_1,n_2\rightarrow\infty,\) _with_ \(\nu_1\neq 0\) _or_ \(\nu_2\neq 0\)_. Then, we have_ \(\{G_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} a(x,y)\left(\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_1)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_2)\right),(x,y)\in[0,1]^2,(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in[-\pi,\pi]^2,\) _with_ \(g_{\eta_1}\) _and_ \(g_{\eta_2}\) _as in Theorem 7.1. Moreover,_ \(\{G_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\lambda a(x,y)\left(\delta_0+\sigma_0\right),(x,y)\in[0,1]^2.\) **Proof:** From the definition in (7.17), we have \(G_\mathbf{n}:=D_\mathbf{n}(a)\left(B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y\right).\) Thus, by GLT 2, we deduce that \(\{D_\mathbf{n}(a)\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}a(x,y),(x,y)\in[0,1]^2.\) Then, using (7.14) and assuming \(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_1}}\rightarrow\nu_1\), by GLT 2, and GLT 7, we obtain \(\{B_\mathbf{n}^x\}_\mathbf{n}=\left\{I_{n_2}\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_1}}B_{n_1}^x\right\}_\mathbf{n}=\left\{T_{n_2}(1)\otimes\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_1}}T_{n_1(g_{\eta_1})}\right\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_1).\) Similarly, using (7.15) and assuming \(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_2}}\rightarrow\nu_2\), by GLT 2, and GLT 7, we obtain \(\{B_\mathbf{n}^y\}_\mathbf{n}=\left\{\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_2}}B_{n_2}^y\otimes I_{n_1}\right\}_\mathbf{n}=\left\{\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_2}}T_{n_2(g_{\eta_2})}\otimes T_{n_1}(1)\right\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_2).\) Invoking the ∗-algebra properties detailed in GLT 3, we obtain that \(\{B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_1)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_2),(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in[-\pi,\pi]^2.\)

Using the product property of GLT 3 applied to the sequences {_D_**n**(_a_)}**n** and \(\{B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y\}_\mathbf{n}\), we conclude that \(\{G_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}a(x,y)\left(\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_1)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_2)\right),(x,y)\in[0,1]^2,(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in[-\pi,\pi]^2,\) By GLT 1, we immediately obtain \(\{G_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\sigma a(x,y)\left(\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_1)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_2)\right),(x,y)\in[0,1]^2,(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in[-\pi,\pi]^2,\) Finally, we observe that \(B_\mathbf{n}^x\) and \(B_\mathbf{n}^y\) are lower triangular matrices. Hence \((B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y)\) is lower triangular, and since _D_**n**(_a_) is diagonal, \(G_\mathbf{n}:=D_\mathbf{n}(a)\left(B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y\right),\) is also lower diagonal. Therefore, the eigenvalues of _G_**n** coincide with its diagonal entries. Since the main diagonal entries of \(B_\mathbf{n}^x\) and \(B_\mathbf{n}^y\) are \(\delta_0\) and \(\sigma_0\), the diagonal entries of _G_**n** are \(\{a(x_i,y_j)\left(\delta_0+\sigma_0\right)\}_{i,j=1}^{n_1,n_2}\). Hence \(\{G_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\lambda a(x,y)\left(\delta_0+\sigma_0\right),(x,y)\in[0,1]^2.\) We are now in a position to compute the GLT symbol of the sequence associated with the full coefficient matrix \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\). To ensure meaningful results, we assume a mild relation among the rates at which the discretization parameters tend to zero. **Theorem 7.3** _With_ \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) _defined in_ (7.18)_, assume that_ \(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_1}}\rightarrow\nu_1,\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_2}}\rightarrow\nu_2,\text{\textit{as}}m,n_1,n_2\rightarrow\infty,\) _with_ \(\nu_1\neq 0\) _or_ \(\nu_2\neq 0\)_. Then, it holds_ \(\{A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} h_\xi(\theta_1)+a(x,y)\left(\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_2)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_3)\right),\)
\((\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)\in[-\pi,\pi]^3,(x,y)\in[0,1]^2,\) _where_ \(h_\xi\) _is given in Theorems 7.1 and_ \(g_{\eta_1}\) _and_ \(g_{\eta_2}\) _are given in Theorems 7.2._ **Proof:** We proceed by decomposing (7.18) as follows \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}=\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c } U_m\otimes I_\mathbf{n} & \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{n}} \\ \mathrm{O}_{\mathbf{n}\times m\mathbf{n}} & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} \end{array}\right]}_{=:C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(1)}}+\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c } I_m\otimes G_\mathbf{n} & \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{n}} \\ \mathrm{O}_{\mathbf{n}\times m\mathbf{n}} & \frac{\lambda}{\alpha_m}G_\mathbf{n} \end{array}\right]}_{=:C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(2)}}+\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c } \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}} & -\alpha_m\mathbf{q}\otimes I_\mathbf{n} \\ \mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_\mathbf{n} & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} \end{array}\right]}_{=:C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(3)}}.\) Thus, we analyze each component separately. For the first component, we have \(C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(1)}=U_{m+1}\otimes I_\mathbf{n}-\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c } \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}} & \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{n}} \\ \gamma_me^{-\rho m\Delta t}I_\mathbf{n} & \cdots \\ \gamma_1e^{-\rho\Delta t}I_\mathbf{n} & \gamma_0I_m \end{array}\right]}_{=:R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(1)}},\)

where \(\mathrm{rank}R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(1)}\le\nu(\mathbf{n})=o(\widetilde{\mathbf{N}})\) as \(m,\mathbf{n}\rightarrow\infty\). According to Theorem 4.1, the sequence \(\{R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(1)}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) is zero-distributed; hence, by GLT 2, we deduce that \(\{R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(1)}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}0.\) Moreover, exploiting the identity \(U_{m+1}\otimes I_\mathbf{n}=T_{m+1}(h_\xi)\otimes T_\mathbf{n}(1)\) and applying the axioms GLT 2-7 yields \(\{C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(1)}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}h_\xi(\theta_1).\) (7.19) Regarding \(C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(2)}\), we observe that \(C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(2)}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } I_m\otimes G_\mathbf{n} & \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{n}} \\ \mathrm{O}_{\mathbf{n}\times m\mathbf{n}} & G_\mathbf{n}+\left(\frac{\lambda}{\alpha_m}-1\right)G_\mathbf{n} \end{array}\right]=I_{m+1}\otimes G_\mathbf{n}+\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ c c } \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}} & \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{n}} \\ \mathrm{O}_{\mathbf{n}\times m\mathbf{n}} & \left(\frac{\lambda}{\alpha_m}-1\right)G_\mathbf{n} \end{array}\right]}_{=:R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(2)}},\) where, once again, \(\mathrm{rank}R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(2)}=\nu(\mathbf{n})=o(\widetilde{\mathbf{N}})\) as \(m,\mathbf{n}\rightarrow\infty\). By Theorem 4.1, the sequence \(\{R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(2)}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) is zero-distributed; therefore, by GLT 2, it follows that \(\{R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(2)}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}0.\) Invoking the assumptions \(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_1}}\rightarrow\nu_1\) and \(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_2}}\rightarrow\nu_2\) together with GLT 2 yields \(\{I_{m+1}\otimes G_\mathbf{n}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}=\{I_{m+1}\otimes D_\mathbf{n}(a)\left(B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y\right)\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\)
\(=\{T_{m+1}(1)\otimes D_\mathbf{n}(a)\left(\nu_1T_\mathbf{n}(g_{\eta_1})+\nu_2T_\mathbf{n}(g_{\eta_2})\right)\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}.\) Then, by GLT 7, we obtain \(\{I_{m+1}\otimes G_\mathbf{n}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}a(x,y)\left(\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_2)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_3)\right).\) By GLT 3, we conclude that \(\{C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(2)}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}a(x,y)\left(\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_2)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_3)\right).\) (7.20) We conclude by observing that \(C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(3)}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}} & -\alpha_m\mathbf{q}\otimes I_\mathbf{n} \\ \mathrm{O}_{\mathbf{n}\times m\mathbf{n}} & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} \end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{ c c } \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}} & \mathrm{O}_{m\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{n}} \\ \mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_\mathbf{n} & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} \end{array}\right],\) where each component has rank at most \(\mathbf{n}=o(\widetilde{\mathbf{N}})\). Hence, we conclude that \(\{C_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{(3)}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}0.\) (7.21) By combining the contributions in (7.19), (7.20), and (7.21), and invoking GLT 3, we obtain the GLT symbol of the matrix sequence \(\{A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) \(\{A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}h_\xi(\theta_1)+a(x,y)\left(\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_2)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_3)\right),\) By GLT 1, the singular value distribution is \(\{A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\sigma h_\xi(\theta_1)+a(x,y)\left(\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_2)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_3)\right),\)

As in the one-dimensional case, the matrices \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) are non-Hermitian, and therefore the GLT symbol obtained in Theorem 7.3 directly yields the singular value distribution but does not automatically imply the eigenvalue distribution. The eigenvalue distribution in this setting follows from Theorem 7.5, where we prove that the preconditioned matrix sequence is weakly clustered at one. This clustering result is based on the low-rank perturbation structure of the preconditioned system, which is sufficient to characterize the eigenvalue behavior. For non-Hermitian matrix sequences in general, eigenvalue distributions require additional assumptions, such as Hermitian structure or suitable perturbation arguments; see \[12, 45\]. In the present work, the weak clustering result ensures fast convergence of the preconditioned GMRES method despite the non-Hermitian nature of the coefficient matrices.

## 7.3 GLT preconditioning

The current section is divided into two parts. The first contains the proposal and the second the related spectral analysis.

### 7.3.1 Block Triangular preconditioning

In this subsection, we propose block triangular preconditioners \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) for the linear system (7.16), aiming to cluster the eigenvalues of \(\{P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) around 1. We define

\(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
U_m\otimes I_\mathbf{n}+I_m\otimes G_\mathbf{n} & \text{O}_{\mathbf{nm}\times\mathbf{n}} \\
\mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_\mathbf{n} & \frac{\lambda}{\alpha_m}G_\mathbf{n}
\end{array}\right].\) (7.22)

Note that both _U<sub>m</sub>_ and _G_**<sub>n</sub>** are invertible, since they are lower triangular matrices with nonzero diagonal entries. The same holds for \(U_m\otimes I_\mathbf{n}+I_m\otimes G_\mathbf{n}\), which is also block lower triangular. Moreover, due to the block triangular structure,<tbc>

the eigenvalues of \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) coincide with those of its diagonal blocks. Therefore, \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) is invertible.
The linear systems with matrix \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) that have to be solved when applying the preconditioned GMRES to the original linear systems can be solved by standard block forward elimination. However we have to specify how the linear systems having as coefficient matrices the diagonal blocks of \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) are solved. Indeed the diagonal blocks have the expression \(\gamma_0I_\mathbf{n}+D_\mathbf{n}(a)B_\mathbf{n}\) and for them we can use several standard preconditioners such as \(\gamma_0I_\mathbf{n}+\hat{a}B_\mathbf{n}\) which is of Toeplitz lower triangular form, with \(\hat{a}\) being the integral average of the function _a_, or the standard circulant preconditioner constructed as \(\gamma_0I_\mathbf{n}+\hat{a}S(B_\mathbf{n})\), _S(B_**n**) being a Strang-like circulant approximation of _B_**n**, constructed by preserving the first column of _B_**n**. The computational features of these choice are discussed at the end of Section 7.4.
The preconditioning strategies developed in this chapter are informed by recent advances in preconditioning for all-at-once systems arising from evolutionary PDEs. Huang, Fung, Hon, and Lin \[56\] introduced an efficient preconditioner for evolutionary PDEs discretized with the \(\theta\)-method in time, providing a comprehensive analysis of its spectral properties. Their approach, which leverages the structure of the time-stepping matrix, is complementary to the block triangular preconditioner proposed here for the ISP in a two-dimensional FDE. Additionally, the matching Schur complement preconditioning technique of Lin, Ke, Hon, and Ng \[81\] for discrete time fractional diffusion ISPs demonstrates the effectiveness of exploiting the block structure of all-at-once systems in the fractional setting. ## 7.3.2 GLT preconditioning analysis The following theorem establishes that \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) has the same GLT symbol, and consequently the same singular value distribution, as the original coefficient matrix sequence. **Theorem 7.4** _With_ \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) _defined in_ (7.22)_, assume that_ \(\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_1}}\rightarrow\nu_1,\frac{\alpha_m}{\beta_{n_2}}\rightarrow\nu_2,\text{\textit{as}}m,n_1,n_2\rightarrow\infty,\) _with_ \(\nu_1\neq 0\) _or_ \(\nu_2\neq 0\)_. Then, it holds_ \(\{P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} h_\xi(\theta_1)+a(x,y)\left(\nu_1g_{\eta_1}(\theta_2)+\nu_2g_{\eta_2}(\theta_3)\right),\)
\((\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)\in[-\pi,\pi]^3,(x,y)\in[0,1]^2,\) _where_ \(h_\xi\) _is given in Theorems 7.1 and_ \(g_{\eta_1}\) _and_ \(g_{\eta_2}\) _are given in Theorems 7.2._ **Proof:** The result follows from the same GLT arguments used in the proof of Theorem 7.3. The GLT symbol and the singular value distribution of the preconditioned matrix sequence follow as a corollary of Theorems 7.3 and 7.4, by exploiting the algebra properties in GLT 3. However, they can also be derived in a more general setting, without assuming specific conditions on the discretization parameters, as shown in the following theorem. Moreover, the eigenvalue distribution can be characterized.

**Theorem 7.5** _With_ \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) _as in_ (7.18) _and_ \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) _as in_ (7.22)_, it holds_<tbc>

\(\{P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_{\mathrm{GLT},\sigma} 1.\)

<tbc>_Moreover,_<tbc>

\(\{P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\lambda 1.\)

<tbc>**Proof:** Define \(R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}:=A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}-P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\). Then,<tbc>

\(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}=I_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}+P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}.\)

<tbc>Since \(\mathrm{rank}R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\le\nu(\mathbf{n})\), it follows that \(\mathrm{rank}(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}})\le\nu(\mathbf{n})=o(\widetilde{\mathbf{N}})\) as \(m,\mathbf{n}\rightarrow\infty\). By Theorem 4.1, the sequence \(\{P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) is zero-distributed; therefore, by GLT 2, it follows that<tbc>

\(\{P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}0.\)

<tbc>Hence, by exploiting part 2 of axiom GLT 3 and by the fact that \(\{I_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}1\), we infer<tbc>

\(\{P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}1.\)

<tbc>Thus, by GLT 1, we immediately obtain<tbc>

\(\{P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\sim_\sigma 1.\)

<tbc>Turning to the eigenvalue distribution, we observe that<tbc>

\(\lambda_n(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}})=1+\lambda_n(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}R_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}),n=1,\dots,\widetilde{\mathbf{N}},\)

<tbc>therefore

\(\#\left\{n=1,\dots,\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}:\lambda_n(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}})\neq 1\right\}\le\mathbf{n}=o(\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}).\)

Thus, the eigenvalues of \(\{P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}^{-1}A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\}_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) are weakly clustered at 1 in the sense of Definition 2.2, which, by Remark 2.1, is equivalent to saying that the sequence is spectrally distributed as 1.

**Remark 7.2** _We emphasize that the given sequence of theoretical steps for studying the distribution and clustering in the eigenvalue and singular value sense can be adapted with little effort to a great variety of different situations. Here we mention two of them, one concerning a generalization of problem_ (7.1) _and one regarding other classes of discretizations for the regularized FDEs in_ (7.2).

1. _If the square_ \([0,1]\times[0,1]\) _is replaced by a bounded_ \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^2\)_, with_ \(\Omega\) _simply Peano-Jordan measurable, then the domain_ \(\Omega_T\) _in_ (7.1)-(7.2) _is replaced by_ \(\Omega\times(0,T)\)_. Hence, simply adapting the steps in Section 7.2 and Section 7.3, the same conclusions are obtained, using the reduced GLT theory \[8\] in place of the classical one; for the reduced GLT theory refer to \[124\]\[pp. 395-399\] and \[125\]\[Section 3.1.4\] for an example, the initial proposal, the related terminology, and \[8\] for a complete theoretical development._<tbc>

_2._ _If the discretization formulae used in Section 7.1 are replaced by high order finite elements in space of order p\>_1 _or by the isogeometric analysis with degree p and regularity k\d or_ (_p-k)d with d_=2_. Again the analysis given here can be performed almost verbatim with minimal technical changes, thanks to the uniform structure of the GLT axioms._ _Of course the directions indicated in 1) and 2) can be combined and even extended to higher space dimensionality with_ \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), \(d\ge 2\)_, so having the potential of providing a very general picture._ ## 7.4 Numerical results and study of the computational cost We evaluate the efficiency of the proposed preconditioner by measuring the number of GMRES iterations required for convergence. Let us consider the two-dimensional problem on the domain \(\Omega=(0,1)^2\) and \(t\in(0,T)\). We set \(T=1,a(x,y)=x+y,q(t)=t^2,\varphi(x,y)=0.\) To construct the noisy final data, we select the source function \(f(x,y)=xy\mathrm{sin}(\pi x)\mathrm{sin}(\pi y).\) and solve the linear system arising from the corresponding direct problem \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } ^T\mathcal{D}_t^{\xi,\rho} u(x,y,t)+a(x,y)\left(^C\mathcal{D}_x^{\eta_1}+^C\mathcal{D}_y^{\eta_2}\right)u(x,y,t)=q(t)f(x,y), & (x,y,t)\in\Omega_T, \\ u(0,y,t)=0=u(1,y,t), & y\in(0,1),t\in(0,T), \\ u(x,0,t)=0=u(x,1,t), & x\in(0,1),t\in(0,T), \\ u(x,y,0)=\varphi(x,y), & x\in(0,1),y\in(0,1). \end{array}\right.\) With the same discretization technique adopted in Section 7.1, we obtain the linear system \(\tilde{A}_{m,\mathbf{n}}\tilde{\mathbf{u}}=\tilde{\mathbf{b}},\) where \(\tilde{A}_{m,\mathbf{n}}:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c } \gamma_0I_\mathbf{n}+G_\mathbf{n} & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} & \cdots & \mathrm{O}_\mathbf{n} \\ \gamma_1e^{-\rho\Delta t}I_\mathbf{n} & \gamma_0I_\mathbf{n}+G_\mathbf{n} & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \mathrm{O}_m \\ \gamma_{m-1}e^{-(m-1)\rho\Delta t}I_\mathbf{n} & \cdots & \gamma_1e^{-\rho\Delta t}I_\mathbf{n} & \gamma_0I_\mathbf{n}+G_\mathbf{n} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{m\mathbf{n}\times m\mathbf{n}},\)
\(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}:=\left[\begin{array}{ c } \mathbf{u}^{(1)} \\ \mathbf{u}^{(2)} \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{u}^{(m)} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{m\mathbf{n}},\tilde{\mathbf{b}}:=\left[\begin{array}{ c } b_0e^{-\rho\Delta t}\varphi+\alpha_mq^1\mathbf{f} \\ b_1e^{-2\rho\Delta t}\varphi+\alpha_mq^2\mathbf{f} \\ \vdots \\ b_{m-1}e^{-m\rho\Delta t}\varphi+\alpha_mq^m\mathbf{f} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{C}^{m\mathbf{n}}.\)

The final time datum **u**_m_ is obtained by solving the forward problem. To model measurement noise, we introduce a perturbation of the form \(\varepsilon\delta(x)\), where \(\delta(x)\) is a random function uniformly distributed in (-1,1). The resulting noisy datum is denoted by \(\unknown\), representing a contaminated version of the exact final time observation. Then, we apply the GMRES method to (7.16) and report in 7.1 the iteration counts and CPU times required by both the nonpreconditioned and preconditioned systems. We set the regularization parameter to \(\lambda=5\cdot 10^{-3}\), the noise level to \(\varepsilon=0.01\), and consider different choices of the fractional orders \(\xi\), \(\eta_1\), and \(\eta_2\). The initial guess is the zero vector, the tolerance is `tol`=10-8, and the maximum number of iterations is equal to the size of the matrix.
Comparing the results obtained for the preconditioned and nonpreconditioned systems, we observe that the preconditioner _PN_ consistently reduces the number of GMRES iterations for all tested values of the fractional orders. The reduction is particularly significant for \(\xi=0.2\), \(\eta_1=0.2\), and \(\eta_2=0.8\), where the iteration counts of the nonpreconditioned system are the largest. For example, when _n_1=_n_2=_m_=25, the number of iterations decreases from 186 to 39, corresponding to a reduction of almost 80%. These results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed preconditioning strategy and are in agreement with the theoretical spectral analysis.
Furthermore, the preconditioner exhibits a remarkable robustness with respect to the problem dimensions. Indeed, for each fixed value of _n_1=_n_2, the number of iterations required by the preconditioned system remains nearly constant as _m_ increases. For instance, when _n_1=_n_2=25 and \((\xi,\eta_1,\eta_2)=(0.2,0.2,0.8)\), the preconditioned iteration counts vary only between 39 and 40, while the corresponding nonpreconditioned iteration counts remain close to 190. Similar behaviour can be observed for all considered choices of the fractional orders.
In addition, for each fixed value of _m_, the number of iterations required by the preconditioned system grows moderately as the spatial discretization parameters _n_1 and _n_2 increase. In contrast, the nonpreconditioned iteration counts increase much more rapidly. This indicates that the preconditioner successfully mitigates the deterioration of the spectral properties associated with mesh refinement, leading to a substantially improved convergence behaviour.
The CPU timings generally reflect the reduction in iteration counts achieved by the preconditioner. Although the gain in computational time is less pronounced in some cases due to the additional cost associated with applying the preconditioner, the preconditioned framework remains competitive and considerably more scalable than the nonpreconditioned one as the problem dimensions increase.
Overall, the numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed preconditioner provides a substantial acceleration of the GMRES method and maintains a robust performance across different discretization levels and fractional-order parameters. ## Study of the computational costs and further proposals In this subsection, we study in detail the computational cost of our preconditioned GMRES method and we discuss further potential proposals regarding the preconditioning.
When applying one step of the preconditioned GMRES with preconditioner \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\), we have to solve a linear system with coefficient matrix \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) and we have to perform matrix-vector products with the original matrix \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\). The related arithmetic costs

are the following

• When performing one matrix-vector multiplication with matrix \(A_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\), we per form \(\frac{m^2}{2}+O(m)\) products of a constant times a vector of size \(\nu(\mathbf{n})\), \(\frac{m^2}{2}+O(m)\) additions between vectors of size \(\nu(\mathbf{n})\), and _m_+1 products of the matrix _D_**<sub>n</sub>**(_a)B_**<sub>n</sub>** times a vector: hence the corresponding arithmetic cost is equal to \(m^2\nu(\mathbf{n})+Cm\nu(\mathbf{n})log[\nu(\mathbf{n})]+o(m^2\nu(\mathbf{n}))=m^2\nu(\mathbf{n})+o(m^2\nu(\mathbf{n}))\) arithmetic operations, if we make the natural assumption that \(log[\nu(\mathbf{n})]=o(m)\) and taking into account that _C_ is a constant;<tbc>

• When solving one linear system with coefficient matrix \(P_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\), we perform \(\frac{m^2}{2}+O(m)\) products of a constant times a vector of size \(\nu(\mathbf{n})\), \(\frac{m^2}{2}+O(m)\) additions between vectors of size \(\nu(\mathbf{n})\), and _m_+1 solutions of linear systems with coefficient matrix \(M_{\nu(\mathbf{n})}:=cI+D_\mathbf{n}(a)B_\mathbf{n}\) times a vector: hence the corresponding arithmetic cost is equal to \(m^2\nu(\mathbf{n})+C'm\nu(\mathbf{n})log[\nu(\mathbf{n})]+o(m^2\nu(\mathbf{n}))=m^2\nu(\mathbf{n})+o(m^2\nu(\mathbf{n}))\) arithmetic operations, if we make the natural assumption that \(log[\nu(\mathbf{n})]=o(m)\) and \(C'\) depends linearly on the number of iterations we need preconditioning with \(\widetilde{P}_{\nu(\mathbf{n})}:=cI+\hat{a}B_\mathbf{n}\) or with \(\widetilde{S}_{\nu(\mathbf{n})}:=cI+\hat{a}S(B_\mathbf{n})\). As it can be seen from  7.2,  7.3,  7.4,  7.5, the number of iterations for both preconditioned GMRES is bounded by a constant independent of the matrix size \(\nu(\mathbf{n})\) so that also \(C'\) can be assumed to be constant.<tbc>

Finally, we introduce an alternative Strang-like preconditioner \(S_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}\) for the linear system (7.16).

A Strang-like preconditioner for our block structure is defined by replacing each lower triangular Toeplitz matrix in the various blocks with its natural circulant approximation and by replacing coefficient _a(x,y_) with its integral average \(\hat{a}\) so that _D_**<sub>n</sub>**(_a_) is replaced by \(\hat{a}I_\mathbf{n}\) and _G_**<sub>n</sub>** reduces to<tbc>

\(G_\mathbf{n}=\hat{a}B_\mathbf{n},B_\mathbf{n}=(B_\mathbf{n}^x+B_\mathbf{n}^y),\)

<tbc>that is

\(S_\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}:=\left[\frac{S(U_m)\otimes I_\mathbf{n}+I_m\otimes\hat{a}S(B_\mathbf{n})}{\mathbf{e}_m^T\otimes I_\mathbf{n}}\right|\text{O}_{\mathbf{n}m\times\mathbf{n}}\frac{\lambda}{\alpha_m}D_\mathbf{n}(a)S(B_\mathbf{n})}\right].\) (7.23)

Since circulant matrices are diagonalizable by the Fourier matrices, we write

\(S(U_m)=F_m\Lambda_m^{(1)}F_m^*,S(B_\mathbf{n})=F_\mathbf{n}\Lambda_\mathbf{n}^{(2)}F_\mathbf{n}^*,\)

where \(\Lambda_m^{(1)}\) and \(\Lambda_\mathbf{n}^{(2)}\) are the diagonal matrices containing the eigenvalues and can be computed starting from the coefficients of _U<sub>m</sub>_, _B_**<sub>n</sub>** via the FFT.

## Chapter 8 ### Structure-preserving preconditioning for variable- coefficient space-fractional diffusion equations and \(\theta\)-Method In this chapter, based on the results presented in [73], we investigate the spectral properties and preconditioning of linear systems arising from the discretization of time-dependent space-FDEs with variable coefficient. Additional details, numerical experiments, and reformulations are included for completeness of the thesis presentation. Fractional diffusion models have become increasingly relevant in the mathematical modeling of anomalous transport processes, especially in situations where the classical diffusion equation fails to capture long-range interactions and nonlocal effects [131]. Such models are particularly valuable for describing superdiffusive behavior, where particles disperse more rapidly than predicted by classical diffusion theory.
The numerical discretization of these equations leads to large linear systems that are dense, nonsymmetric, and often severely ill-conditioned. To address these challenges, we develop a preconditioning strategy based on the structural properties of the discretized operator. A detailed spectral analysis of the associated matrix sequences is carried out using the GLT theory, which provides a unified framework for describing the asymptotic singular value and spectral distributions of both the original and preconditioned matrices [41, 42]. The main novelty is that the analysis fully covers the nonconstant variable coefficient case, both in one and two spatial dimensions. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of the proposed preconditioners in accelerating the convergence of GMRES.
In this chapter, we consider the following class of evolutionary partial differential equations: \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } \frac{\partial}{\partial t}u(x,y,t)=\mathcal{L}u(x,y,t)+f(x,y,t), & (x,y,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T], \\ u(x,y,t)=0, & (x,y)\in\partial\Omega,t\in[0,T], \\ u(x,y,0)=\phi(x,y), & (x,y)\in\Omega, \end{array}\right.\) (8.1) where \(\Omega=(L_1,R_1)\times(L_2,R_2)\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) is open, _f(x,y,t_) is a given source term, _u(x,y,t_) denotes the unknown solution, and \(\phi(x,y)\) is the prescribed initial condition.
More specifically, we consider the operator \(\mathcal{L}=a(x,y)\left(\mathcal{D}_x^{\alpha_1}+\mathcal{D}_y^{\alpha_2}\right),\) where _a(x,y_) is a smooth variable diffusion coefficient, \(\mathcal{D}_x^{\alpha_1}\) denotes the left-sided Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative of order \(\alpha_1\in(1,2)\) with respect to _x_, and \(\mathcal{D}_y^{\alpha_2}\) denotes the left-sided Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative of order \(\alpha_2\in(1,2)\) with respect to _y_.

In the one-dimensional case, the model reduces to \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } \frac{\partial}{\partial t}u(x,t)=a(x)\mathcal{D}_x^\alpha u(x,t)+f(x,t), & (x,t)\in(L_1,R_1)\times(0,T], \\ u(x,t)=0, & x\in\partial(L_1,R_1),t\in[0,T], \\ u(x,0)=\phi(x), & x\in(L_1,R_1). \end{array}\right.\) (8.2) The chapter is organized as follows. Section 8.1 contains the structural and spectral analysis of the relevant matrix sequences. In Sections 8.2 and 8.3, we introduce suitable preconditioners and study their spectral behavior. Finally, in Section 8.4, we present spectral visualizations and numerical experiments, and discuss the numerical results. ## 8.1 Discretized problem and GLT analysis In this section, we present the discretization of the variable-coefficient space-fractional diffusion equation (8.1), posed on the spatial domain \(\Omega=(L_1,R_1)\times(L_2,R_2)\subset\mathbb{R}^2\). The equation is first reformulated on a discrete space-time grid, leading to a sequence of linear systems governed by structured coefficient matrices that encode the nonlocal behavior of the model. We then analyze the spectral properties of these matrices using the GLT framework. In particular, we compute the GLT symbol of the resulting matrix sequence, which characterizes the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues and singular values. ### 8.1.1 Discretization We first treat the one-dimensional space setting and then the two-dimensional space setting. ### One-dimensional Let _M_ and _N_ be positive integers representing the number of temporal steps and the number of interior spatial grid points, respectively. The spatial and temporal meshes are defined as \(x_i=L_1+i\Delta x,\Delta x=\frac{(R_1-L_1)}{(N+1)},0\le i\le N+1,\)
\(t_m=m\Delta t,\Delta t=\frac{T}{M},0\le m\le M.\) To approximate the left-sided Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative, we adopt the shifted Grünwald finite difference scheme [91], which is widely recognized for its improved stability and accuracy compared to the standard Grünwald approach. The continuous fractional operator \(\mathcal{D}_x^\alpha u(x,t)\) is discretized at each interior point _xi_ using the following expression \(\mathcal{D}_x^\alpha u(x,t)\big|_{x=x_i,t=t_m}=\frac{1}{(\Delta x)^\alpha}\sum_{k=0}^{i+1}g_{i-k+1}^{(\alpha)}u(x_k,t_m)+\mathcal{O}(\Delta x),\) (8.3)

where

\(g_0^{(\alpha)}=1,g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}=\left(1-\frac{\alpha+1}{k+1}\right)g_k^{(\alpha)},k\ge 0.\) (8.4)

This recurrence can be rewritten in closed form as

\(g_k^{(\alpha)}=(-1)^k\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\alpha}{k},k\ge 0,\) (8.5)

where

\(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\alpha}{k}=\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)\cdots(\alpha-k+1)}{k!}\)

denotes the generalized binomial coefficient.

**Proposition 8.1** _Let_ \(\alpha\in(1,2)\) _and_ \(g_k^{(\alpha)}\) _be defined as in_ (8.4)_. Then we have_

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
g_0^{(\alpha)}=1, & g_1^{(\alpha)}=-\alpha, \\
\sum_{k=0}^\infty g_k^{(\alpha)}=0, & \sum_{k=0}^ng_k^{(\alpha)}<0,
\end{array}\right.\)

When combined with the variable diffusion coefficient _a(x_), the spatial discretization for the fractional diffusion term at time level _m_ becomes

\(a(x)\mathcal{D}_x^\alpha u(x,t)\big|_{x=x_i,t=t_m}=\frac{a(x_i)}{(\Delta x)^\alpha}\sum_{k=0}^{i+1}g_{i-k+1}^{(\alpha)}u(x_k,t_m)+\mathcal{O}(\Delta x).\) (8.6)

Finally, by coupling the \(\theta\)-method \[101\] to discretize the temporal derivative in (8.2) with the approximation in (8.6), we obtain the following time-stepping scheme

\(\frac{u_i^{(m+1)}-u_i^{(m)}}{\Delta t}=\theta\left(\frac{a(x_i)}{(\Delta x)^\alpha}\sum_{k=0}^{i+1}g_k^{(\alpha)}u_{i-k+1}^{(m+1)}\right)+(1-\theta)\left(\frac{a(x_i)}{(\Delta x)^\alpha}\sum_{k=0}^{i+1}g_k^{(\alpha)}u_{i-k+1}^{(m)}\right)+f_i^{(m,\theta)},\) (8.7)

where \(0\le\theta\le 1\) is a weighting parameter, \(u_i^{(m)}\) approximates _u(x<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>m</sub>_), and \(f_i^{(m,\theta)}=\theta f(x_i,t_{m+1})+(1-\theta)f(x_i,t_m)\). The value of \(\theta\) determines the nature of the method: \(\theta=0\) corresponds to the Forward Euler method, \(\theta=1\) yields the Backward Euler method, and \(\theta=\frac{1}{2}\) gives the Crank-Nicolson scheme.

By defining \(u_N^{(m)}=\left[u_i^{(m)}\right]_{i=1,\dots,N}^T\), that is the numerical approximation of the solution _u(x,t<sub>m</sub>_) at all points of the interior spatial grid _x<sub>i</sub>,i_=1_,...,N_, and accordingly, the vector \(f_N^{(m,\theta)}=\left[f_i^{(m,\theta)}\right]_{i=1,\dots,N}^T\), and by multiplying both sides of (8.7) by \(\Delta t\) and simplifying, we obtain<tbc>

\(u_n^{(m+1)}-u_n^{(m)}=\theta G_{\alpha,N}u_N^{(m+1)}+(1-\theta)G_{\alpha,N}u_N^{(m)}+\Delta tf_N^{(m,\theta)},m=0,\dots,M-1,\)

<tbc>where<tbc>

\(G_{\alpha,N}=\gamma\mathcal{D}_N(a)\overline{G_{\alpha,N}},\) (8.8)

with \(\gamma=\Delta t/(\Delta x)^\alpha\), D_N(a_)=diag(_a(xi_))_i_=1_,...,N_ denoting the _N_-th diagonal sampling matrix and \(\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c } g_1^{(\alpha)} & g_0^{(\alpha)} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ g_2^{(\alpha)} & g_1^{(\alpha)} & g_0^{(\alpha)} & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & g_2^{(\alpha)} & g_1^{(\alpha)} & \ddots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & g_0^{(\alpha)} \\ g_N^{(\alpha)} & \ddots & \cdots & g_2^{(\alpha)} & g_1^{(\alpha)} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N},\) (8.9) denoting the Hessenberg Toeplitz matrix, that is \((I_N-\theta G_{\alpha,N})u_N^{(m+1)}=(I_N+(1-\theta)G_{\alpha,N})u_N^{(m)}+\Delta tf_N^{(m,\theta)}.\) (8.10) In terms of notations, notice that D_N(a_) coincides with _DN(a_) as in (4.1) with _d=r_=1 if the domain of definition of the function _a_ is \[0,1\]. In general \([L_1,R_1]\neq[0,1]\) and hence \(\mathcal{D}_N(a)=D_N(\hat{a})\) with \(\hat{a}(\hat{x})=a(L_1+(R_1-L_1)\hat{x})\) and \(x=L_1+(R_1-L_1)\hat{x}\), \(\hat{x}\in[0,1]\): this specification is useful for applying the GLT axioms when deducing the Weyl distributions of the related matrix sequences, as indicated in Remark 8.2. Equation (8.10) leads to the following all-at-once formulation linear system \(\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c } I_N-\theta G_{\alpha,N} & & & \\ -(I_N+(1-\theta)G_{\alpha,N}) & I_N-\theta G_{\alpha,N} & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & -(I_N+(1-\theta)G_{\alpha,N}) & I_N-\theta G_{\alpha,N} \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ c } u_N^{(1)} \\ u_N^{(2)} \\ \vdots \\ u_N^{(M)} \end{array}\right]\)
\(=\left[\begin{array}{ c } \Delta tf_N^{(1,\theta)}+(I_N+(1-\theta)G_{\alpha,N})u_N^{(0)} \\ \Delta tf_N^{(2,\theta)} \\ \vdots \\ \Delta tf_N^{(M,\theta)} \end{array}\right].\) (8.11) This system can be compactly expressed using Kronecker products in the following form \(\bar{A}\bar{\mathbf{u}}=\bar{\mathbf{f}},\) (8.12) where \(\bar{A}=(I_M\otimes(I_N-\theta G_{\alpha,N})-Z_M\otimes(I_N+(1-\theta)G_{\alpha,N}))\in\mathbb{R}^{NM\times NM},\) (8.13) \(Z_N=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c } 0 & & & \\ 1 & 0 & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M},\) and \(\bar{\mathbf{u}},\bar{\mathbf{f}}\in\mathbb{R}^{NM\times 1}\). The coefficient matrix in (8.13) can therefore be expressed compactly using Kronecker products as \(\bar{A}=H_{\theta,M}\otimes G_{\alpha,N}+H_M\otimes I_N.\)

where the matrices _HM_ and \(H_{\theta,M}\) are defined as follows \(H_M=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c } 1 & & & \\ -1 & 1 & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M},H_{\theta,M}=-\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c } \theta & & & \\ 1-\theta & \theta & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & 1-\theta & \theta \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}.\) To calculate the solution of (8.12) in a parallel pattern form, we exchange the order of the Kronecker product in \(\bar{A}\). By pre-multiplying both sides of (8.14) with \((I_N\otimes H_{\theta,M})^{-1}\), we obtain an equivalent formulation \(A_{\alpha,N,M}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f},\) (8.15) where \(A_{\alpha,N,M}=G_{\alpha,N}\otimes I_M+I_N\otimes H_{\theta,M}^{-1}H_M=G_{\alpha,N}\otimes I_M+I_N\otimes Q_{\theta,M},\) with the matrix \(Q_{\theta,M}=H_{\theta,M}^{-1}H_M\) defined as \(Q_{\theta,M}=-\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c } \frac{1}{\theta} & & & & \\ \frac{-1}{\theta^2} & & \frac{1}{\theta} & & \\ \frac{-(\theta-1)}{\theta^3} & & \frac{-1}{\theta^2} & & \frac{1}{\theta} & \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\ \vdots & \ddots & \frac{-(\theta-1)}{\theta^3} & & \frac{-1}{\theta^2} & \frac{1}{\theta} \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}.\) (8.16) The transformed right-hand side is given by \(\mathbf{f}=(I_N\otimes H_{\theta,M})^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf{f}}=(I_N\otimes H_{\theta,M}^{-1})\widetilde{\mathbf{f}}\). ## Two-dimensional Let _N_1, _N_2 and _M_ be positive integers representing the number of interior spatial and temporal steps, respectively. \(y_j=L_2+j\Delta y,\Delta y=\frac{(R_2-L_2)}{(N_2+1)},0\le j\le N_2+1,\)

As in the one-dimensional setting, we adopt the shifted Grünwald finite difference scheme \[91\] to approximate the left-sided Riemann-Liouville fractional derivatives.
