Equivalently, \(\widetilde{\mathbf{f}}\) is formed by stacking the columns of the transpose of the reshaped matrix. ## 8.1.2 GLT, singular value, and eigenvalue analysis In the current section, we first introduce a basic definition, and then proceed with the GLT analysis of the coefficient matrix sequences derived from the previous approximation methods. More precisely the section is divided into two parts: in the first we study the matrix sequences arising from the space discretizations, both in 1D and 2D. Then, in the second part, we provide the GLT analysis for the global matrix sequences, incorporating also the term coming from the time discretization. ### GLT analysis of the space matrix sequences **Definition 8.1** _The Wiener class is the set of functions_ \(f(\theta)=\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^d}f_\mathbf{k}e^{i\langle\mathbf{k},\theta\rangle},\theta\in[-\pi,\pi]^d,\) _such that_ \(\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^d}|f_\mathbf{k}|<\infty,\) _where_ \(i=\sqrt{-1}\) _and_ \(\langle\mathbf{k},\theta\rangle=k_1\theta_1+\cdots+k_d\theta_d\)_. The Wiener class forms a sub-algebra of the continuous_ \(2\pi\)_-periodic functions defined on_ \([-\pi,\pi]^d\).

In this view, we begin by reporting the symbol associated with the matrix sequence \(\overline{G_{\alpha,n}}\) defined in equation (8.8). **Proposition 8.2** _Let_ \(\alpha\in(1,2)\)_. The symbol associated with_ \(\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\) _belongs to the Wiener class, and_ \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)=\sum_{k=-1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}e^{ik\xi_1}=e^{-i\xi_1}\left(1+e^{i(\xi_1+\pi)}\right)^\alpha,\xi_1\in[-\pi,\pi].\) **Proof:** Let us observe that \(\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}=[g_{i-j+1}^{(\alpha)}]_{i,j=1}^N\) with \(g_k^{(\alpha)}=0\) for _k\<_0, and let us define the function \(\sum_{k=-1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}e^{ik\xi_1}\). When \(\alpha\in(1,2)\), it is easy to see that \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)\) lies in the Wiener class. In detail, from Proposition 8.1 we know that \(g_0^{(\alpha)}=1>0,g_1^{(\alpha)}=-\alpha<0,g_k^{(\alpha)}>0\forall k\ge 2,g_k^{(\alpha)}=0\forall k<0.\) Then \(\sum_{k=-1}^\infty\left|g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}\right|=\left|g_0^{(\alpha)}\right|+\left|g_1^{(\alpha)}\right|+\sum_{k=1}^\infty\left|g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}\right|\)
\(=g_0^{(\alpha)}+\left(-g_1^{(\alpha)}\right)+\sum_{k=1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}\text{(since}g_0^{(\alpha)}>0,g_1^{(\alpha)}<0,g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}>0\text{for}k\ge 1\right)\)
\(=g_0^{(\alpha)}-g_1^{(\alpha)}+\sum_{k=1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}.\) (8.25) From Proposition (8.1), we have \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty g_k^{(\alpha)}=0\). Therefore, \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}=\sum_{k=2}^\infty g_k^{(\alpha)}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty g_k^{(\alpha)}-g_0^{(\alpha)}-g_1^{(\alpha)}=-g_0^{(\alpha)}-g_1^{(\alpha)}=-1+\alpha\) (8.26) Now, plugging (8.26) in (8.25), we find \(\sum_{k=-1}^\infty\left|g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}\right|=g_0^{(\alpha)}-g_1^{(\alpha)}+\left(-1+\alpha\right)=1+\alpha+\left(-1+\alpha\right)=2\alpha.\) (8.27) Since this sum is finite, \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)\) belongs to the Wiener class for \(\alpha\in(1,2)\).
To obtain an explicit formula for the symbol \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)\), let us recall the definition of \(g_k^{(\alpha)}\) given in (8.5) and rewrite \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)\) in the following manner \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)=\sum_{k=-1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\alpha)}e^{ik\xi_1}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty g_k^{(\alpha)}e^{i(k-1)\xi_1}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\left(-1\right)^k\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\alpha}{k}e^{i(k-1)\xi_1}.\) We now write (-1)_k_ as \(e^{ik\pi}\) so that \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\alpha}{k}e^{i(k-1)\xi_1}e^{ik\pi}=e^{-i\xi_1}\sum_{k=0}^\infty\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\alpha}{k}e^{ik(\xi_1+\pi)}.\)

Applying the well-known binomial series<tbc>

\((1+z)^\alpha=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\alpha}{k}z^k,z\in\mathbb{C},|z|\le 1,\alpha>0,\)

<tbc>with \(z=e^{i(\xi_1+\pi)}\), we finally deduce a very informative expression i.e.

\(f_\alpha(\xi_1)=e^{-i\xi_1}\left(1+e^{i(\xi_1+\pi)}\right)^\alpha.\)

In the two-dimensional case, \(\overline{G_{\alpha_1,N_1}}\) has the same symbol as obtained in Proposition 8.2. Similarly, the matrix \(\overline{G_{\alpha_2,N_2}}\) has the same Toeplitz-like structure as \(\overline{G_{\alpha_1,N_1}}\), with parameter \(\alpha_2\) in place of \(\alpha_1\). Therefore, its associated symbol is given by

\(f_{\alpha_2}(\xi_2)=e^{-i\xi_2}\left(1+e^{i(\xi_2+\pi)}\right)^{\alpha_2},\xi_2\in[-\pi,\pi],\)

which is the exact analogue of \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)\) obtained in Proposition 8.2.

**Proposition 8.3** _Let_ \(Q_{\theta,M}=H_{\theta,M}^{-1}H_M\)_. Then,_

\(\{Q_{\theta,M}\}_M\sim_\mathrm{GLT}q_\theta(\xi_3)\) (8.28)

_where_ \(q_\theta(\xi_3)=\frac{1-e^{i\xi_3}}{\theta+(1-\theta)e^{i\xi_3}}\).

**Proof:** In both the one and two-dimensional cases, both _H<sub>M</sub>_ and \(H_{\theta,M}\) are Toeplitz matrices generated by the symbols<tbc>

\(\rho_1(\xi_3)=1-e^{i\xi_3},\rho_2(\xi_3)=\theta+(1-\theta)e^{i\xi_3},\)

<tbc>respectively, where \(\xi_3\in[-\pi,\pi]\). According to the GLT algebra and the standard properties of Toeplitz sequences \[41, Section 6.2\], the matrix sequence \(Q_{\theta,M}=H_{\theta,M}^{-1}H_M\) is associated with the GLT symbol<tbc>

\(q_\theta(\xi_3)=\frac{\rho_1(\xi_3)}{\rho_2(\xi_3)}.\)

<tbc>Therefore,

\(\{Q_{\theta,M}\}_M\sim_\mathrm{GLT}q_\theta(\xi_3).\)

**Theorem 8.1** _If_ \(a:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) _is continuous a.e., then_

_a_1) \(\{\mathcal{D}_N(a)\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}a(x)f_\alpha(\xi_1),\)<tbc>

_a_2) \(\{\mathcal{D}_N(a)\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\}_N\sim_\sigma a(x)f_\alpha(\xi_1),\)

_with_ \(f_\alpha\) _as in Proposition 8.2._

**Proof:** To prove _a_1), we first recall that the argument relies on the fundamental properties of the GLT class, in particular the second part in GLT 2 and the third part stated in GLT 3. More precisely, we have \(\mathcal{D}_N(a)=D_N(a)=\mathrm{diag}_{i=1,2,\dots,N}a(x_i)\) and hence \(\{\mathcal{D}_N(a)=D_N(a)\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}a(x)\) by using GLT 2. Furthermore, by Proposition 8.2 via axiom GLT 2, we find \(\{\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}f_\alpha(\xi_1).\) In conclusion by equation (8.8) and GLT 3, we obtain _a_1) i.e. \(\{\mathcal{D}_N(a)\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}a(x)f_\alpha(\xi_1),\) so that, by invoking GLT 1, we infer _a_2). And what about _a3_) \(\{\mathcal{D}_N(a)\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\}_N\sim_\lambda a(x)f_\alpha(\xi_1)?\) Since \(G_{\alpha,N}\) is not Hermitian, its eigenvalue distribution cannot be immediately deduced from GLT 1, even if other tools are available \[21\].
To illustrate the relationship between the eigenvalue distributions and the associated symbols, we present two representative examples for which Figures 8.1-8.2 indicate that the question in _a_3) has a positive answer, which is clear in the constant coefficient case. Indeed, although the convergence is slow, we believe that the answer is positive even in the variable coefficient case.
In the one-dimensional case, we first consider the constant-coefficient matrix \(\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\) and compare its eigenvalues with sampled values of the symbol \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)\) (Figure 8.1). The two graphs almost superpose and hence we observe a positive answer to the question in _a_3) when _a(x_) is a constant function. The fact holds also formally because of the results in \[21\], where the authors study the canonical distribution of Toeplitz matrix sequences for a rich class of parametric generating functions which includes \(f_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\in(1,2)\). Hence \(\{\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\}_N\sim_\lambda f_\alpha(\xi_1).\) We then examine the variable-coefficient case \(D_N(a)\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\) with _a(x_)=_x_2+1, comparing the eigenvalues with sampled values of the symbol \(a(x)f_\alpha(\xi_1)\) (Figure 8.2). Also in this more complicate setting, the numerics suggest that the answer to the question in _a_3) is positive as reported Figure 8.2. We also tried the more degenerate case of _a(x_)=_x_2 and also in this case the agreement is remarkable. In fact, since _a(x_) is continuous with range \[0,1\], the range of \(a(x)f_\alpha(\xi_1)\) for fixed \(\xi_1\) is exactly the segment connecting the complex zero with the value \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)\): as a consequence the total range of the GLT symbol \(a(x)f_\alpha(\xi_1)\) is exactly the convex hull of the range of \(f_\alpha(\xi_1)\). On the other hand, since 1+_x_2 is continuous with range \[1,2\], the eigenvalues fill the disconnected (highly nonconvex) region \(\bigcup_{y\in[1,2]}y\mathrm{range}(f_\alpha)=\big\{yz:y\in[1,2],z\in\mathrm{range}(f_\alpha)\big\},\)

i.e. the union of the scaled copies of range\((f_\alpha)\) by the real factors \(y\in[1,2]\), in agreement with the behaviour depicted in Figure 8.2.

Conversely, the theoretical proof is not available yet and it will be the subject of future investigations, starting from the key tools given in \[21\].

The question _a_3) concerning the eigenvalue distribution of the non-Hermitian matrix sequence \(\{\mathcal{D}_N(a)\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\}_N\) deserves careful attention. Since the matrices are non-Hermitian, the GLT symbol obtained in _a_1) directly yields the singular value distribution but does not automatically imply the eigenvalue distribution. The numerical evidence presented in Figures 8.1-8.2 suggests that the same symbol may describe the eigenvalue distribution in this setting, and this is indeed rigorously established in the constant coefficient case by the results of Bogoya, Böttcher, and Grudsky \[21\]. However, for the variable coefficient case, a rigorous proof remains open. Thus, while the numerical observations are compelling, the eigenvalue distribution should be regarded as a conjecture supported by numerical evidence rather than a proven result.

As noted in the discussion following Theorems 8.3 and 8.4, the eigenvalue distribution of the space-time matrix sequences \(\{A_{\alpha,N,M}\}_{N,M}\) and \(\{A_{\alpha,\mathbf{n},M}\}_{\mathbf{n},M}\) is not

guaranteed by the GLT theory, since these matrices are non-Hermitian. The numerical results reported in this chapter indicate that the eigenvalue distribution may not follow the GLT symbol in the current setting, even when _a_ is chosen as a constant function. This contrasts with the spatial discretization case, where the numerical evidence was consistent with the symbol. The distinction is important: for non- Hermitian matrices, the GLT symbol provides a rigorous description of the singular value distribution, but the eigenvalue distribution requires additional analysis. In this work, we focus on preconditioning strategies that ensure weak clustering at one for the preconditioned matrix sequences, which is sufficient to guarantee fast convergence of the GMRES method without requiring a full characterization of the eigenvalue distribution of the original coefficient matrices. ## 8.2 Preconditioning strategy: 1D space setting Since the considered coefficient matrices are non-symmetric and exhibit a Toeplitz- like structure, Krylov subspace methods such as GMRES \[107\] are well-suited for solving the linear systems in (8.15), benefiting from efficient fast matrix-vector products. To further enhance the efficiency and robustness of these iterative solvers, the use of preconditioning techniques is an essential strategy \[15\].
Here, we propose a block circulant preconditioner for _AN,M_, obtained by replacing the Toeplitz block \(\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\) with a circulant counterpart \(C_{\alpha,N}\), while keeping \(Q_{\theta,M}\) unchanged. Since our constant term \(\gamma=\Delta t/(\Delta x)^\alpha\) is sufficiently large, we apply the circulant approximation only to \(\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\) and retain \(Q_{\theta,M}\) as it is. In order to preserve the circulant structure, instead of using the diagonal matrix _DN(a_), we replace it with a constant scalar multiplier given by the average of the diffusion coefficients \(d=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^Nd_i,\) where _di_ are the diagonal entries of _DN(a_). Of course the choice of the circulant counterpart is far from unique and several proposals are treated in three decades of relevant literature. From theoretical studies, we know that Strang-type approaches are better than Frobenius optimal approximations, especially for matching the small eigenvalues and especially when the generating functions are smooth. However, here we have lower Hessenberg structures and hence, together with the usual Strang approximation, we take the Strang-type matrix chosen taking into account the largest coefficients, i.e. those on the first column, except the last which is replaced by that on upper main diagonal. More precisely, we consider these two possible circulant approximations, where the first preconditioner is defined as \(\widetilde{P}_{\alpha,N,M}=\gamma d\widetilde{C}_{\alpha,N}\otimes I_M+I_N\otimes Q_{\theta,M}\) (8.35) where \(\widetilde{C}_{\alpha,N}\) is the standard Strang circulant approximation, while the latter is defined as \(\widehat{P}_{\alpha,N,M}=\gamma d\widehat{C}_{\alpha,N}\otimes I_M+I_N\otimes Q_{\theta,M}\) (8.36) where \(\widehat{C}_{\alpha,N}\) is the circulant matrix generated by the vector \(\left[g_1^{(\alpha)},\dots,g_{N-1}^{(\alpha)},g_0^{(\alpha)}\right]\), that is by the first column of \(\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\) where the last entry \(g_N^{(\alpha)}\) has been replaced by

the coefficient \(g_0^{(\alpha)}\), which is nonnegligible while \(g_N^{(\alpha)}\) tends to zero as _N_ tends to infinity; see also the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma \[141\].
It is well known that any circulant matrix _CN_ can be diagonalized by the Fourier matrix, i.e., \(C_N=F_N\Lambda_NF_N^*,\) where _FN_ is the unitary matrix given by (3.3) and \(\Lambda_N\) is a diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of _CN_. **Theorem 8.5** _Let_ \(P\in\{\widetilde{P}_{\alpha,N,M},\widehat{P}_{\alpha,N,M}\}\) _as defined in_ (8.35) _and in_ (8.36)_, respectively. Set_ \(U=F_N\otimes I_M\)_. Then P is unitarily similar to a block diagonal matrix, namely_ \(U^*PU=\mathrm{blkdiag}\big(\gamma d\lambda_jI_M+Q_{\theta,M}\big)_{j=1}^N,\) (8.37) _where_ \(\lambda_j\)_, j_=1_,...,N, denote the eigenvalues of the circulant block_ \(\tilde{C}_{\alpha,N}\) _or_ \(\hat{C}_{\alpha,N}\)_, respectively. Moreover, each diagonal block_ \(D_j=\gamma d\lambda_jI_M+Q_{\theta,M},j=1,\dots,N,\) (8.38) _is an invertible lower triangular Toeplitz matrix (ILTT)._ **Proof:** Substituting the diagonalization of the circulant matrix into (8.35) (or into (8.36) equivalently) gives \(P=\gamma dF_N\Lambda_{\alpha,N}F_N^*\otimes I_M+I_N\otimes Q_{\theta,M}.\) Then, using the mixed-product property \((A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=AC\otimes BD\), it holds that \(U^*PU=\left(F_N^*\otimes I_M\right)\left(\gamma dF_N\Lambda_{\alpha,N}F_N^*\otimes I_M+I_N\otimes Q_{\theta,M}\right)\left(F_N\otimes I_M\right)\)
\(=\gamma dF_N^*F_N\Lambda_{\alpha,N}F_N^*F_N\otimes I_M+F_N^*F_N\otimes Q_{\theta,M}\)
\(=\gamma d\Lambda_{\alpha,N}\otimes I_M+I_N\otimes Q_{\theta,M}.\) Since \(\Lambda_{\alpha,N}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N)\), it follows that \(\Lambda_{\alpha,N}\otimes I_M=\mathrm{blkdiag}(\lambda_1I_M,\dots,\lambda_NI_M),I_N\otimes Q_{\theta,M}=\mathrm{blkdiag}(Q_{\theta,M},\dots,Q_{\theta,M}).\) Hence their sum is block diagonal with blocks \(\gamma d\lambda_jI_M+Q_{\theta,M}\), _j_=1_,...,N_. Finally, note that \(Q_{\theta,M}\) is a lower triangular Toeplitz matrix, and adding a scalar multiple of the identity preserves both the Toeplitz and lower triangular structure. Thus, taking into account that \(H_{\theta,M}\) is invertible, each block \(D_j=\gamma d\lambda_jI_M+Q_{\theta,M}=H_{\theta,M}^{-1}\left(\gamma d\lambda_jH_{\theta,M}+H_M\right)\) is lower triangular Toeplitz. Now we can conclude that _Dj_ is nonsingular because \(\gamma d\lambda_jH_{\theta,M}+H_M\) is lower bidiagonal and its invertibility is decided by the diagonal elements, which are of the form \(1-\gamma d\lambda_j\theta\) which can not vanish since the eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) have all nonzero imaginary part. With the latter the proof is concluded. **Remark 8.3** _The block diagonalization in Theorem 8.5 shows that applying P_-1 _to a given vector v can be performed through the following three steps._ 1. _Step 1: compute_ \(\dot{v}=(F_N^*\otimes I_M)v\).

2. _Step 2: compute_ \(\ddot{v}=\mathrm{blkdiag}\left(D_j^{-1}\right)_{j=1}^N\dot{v},D_j=\gamma d\lambda_jI_M+Q_{\theta,M}\). _3._ _Step 3: compute_ \(\ddot{v}=(F_N\otimes I_M)\ddot{v}\). _The resulting total cost is of the order O(NM_log(_N_)) _which is optimal in our setting, since it is the same order of the cost of a matrix-vector product with the original coefficient matrix._
_From Theorem 8.5, both Steps 1 and 3 involve Fourier transforms in the spatial dimension and can be performed in_ O(_NM_log_N_) _operations using FFT. Step 2 requires solving N independent systems with coefficient matrices Dj, which are ILTT matrices. Since the inverse of an ILTT matrix is also ILTT, its first column can be computed in_ O(_M_log_M_) _operations by the divide-and-conquer inversion algorithm \[28\]. Therefore, Step 2 can be carried out in_ O(_NM_log_M_) _operations. In total, applying P_-1_v requires_ O(_NM_log_N+NM_log_M), which is nearly linear in the problem size. Moreover, the N systems in Step 2 are completely independent and can be solved in parallel, making the preconditioner highly efficient in practice. Of course, if the matrix_ \(Q_{\theta,M}\) _is not stored explicitly as in (8.16), then it can be viewed as_ \(H_{\theta,M}^{-1}H_M\) _so that_ \(D_j=H_{\theta,M}^{-1}\left(\gamma d\lambda_jH_{\theta,M}+H_M\right),\) _which leads to a more efficient computation since_ \(H_{\theta,M}\) _and_ \(\gamma d\lambda_jH_{\theta,M}+H_M\)_, j_=1_,...,N, are all lower bidiagonal. With this choice, for solving n linear systems with coefficient matrices Dj, j_=1_,...,N, the related cost is reduced from_ O(_NM_log_M_) _to_ O(_NM)._ We conclude the current section with a GLT/clustering analysis of the preconditioned matrix sequences. **Theorem 8.6** _Let_ \(P_{N,M}\in\{\widetilde{P}_{\alpha,N,M},\widehat{P}_{\alpha,N,M}\}\)_, as defined in_ (8.35) _and in_ (8.36)_, respectively. Then,_ \(\{P_{N,M}\}_{N,M}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\gamma^*\hat{d}f_\alpha(\xi_1)+q_\theta(\xi_3),\) _with_ \(\hat{d}=\int_\Omega a(x)\) _and d=dN converging to_ \(\hat{d}\) _as N tends to infinity and_ \(\{P_{N,M}^{-1}A_{\alpha,N,M}\}_{N,M}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\frac{\gamma^*a(x)f_\alpha(\xi_1)+q_\theta(\xi_3)}{\gamma^*\hat{d}f_\alpha(\xi_1)+q_\theta(\xi_3)}.\) **Proof:** From the literature \[27, 35\], it is known that \(\{\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}-\widetilde{C}_{\alpha,N}\}_N\sim_\sigma 0\). The same clustering at zero is true for \(\{\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}-\widehat{C}_{\alpha,N}\}_N\) since the approximation is even better (the only neglected coefficient is \(g_N^{(\alpha)}\)). In both cases the clustering is strong since the generating function is continuous and \(2\pi\)-periodic \[27, 35\]. Now by axiom GLT 2, part 3, \(\{\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}-C_{\alpha,N}\}_N\sim_\sigma 0\) if and only if \(\{\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}-C_{\alpha,N}\}_N\sim_\mathrm{GLT}0\), \(C_{\alpha,N}\in\{\widetilde{C}_{\alpha,N},\widehat{C}_{\alpha,N}\}\). Since \(\{\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\}_N\) is also a GLT matrix sequence, by axiom GLT 3, part 3, it is clear that both the approximating matrix sequences \(\{\widetilde{C}_{\alpha,N}\}_N\), \(\{\widehat{C}_{\alpha,N}\}_N\) are both GLT matrix sequences with the same GLT symbol as \(\{\overline{G_{\alpha,N}}\}_N\), as in Theorem 8.1 and Remark 8.1.
By following the very same steps as in the proof of Theorem 8.1, Theorem 8.3 and of the reasoning in Remark 8.1, we end up with the conclusion \(\{P_{N,M}\}_{N,M}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\gamma^*\hat{d}f_\alpha(\xi_1)+q_\theta(\xi_3)\)

with \(\hat{d}=\int_\Omega a(x)\) and _d=d<sub>N</sub>_ converging to \(\hat{d}\) as _N_ tends to infinity. As a consequence

\(\{P_{N,M}^{-1}A_{\alpha,N,M}\}_{N,M}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\frac{\gamma^*a(x)f_\alpha(\xi_1)+q_\theta(\xi_3)}{\gamma^*\hat{d}f_\alpha(\xi_1)+q_\theta(\xi_3)},\)

by using axiom GLT 3, part 4 and part 3.

Notice that this GLT symbol is equal to 1 in the constant coefficient case since \(a=\hat{d}\), so ensuring a clustering at 1 for the preconditioned matrix sequence.

## 8.3 Preconditioning strategy: 2D space setting

In the two-dimensional case, the spatial discretization yields a two-level Toeplitz structure, while the temporal discretization adds a further level so that a three-level matrix is obtained, in the all-at-once formulation. To construct an efficient preconditioner for this system, we approximate only the spatial part using a multilevel circulant matrix, while the temporal block \(Q_{\theta,M}\) remains unchanged. The spatial operator \(G_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}\) is the diagonal sampling matrix _D_**<sub>n</sub>**(_a_) multiplied with the two-level Toeplitz matrix<tbc>

\(U_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}=\gamma_1\overline{G_{\alpha_1,N_1}}\otimes I_{N_2}+I_{N_1}\otimes\gamma_2\overline{G_{\alpha_2,N_2}}.\)

<tbc>To form the preconditioner, we replace \(U_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}\) with its two-level circulant approximation

\(C_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}=\gamma_1C_{\alpha_1,N_1}\otimes I_{N_2}+I_{N_1}\otimes\gamma_2C_{\alpha_2,N_2},\)

where \(C_{\alpha_r,N_r}\), _r_=1,2 are the circulant matrices already considered in the one- dimensional case, i.e., \(C_{\alpha_r,N_r}\in\{\widetilde{C}_{\alpha_r,N_r},\widehat{C}_{\alpha_r,N_r}\}\).

Since the constants \(\gamma_1=\Delta t/(\Delta x)^{\alpha_1}\) and \(\gamma_2=\Delta t/(\Delta y)^{\alpha_2}\) are sufficiently large, the circulant approximation is applied only to the spatial blocks, while the time stepping matrix \(Q_{\theta,M}\) is left unchanged. As before, to preserve the circulant structure, the diagonal sampling matrix _D_**<sub>n</sub>**(_a_) is replaced by the spatial average of the diffusion coefficient<tbc>

\(d=\frac{1}{N_1N_2}\sum_{i_1=1}^{N_1}\sum_{i_2=1}^{N_2}a_{i_1,i_2},\)

<tbc>and the preconditioner is defined as

\(\widetilde{P}_{\alpha,\mathbf{n},M}=d\widetilde{C}_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}\otimes I_M+I_\mathbf{n}\otimes Q_{\theta,M},\) (8.39)

or

\(\widehat{P}_{\alpha,\mathbf{n},M}=d\widehat{C}_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}\otimes I_M+I_\mathbf{n}\otimes Q_{\theta,M},\) (8.40)

where, clearly, it holds

\(C_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}=F_\mathbf{n}^*\Lambda_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}F_\mathbf{n}\)

with \(C_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}\in\{\widetilde{C}_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}},\widehat{C}_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}\}\), \(F_\mathbf{n}=F_{N_1}\otimes F_{N_2}\) and \(\Lambda_{\alpha,\mathbf{n}}=\gamma_1\Lambda_{\alpha_1,N_1}\otimes I_{N_2}+I_{N_1}\otimes\gamma_2\Lambda_{\alpha_2,N_2}\). Now we give only the statement of results regarding the invertibility of _P_, the computation cost related to the chosen preconditioner, and the clustering results for the related preconditioned matrix sequence. The tools and the structure of the proofs follow verbatim those of Section 8.2.

**Theorem 8.7** _Let_ \(P\in\{\widetilde{P}_{\unknown,\mathbf{n},M},\widehat{P}_{\unknown,\mathbf{n},M}\}\) _be defined as in_ (8.39) _and as in_ (8.40)_, respectively. Set_ \(U=F_\mathbf{n}\otimes I_M\)_. ## 8.4.2 GMRES performance in the _d_-dimensional space setting, _d_=1,2

We consider the one-dimensional variable-coefficient space-fractional diffusion equation (8.2):

\(\frac{\partial u(x,t)}{\partial t}=x^2D_x^\alpha u(x,t)+f(x,t),x\in(0,1),t\in(0,1],\)

with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions _u_(0_,t_)=_u_(1_,t_)=0 and initial condition _u(x,_0)=0.

We choose the exact solution as

\(u(x,t)=t^2x^2(1-x)^2.\)

The corresponding source term is given by

\(f(x,t)=2tx^2(1-x)^2-x^2t^2\left[\frac{2}{\Gamma(3-\alpha)}x^{2-\alpha}-\frac{12}{\Gamma(4-\alpha)}x^{3-\alpha}+\frac{24}{\Gamma(5-\alpha)}x^{4-\alpha}\right].\)

Thus, in this section, we investigate the practical performance of the GMRES iterative solver for the all-at-once linear system arising from the one-dimensional discretization given in equation (8.15), with the time-stepping parameter set to \(\theta=0.5\) (Crank–Nicolson method). We compare the behavior of GMRES applied to both the original (non-preconditioned) system and the system preconditioned by a circulant structure-preserving preconditioners as defined in Section 8.2, to illustrate the impact of preconditioning on convergence and computational efficiency. First, the experiments are conducted for the one-dimensional constant-coefficient fractional diffusion problem (_a(x_)=1), and then for the one-dimensional variable-coefficient fractional diffusion problem with coefficient _a(x_)=_x_<sup>2</sup>+1, and _a(x_)=_x_<sup>2</sup>. The initial vector is set to zero, the tolerance is 10<sup>-8</sup>, and the maximum number of iterations equals the matrix dimension. s 8.3, 8.5, and 8.7 summarize the numerical performance of the GMRES method both for the unpreconditioned system and the preconditioned ones. Here, _N_ denotes the number of spatial grid points and _M_ the number of time levels and the average number of GMRES iterations per time step are reported in the columns. s 8.4 and 8.6 report the averaged total computational time (in seconds) for solving the entire problem 10 times.

As the discretization becomes finer, the unpreconditioned system exhibits a substantial growth in both iteration counts and CPU times, reflecting the increasing ill-conditioning of the coefficient matrix. The computational effort is mainly influenced by the spatial parameter _N_, as larger _N_ values lead to denser matrices and slower convergence, while variations in _M_ have a comparatively smaller effect.

When the preconditioners are applied, GMRES shows a significant improvement in convergence. The iteration numbers remain nearly constant for increasing _N_ and _M_, and the corresponding CPU times grow only mildly with the problem size. This behavior demonstrates the mesh-independent convergence of the preconditioned system and confirms that the preconditioners effectively captures the spectral structure of the matrix, resulting in a well-clustered spectrum and reduced computational cost.

## Chapter 9

### Maximal results for geometric means of GLT sequences

This chapter presents and discusses the main contributions of our recent work [65] on the spectral distribution of geometric means of HPD GLT matrix sequences. The spectral distribution of the geometric mean for two HPD GLT matrix sequences was studied in [1]. It was shown that if at least one of the GLT symbols \(\kappa\) and \(\xi\) is invertible almost everywhere, the geometric mean sequence remains GLT. In the scalar case _r_=1, this hypothesis is equivalent to requiring that at least one of \(\kappa,\xi\) is nonzero almost everywhere; for matrix-valued symbols _r\>_1, the correct condition is invertibility a.e., i.e. the smallest eigenvalue of the symbol is positive on a set of full measure. The symbol is \((\kappa\xi)^{1/2}\) in the scalar or commuting case, and more generally \(G(\kappa,\xi)=\kappa^{1/2}\left(\kappa^{-1/2}\xi\kappa^{-1/2}\right)^{1/2}\kappa^{1/2}\) in the noncommutative case. In this chapter, we address the open question of whether these assumptions can be relaxed. Motivated by the observation that invertibility is primarily required due to noncommutativity, we rigorously prove that when the GLT symbols \(\kappa\) and \(\xi\) commute, the invertibility condition can be completely removed in the case where _r_=1 and \(d\ge 1\).

Furthermore, we investigate the limitations of this maximal result through both theoretical analysis and extensive numerical experiments. We show that, in the general block case (_r\>_1), if the GLT symbols \(\kappa\) and \(\xi\) are both non-invertible and do not commute, the geometric mean sequence {_G(A<sub>n</sub>,B<sub>n</sub>_)}_<sub>n</sub>_ still forms a GLT matrix sequence with some symbol \(\psi\); however, this symbol may not coincide with the classical geometric mean \(G(\kappa,\xi)\), or, in some cases, \(G(\kappa,\xi)\) may not be well defined. These findings demonstrate that our main results are indeed maximal: relaxing either the commutativity or invertibility assumptions can lead to fundamentally different or ill-posed spectral behavior.

A significant advance in this paper is the introduction and use of momentary GLT symbols (see [23, 24, 7]), which provide a finer description of the spectral distribution, especially for finite-size matrices and cases where the product \(\kappa\xi\) is zero or the symbols are rank-deficient. Momentary symbols incorporate the effects of small-norm perturbations, allowing the observed richer spectral structures such as secondary eigenvalue distributions in numerical experiments to be explained within an extended GLT framework.

The work further investigates the extremal spectral behavior of the geometric mean, with particular focus on the asymptotic rate at which the minimal eigenvalues decay as the matrix size increases. Through detailed numerical experiments, we observe that the decay rate of the minimal eigenvalue is intimately connected to the order of vanishing (i.e., the multiplicity of zeros) of the associated GLT symbol.

## 9.1 Geometric mean of GLT matrix sequences We begin by recalling the definition of the geometric mean of two HPD matrices. Given two HPD matrices \(A,B\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\), their geometric mean is defined by \(G(A,B):=A^{1/2}\big(A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}\big)^{1/2}A^{1/2}=G(B,A).\) (9.1) This definition preserves symmetry, positive definiteness, and the key variational properties of the two arguments \[3, 16\]. For matrix sequences {_An}n_ and {_Bn}n_ of HPD matrices, we write {_G(An,Bn_)}_n_ for the corresponding sequence of geometric means. The following result, due to \[1, Theorem 4\], extends \[41, Theorem 10.2\] to a broader setting. **Theorem 9.1 \[1\], Theorem 4)** _Let r_=1 _and_ \(d\ge 1\)_. Suppose_ \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\) _and_ \(\{B_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\xi\)_, where_ \(A_\mathbf{n},B_\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{n}\) _for every multi-index **n**, with_ P**n** _denoting the set of HPD matrices of multi-index **n**. Assume that at least one of between_ \(\kappa\) _and_ \(\xi\) _is nonzero almost everywhere. Then_ \(\{G(A_\mathbf{n},B_\mathbf{n})\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\left(\kappa\xi\right)^{1/2},\) (9.2) _and_ \(\{G(A_\mathbf{n},B_\mathbf{n})\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_{\sigma,\lambda}\left(\kappa\xi\right)^{1/2}.\) (9.3) Using the topological a.c.s. notion, we now show that the thesis of the previous theorem holds without assuming that at least one between \(\kappa\) and \(\xi\) is invertible almost everywhere (a.e.), thus proving \[41, Conjecture 10.1\]. We make use of Axioms GLT 1, GLT 2, GLT 3, GLT 4, GLT 5, GLT 6 as reported in Section 4.6. **Theorem 9.2** _Let r_=1 _and_ \(d\ge 1\)_. Assume_ \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa\) _and_ \(\{B_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\xi\)_, where_ \(A_\mathbf{n},B_\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{n}\) _for every multi-index **n**. Then_ \(\{G(A_\mathbf{n},B_\mathbf{n})\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\left(\kappa\xi\right)^{1/2},\)
\(\{G(A_\mathbf{n},B_\mathbf{n})\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_{\sigma,\lambda}\left(\kappa\xi\right)^{1/2}.\) **Proof:** We have \(\{A_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa,\) (9.4) \(\{B_\mathbf{n}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\xi,\) (9.5) where \(\kappa,\xi:[0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{C}\) and _A_**n**_,B_**n** are Hermitian positive definite matrices \(\forall\mathbf{n}\). Therefore \(\kappa,\xi:[0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_0^+\) almost everywhere: furthermore, we assume that \(\mu_{2d}(\kappa\equiv 0)>0\) and \(\mu_{2d}(\xi\equiv 0)>0\), so that the hypotheses of \[41, Theorem 10.2\] for _d_=1 and of Theorem 9.1 for _d\>_1 are violated. Let \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(\kappa_\varepsilon=\kappa+\varepsilon\) and let \(A_{\mathbf{n},\varepsilon}=A_\mathbf{n}+\varepsilon I_{N(\mathbf{n})}\), where _I__N_(**_n_**) denotes the identity matrix of size _N_(**_n_**). By the first part of GLT 2 (the identity is a special Toeplitz matrix with GLT symbol 1), we have \(\{\varepsilon I_{\nu(\mathbf{n})}=T_\mathbf{n}(\varepsilon)\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\varepsilon\), where \(T_\mathbf{n}(\varepsilon)\) denotes the Toeplitz matrix generated by the constant function \(\varepsilon\). Now, by exploiting linearity, i.e. the second item of GLT 3, it follows that \(\{A_{\mathbf{n},\varepsilon}\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\kappa_\varepsilon,\kappa_\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon\text{a.e.},\)

since \(\kappa,\xi\ge 0\) a.e. due to (9.4) and (9.5). Hence, we are again in the framework of Theorem 9.1. Therefore, by Theorem 9.1 we conclude that the sequence of geometric means satisfies the GLT relation<tbc>

\(\{G(A_{\mathbf{n},\varepsilon},B_\mathbf{n})\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\left(\kappa_\varepsilon\xi\right)^\frac{1}{2}.\)

<tbc>Furthermore, we apply the full ∗-algebra framework of the GLT matrix sequences as in \[1, Section 2.9\]. More precisely, by third item of GLT 3 followed by GLT 6 with the function \(f(z)=z^\frac{1}{4}\), we obtain<tbc>

\(\{G(A_\mathbf{n},B_\mathbf{n})\}_\mathbf{n}\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\left(\kappa\xi\right)^{1/2},\)

**Remark 9.1 (Intuition on the generalization)** _One of the basic but key ingredients of the previous proof is that scalar-valued functions commute. Hence, it is reasonable to expect that the same proof also works in the case of d-level r-block GLT matrix sequences, when assuming that the symbols commute. In turn, the generating function is also the _d_-variate, \(r\times r\) matrix-valued GLT symbol of the _d_-level, _r_-block Toeplitz matrix sequence.
Although the distribution results are also valid for general _d_-level, _r_-block GLT matrix sequences, this is no longer true in general for the extremal behavior and for the localization results, unless we add supplementary assumptions, such as requiring the sequence to be generated by a _matrix-valued linear positive operator_ (LPO), i.e. a linear operator from the space of matrix-valued functions to the space of matrices that preserves positive semidefiniteness; see \[120, 128\]. We observe that the geometric mean can be seen as a monotone operator with respect to its two variables, and the monotonicity is implied when we consider an LPO, even if the converse is not true. Hence, it is also interesting to verify which properties are maintained by a geometric mean of two _d_-level, _r_-block GLT matrix sequences in terms of its GLT symbol, when the latter exists. According to the previous discussion, the remainder of the section considers numerical experiments in the following directions: • the validation of the distribution results in the commuting setting as in Theorem 9.2 and Theorem 9.4; • connections of the previous results with the notion of Toeplitz and GLT momentary symbols and the extremal behavior compared to the GLT symbol; • evidence that Theorem 9.2 and Theorem 9.4 are maximal, by taking GLT matrix sequences with noncommuting symbols which are both not invertible almost everywhere. All numerical experiments are performed using MATLAB R2022b on a laptop equipped with an 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-1155G7 CPU running at 2.50 GHz, with 16 GB of RAM. The operating system was Windows 11 Pro (version 23H2, build 22631.5189).

## 9.2.1 Validation of the distribution results

**Example 1**

Let _d_=1 and consider the following two matrix-sequences {_A<sub>n</sub>}<sub>n</sub>_, {_B<sub>n</sub>}<sub>n</sub>_, with \(A_n=D_n(a)+\frac{1}{n^4}I_n\) and \(B_n=T_n(3+2cos(\theta))\), where \(T_n(\cdot)\) denotes the Toeplitz operator for _d_=1, as introduced in Section 3.1, _D<sub>n</sub>(a_) represents the diagonal matrix generated by the continuous function<tbc>

\(a(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
0, & x\in[0,\frac{1}{2}), \\
1, & x\in[\frac{1}{2},1].
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>Because of Theorem 9.2, the geometric mean of these two sequences, that is {_G(A<sub>n</sub>,B<sub>n</sub>_)}_<sub>n</sub>_, satisfies the GLT relation:

\(\left\{G\left(A_n,B_n\right)\right\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\sqrt{a(x)(3+2cos(\theta))},\)

where the corresponding GLT symbols are explicitly given by \(\kappa=a(x)\) and \(\xi=3+2cos(\theta)\).

**Eigenvalue distribution**

We numerically analyze the spectral behavior of the geometric mean _G(A<sub>n</sub>,B<sub>n</sub>_) from **Example 1**. The eigenvalues of this geometric mean are computed for various increasing dimensions _n_ and compared with the uniformly sampled points from the GLT symbol \(\sqrt{a(x)(3+2cos(\theta))}\). In Figure 9.1, numerical results strongly indicate that the GLT symbol accurately characterizes the eigenvalue distribution of the geometric mean. As _n_ grows, the eigenvalue distribution closely matches the GLT symbol, giving evidence of the theoretical findings in Theorem 9.2.

## 9.2.2 Distribution results and momentary symbols ### Example 2 Let _d_=1 and define the matrix sequences {_An}n_, {_Bn}n_, with \(A_n=D_n(a)+\frac{1}{n^4}I_n\), \(C_n=T_n(3+2cos(\theta))\) and \(B_n=\left(D_n(1-a)+\frac{1}{n^4}I_n\right)C_n\left(D_n(1-a)+\frac{1}{n^4}I_n\right)\), where _Dn(a_) is the diagonal matrix generated by the piecewise continuous function _a(x_) given in **Example 1**. Then, the geometric mean sequence explicitly satisfies the GLT relation: \(\left\{G\left(A_n,B_n\right)\right\}_n\sim_\mathrm{GLT}\sqrt{a(x)(1-a(x))(3+2cos\theta)}\)
\(=a(x)(1-a(x))\sqrt{3+2cos\theta}=0\) where \(\kappa=a(x),\xi=(1-a(x))(3+2cos(\theta)).\) The zero-valued symbol arises naturally due to the definition of the piecewise function _a(x_): \(\bullet\) For \(x\in[0,\frac{1}{2})\), we have _a(x_)=0. Thus, the term _a(x_)(1-_a(x_)) becomes zero. \(\bullet\) For \(x\in[\frac{1}{2},1]\), we have _a(x_)=1. In this interval, the factor 1-_a(x_) becomes zero, making _a(x_)(1-_a(x_))=0. ### Eigenvalue distribution The eigenvalue distribution of {_G(An,Bn_)}_n_ is numerically analyzed for increasing matrix dimensions _n_. Since the GLT symbol for this example is zero, by Theorem 9.2 we expect the eigenvalues to concentrate along the zero line. Interestingly, numerical results reveal an additional spectral structure beyond Theorem 9.2. For smaller values of _n_, eigenvalues align closely with zero, as predicted by the GLT symbol. However, some eigenvalues appear above this level, forming a secondary symbol. This phenomenon is attributed to momentary symbols, as discussed in the introduction (see [23, 24, 7]). As _n_ increases, these elevated eigenvalues shift upwards reaching approximately 10-3 for _n_=40 (shown in the Figure 9.2) and 10-4 for _n_=80.

## 9.2.3 Minimal eigenvalues and conditioning

In this section, we analyze the extremal spectral behavior and conditioning of the geometric mean sequence {_G(A<sub>n</sub>,B<sub>n</sub>_)}_<sub>n</sub>_, focusing on its dependence on the analytical properties of the corresponding GLT symbol. This approach follows prior studies on extremal eigenvalues in structured matrix settings, particularly in Toeplitz matrices \[25, 115, 116, 127\] and block Toeplitz matrices \[117, 118\], as well as variable coefficient differential operators, including multilevel cases with _d\>_1 \[98, 139, 126\]. In the case of variable coefficient differential operators it is worth noticing that extremal spectral results do not stem from the GLT theory but from a combination of GLT tools and properties which are typical of linear positive operators \[128, 120\]. Here, we restrict our attention to the unilevel scalar setting with _d=r_=1, considering **Example 1** and **Example 2**.

**Example 1: minimal eigenvalue**

## 9.2.4 Numerical study: noncommuting, rank-deficient symbols

In this section, through numerical test, we investigate the eigenvalue distribution of the geometric means {_G(A<sub>n</sub>,B<sub>n</sub>_)}_<sub>n</sub>_ with

\(G(A_n,B_n)=A_n^{1/2}\big(A_n^{-1/2}B_nA_n^{-1/2}\big)^{1/2}A_n^{1/2},\)

where {_A<sub>n</sub>}<sub>n</sub>_ and {_B<sub>n</sub>}<sub>n</sub>_ are HPD GLT matrix sequences with \(r\times r\) matrix-valued symbols \(\kappa,\xi\). The GLT matrix sequences are specifically chosen with GLT symbols so that:

1. they are rank-deficient on a subset of positive Lebesgue measure; and

2. they do not commute pointwise on a set of positive measure.

These hypotheses clearly set the problem outside the scope of commuting or almost everywhere invertible cases treated in Theorems 9.2 and in Theorem 9.4.

Our tests provide evidence for two phenomena:

\begin{tabular}{ccc}
_n_ & \(\tau_j\) & \(\alpha_j\) \\ 40 & \(3.9177\times 10^{-7}\) & 4.0003 \\ 80 & \(2.4480\times 10^{-8}\) & 4.0040 \\ 160 & \(1.5259\times 10^{-9}\) & 4.0009 \\ 320 & \(9.5367\times 10^{-11}\) & \\ \end{tabular}

9.2: Numerical behaviour of the minimal eigenvalue.

**(i)** The support of the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution of {_G(An,Bn_)}_n_ coincides with the intersection set \(\text{essRan}(\kappa)\cap\text{essRan}(\xi)\) see Section 9.2.4. **(ii)** The eigenvalues appear to converge in distribution to a candidate symbol which is rank-deficient and, in general, distinct from the classical geometric mean \(G(\kappa,\xi)\). Clearly, the relation \(G(A_n,B_n)\sim_\text{GLT}G(\kappa,\xi)\) cannot hold under hypotheses 1.-2., and the experiments show the substantial differences in this case compared to the commuting or invertible scenarios. If this case can be studied within the GLT framework, it requires a more technical application of GLT and a.c.s. theory, along with a deeper functional calculus of matrix means. ## Setup of the numerical experiments Below, we provide the setup of the numerical tets.
We construct four pairs of unilevel GLT matrix sequences {_An}n,{Bn}n_, whose symbols simultaneously satisfy the hypothesis stated at the beginning of Section 9.2.4 (rank deficiency and non-commutation). These examples are organized according to the property of rank loss: • **Case 1** - each symbol is full rank on a set of positive measure; • **Case 2** - each symbol is rank-deficient almost everywhere. **Case 1, Example 1.**
Define \(f(\theta)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } 0, & \theta\in[-\pi,0], \\ \theta, & \theta\in(0,\pi], \end{array}\right.g(\theta)=f(-\theta),\) and set \(F(\theta)=f(\theta)\otimes\left[\begin{array}{ c c } 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{array}\right],G(\theta)=g(\theta)\otimes\left[\begin{array}{ c c } 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{array}\right].\) With the \(2n\times 2n\) Toeplitz matrices _Tn(F_) and _Tn(G_), define \(A_n=T_n(F)+\frac{1}{n^3}I_{2n},B_n=T_n(G)+\frac{1}{n^3}I_{2n}.\) (9.10) **Case 1, Example 2.**
Let \(\chi_{[-a,a]}\) be the characteristic function of [-_a,a_], \(0 \(f(\theta)=\chi_{[-1/2,1/2]}(\theta),g(\theta)=\chi_{[-1/4,1/4]}(\theta),\)
\(A=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{array}\right],B=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{array}\right],\)
\(F(\theta)=f(\theta)\otimes A,G(\theta)=g(\theta)\otimes B.\) Define \(A_n=T_n(F)+\frac{1}{n^3}I_{2n},B_n=T_n(G)+\frac{1}{n^3}I_{2n}.\) (9.11)

**Case 2, Example 1.**
With \(f(\theta)=2-cos\theta\), \(g(\theta)=3+cos\theta\) and rank one blocks \(A=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{array}\right],B=\left[\begin{array}{ c c } 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{array}\right],\) let \(F(\theta)=f(\theta)\otimes A\) and \(G(\theta)=g(\theta)\otimes B\). Set \(A_n=T_n(F)+\frac{1}{n^2}I_{2n},B_n=T_n(G)+\frac{1}{n^2}D_n(b),b(x)=(1+x)I_2.\) Here, both symbols are rank 1 almost everywhere. **Case 2, Example 2.**
Define piecewise-linear scalar functions in \[0,1\]: \(a(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } 1-2x, & 0\le x\le\frac{1}{2}, \\ 0, & \frac{1}{2}and let _Dn(a_), _Dn(b_) be the corresponding sampling matrices. With \(f(\theta)=2+cos\theta\), \(g(\theta)=3+cos\theta\) and \(A=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c } 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{array}\right],B=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c } 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{array}\right],\) define \(F(\theta)=f(\theta)\otimes A\) and \(G(\theta)=g(\theta)\otimes B\), and set \(A_n=\left(D_n^{1/2}(a)\otimes I_3\right)T_n(F)\left(D_n^{1/2}(a)\otimes I_3\right)+\frac{1}{5n}I_{3n},\) (9.12) \(B_n=\left(D_n^{1/2}(b)\otimes I_3\right)T_n(G)\left(D_n^{1/2}(b)\otimes I_3\right)+\frac{1}{5n}I_{3n}.\) (9.13) In every example we denote by \(\kappa\) and \(\xi\) the GLT symbols of {_An}n_ and {_Bn}n_, respectively. ## A candidate symbol for the geometric mean Let {_An}n_ and {_Bn}n_ be GLT matrix sequences whose matrix-valued symbols \(\kappa,\xi:[0,1]^d\times[-\pi,\pi]^d\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r\times r},\) are positive-semidefinite.
For any \(\varepsilon>0\), define the strictly positive symbols \(\kappa_\varepsilon=\kappa+\varepsilon I_r\), \(\xi_\varepsilon=\xi+\varepsilon I_r\). Since the matrix geometric mean is monotone continuous in each argument, the limit below exists point-wise and it is unique (\[3, p.3\]): **Definition 9.1 (Candidate symbol)** _For almost every_ \((x,\theta)\) _set_ \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)(x,\theta):=lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}G\big(\kappa_\varepsilon(x,\theta),\xi_\varepsilon(x,\theta)\big).\) (9.14)

The matrix-valued symbol \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)\) is _essentially_ positive semidefinite (see \[3\]) and satisfies the essential support identity \(\text{essRan}\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)=\text{essRan}\big[(x,\theta)\mapsto\text{ran}\kappa(x,\theta)\cap\text{ran}\xi(x,\theta)\big].\) Here ran_M_ denotes the column space of an individual matrix _M_, whereas essRan(.) is the essential range of a Grassmannian valued measurable map. The essential formulation of the subspace condition can also be formulated as the pre-image of the essential numerical range in the style of \[\[32\], Definition 1\]. Taking into account the Definition 9.1 of the candidate symbol, we propose the following conjecture: **Conjecture 9.2.1 (GLT closure under geometric mean)** _Let_ {_An}n and_ {_Bn}n be HPD GLT matrix sequences with_ \(\{A_n\}_n\sim_\text{GLT}\kappa,\{B_n\}_n\sim_\text{GLT}\xi.\) _Then the geometric mean matrix sequence is again GLT and_ \(\{G(A_n,B_n)\}_n\sim_\text{GLT}\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi),\) _where_ \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)\) _is the candidate symbol defined in_ (9.14). The heuristic justification of the conjecture is the following. For each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) the shifted sequences \(\{A_n+\varepsilon I\}_n\) and \(\{B_n+\varepsilon I\}_n\) are GLT sequences symbols \(\kappa_\varepsilon\) and \(\xi_\varepsilon\) and their geometric mean sequences satisfy \(\{G(A_n+\varepsilon I,B_n+\varepsilon I)\}_n\sim_\text{GLT}G(\kappa_\varepsilon,\xi_\varepsilon)\). Properties of monotone functions and the matrix geometric mean axioms described in \[3\], combined with closeness of the GLT ∗-algebra (GLT 4) under a.c.s convergence, suggest that letting \(\varepsilon\rightarrow 0\) the limit of \(\{G(A_n+\varepsilon I,B_n+\varepsilon I)\}_n\) is well defined in the a.c.s topology and this limit is {_G(An,Bn_)}_n_, up to zero-distributed perturbations , leading to the GLT algebraic part of Conjecture 9.2.1, a full proof when \(\kappa\) and \(\xi\) do not commute point-wise remains open. Meanwhile, all numerical evidence below supports the conjecture on the spectral distribution part of our hypothesis. ## Candidate symbols predicted by Conjecture 9.2.1 For the four test pairs introduced in Section 9.2.4, Conjecture 9.2.1 predicts the following GLT symbols for {_G(An,Bn_)}_n_. Throughout **1**=(1,1,1)T, \(J=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}\in\mathbb{C}^{3\times 3}\). **Case 1, Example 1.** \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)(x,\theta)=0_{2\times 2}.\) **Case 1, Example 2.** \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)(x,\theta)=\chi_{[-\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{4}]}(\theta)\otimes C,\)
\(C=\frac{1}{6^{1/4}\sqrt{2+\sqrt{6}}}\left[\begin{array}{ c c } 2\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3} & 2\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3} \end{array}\right].\)

**Case 2, Example 1.** \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)(x,\theta)=0_{2\times 2}.\) **Case 2, Example 2.** \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)(x,\theta)=\sqrt{\left(2+\mathrm{cos}\theta\right)\left(3+\mathrm{cos}\theta\right)h(x)k(x)}\otimes J.\) **Numerical verification of the Conjecture** Let \(G_n:=G(A_n,B_n)\in\mathbb{C}^{d_n\times d_n},d_n=\mathrm{size}(G_n).\) We test whether the empirical eigenvalue distribution of {_Gn}n_ converges to the distribution induced by the candidate symbol \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)(x,\theta)\) defined in Section 9.2.4. The comparison follows the standard rearrangement strategy. **1. Sampling the symbol.** Evaluate \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)\) on a tensor grid \(\{x_j\}_{j=1}^{M_x}\subset[0,1]\), \(\{\theta_i\}_{i=1}^{M_\theta}\subset[-\pi,\pi]\) with a total number of \(M_x\times M_\theta\simeq 2000\) samples. For each point \((x_j,\theta_i)\) compute the _r_ eigenvalues of the function; then merge and sort in non-decreasing order all the computed values. This yields the empirical quantile function of the eigenvalues. **2. Eigenvalue computation.** Matrices _An,Bn_ are generated for \(n\in\{40,80,160,320\}\), and eigenvalues are ordered in non-decreasing order, to obtain the quantile spectral distribution function of {_Gn}n_.
We also record \(\lambda_\mathrm{min}(G_n)\), \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}(G_n)\) and the condition number cond2(_Gn_) for later stability analysis. **3. Quantile plot matching.** For each _n_ we plot the sorted eigenvalues \(\left(\lambda_i(G_n)\right)\) against the corresponding rearranged eigenvalues of the sample values of \(\widetilde{G}\). A superposition of the two plots for growing values of _n_ gives an experimental indication of the asymptotic convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of {_Gn}n_ to that of the symbol. **4. Support analysis.** To estimate the measure of the zero set \(\{(x,\theta):\widetilde{G}=0\}\), we count the fraction of eigenvalues below the threshold 0.1 compared to the matrix size; the value is an estimate of the complement of the predicted measure of the support as _n_ grows. All tests for this section are run on an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H CPU (22 threads, 30.9 GiB RAM) under Ubuntu 24.10, Linux 6.11.0-29, with Python 3.12.7, NumPy 1.26.4 and SciPy 1.13.1 linked against OpenBLAS. **Remark 9.2 (Measure-theoretic meaning of the rearrangement test)** _As anticipated implicitly, the comparison of sorted eigenvalues versus the sorted eigenvalues of the sampled symbol has a precise measure-theoretic foundation based on the quantile approximation theory \[22\]. For completeness, we report the construction in \[22\] for the unilevel setting d_=1_; the multilevel case is analogous. Let r denote the size of_

<tbc>_the matrix_ \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)(x,\theta)\) _and put_ \(D=[0,1]\times[-\pi,\pi]\) _(so_ \(\mu(D)=2\pi\)_). Define the probability space by the triple_<tbc>

\((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}),\Omega=D\times\{1,\dots,r\},\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{B}(D)\otimes 2^{\{1,\dots,r\}}.\)

<tbc>_Here,_ B(_D_) _denotes the Borel_ \(\sigma\)_-algebra on D,_ 2<sup>{1_,...,r_}</sup> _denotes the power set of_ {1_,...,r}, and the product measure is_<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}(A\times B)=\frac{\mu(A)}{2\pi}\frac{|B|}{r},A\in\mathcal{B}(D),B\subseteq\{1,\dots,r\}.\)

<tbc>_With this choice,_

\(\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=\frac{\mu(D)}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{r}{r}=1,\)

_so that_ \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\) _is indeed a probability space._

_Introduce the random variable_

\(X(x,\theta,i):=\lambda_i\big(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)(x,\theta)\big),(x,\theta,i)\in\Omega,\)

_where the eigenvalues are ordered non-decreasingly. The quantile function of X is precisely the_ non-decreasing rearrangement \(\widetilde{G}^\dagger\) _of the matrix-valued symbol._

_Because spectral distributions are defined only up to measure-preserving rearrangements, we deduce that_

\(\{G_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\widetilde{G}\Longrightarrow\{G_n\}_n\sim_\lambda\widetilde{G}^\dagger,\)

_so verifying convergence to the quantile_ \(\widetilde{G}^\dagger\) _is equivalent and numerically simpler than verifying convergence to the symbol_ \(\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)\) _itself._

_Furthermore, whenever_ \(\widetilde{G}^\dagger\) _is continuous at_ \(t\in(0,1)\)_, the sorted eigenvalues satisfy_ \(\lambda_{\lceil tdn_n\rceil}(G_n)\rightarrow\widetilde{G}^\dagger(t)\) _as_ \(n\rightarrow\infty\)_, and the empirical proportion of eigenvalues below a small threshold t_<sub>0</sub> _(we take t_<sub>0</sub>=0.1_) converges to_ \(\mathbb{P}[X\le t_0]\)_, therefore it can be used as an estimate of the measure of the rank-deficient subset_ \(\{(x,\theta):\widetilde{G}(\kappa,\xi)(x,\theta)=0\}\).

## Conclusions and future work

Throughout the dissertation, we analyzed various structured matrix sequences arising from the discretization of multi-dimensional fractional partial differential equations. After introducing the analytical foundations of fractional operators, the spectral framework of matrix sequences, the main classes of structured matrices, and the GLT theory in Part I to provide a foundation for the numerical applications, in Part II we discretized several types of equations and addressed both direct and inverse problems. The associated linear systems are generally computationally challenging due to the dense and ill-conditioned nature of the coefficient matrices. However, we showed that the rich framework of GLT theory can effectively support the development of fast solvers, focusing in particular on preconditioning strategies. This final chapter summarizes our findings, highlights key similarities and differences across the studied scenarios, and suggests possible directions for future research.

### Summary of research contributions

In Chapter 5, we studied ISPs for a two-dimensional generalized diffusion equation involving a Caputo-type time-fractional derivative with a general memory kernel and nonlocal boundary conditions. Using the spectral decomposition of the associated elliptic operator, we derived explicit series representations of the solutions in terms of bi-orthogonal systems of eigenfunctions. We established rigorous existence and uniqueness results for regular solutions and demonstrated that both ISPs are ill- posed in the Hadamard sense. Several special cases, including tempered, multi-term, mono-term, and classical diffusion models, were obtained as particular choices of the memory kernel, illustrating the unifying nature of the generalized formulation. An interesting direction for future research would be to combine the present theoretical study with the computational features of structured matrices and the asymptotic spectral theory for matrix sequences, in the spirit of the works [33, 88, 102]. The design of fast regularization algorithms for the ISPs examined in this chapter presents a significant challenge.

In Chapter 6, we addressed an ISP for a space-time FDE involving a tempered fractional derivative in time and a Caputo fractional derivative in space. The ill-posed ISP was regularized using the quasi-boundary value method. The finite difference discretization led to a large-scale two-by-two block linear system with structured coefficients, for which we developed an efficient preconditioning strategy based on the block triangular structure. A detailed spectral analysis of the associated matrix sequences was conducted using the GLT framework, which provided a rigorous description of their asymptotic spectral behavior despite the presence of the variable coefficient that spoils the pure Toeplitz structure. Numerical experiments confirmed the stability, accuracy, and computational efficiency of the proposed approach in reconstructing the source term from noisy data. For future work, we plan to construct a more accurate preconditioner that accounts for the remaining outliers and possibly leads to a strong eigenvalue cluster at 1. In fact, even in presence of negative findings concerning matrix algebra preconditioners for multilevel Toeplitz systems,<tbc>

there exist cases especially in the fractional setting where optimality can still be reached [5, 99]. As a further step, a theoretical and practical comparison of our technique with direct-like solvers stemming either from block Gaussian elimination or from Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury methods would be valuable.

In Chapter 7, we considered an ISP for a time-space FDE with variable coefficients, extending the previous work from the uni-dimensional to the two-dimensional setting. A comprehensive spectral analysis of the coefficient matrix sequences was conducted using GLT theory, which guided the construction of an effective preconditioner. We introduced a block triangular preconditioner and proved that the preconditioned matrix sequence was weakly clustered at one in the GLT, singular value and eigenvalue sense, ensuring fast convergence of the preconditioned GMRES method. Numerical experiments demonstrated the accuracy of the source reconstruction and the efficiency of the proposed preconditioning strategy across various fractional orders and problem sizes. The convergence behavior depends mainly on the spatial discretization, with limited sensitivity to temporal refinement, which is reasonable considering that the number of outliers in the cluster at one of the preconditioned matrix depends only on the spatial dimension. Future work will address extensions to more complex geometries, high-order finite elements or isogeometric analysis with intermediate regularity, and higher dimensions. Additionally, taking inspiration from the variable-coefficient approach in [119] and from the \(\omega\)-circulant approach [31], other options for the choice of the preconditioners should be considered.

In Chapter 8, we studied the spectral properties and preconditioning of linear systems arising from the finite difference discretization of time-dependent space-FDEs with variable coefficients. The model involved a one-sided Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative multiplied by a variable coefficient, discretized using the shifted Grünwald formula in space and the \(\theta\)-method in time. The resulting all-at-once systems exhibited a (_d_+1)-level Toeplitz-like matrix structure. Using GLT theory, we provided a detailed analysis of the spectral distribution of both the original and preconditioned matrix sequences and proposed structure-preserving preconditioners based on circulant approximations. The main novelty was that the analysis fully covered the nonconstant variable coefficient case, both in one and two spatial dimensions, extending several existing results in the literature which were often restricted to more simplified settings. Numerical experiments confirmed the theoretical predictions and demonstrated significant reductions in GMRES iteration counts and computational cost. Several open problems remain. The extension of the eigenvalue distribution results for non-Hermitian Toeplitz matrices to the variable coefficient case seems not trivial and is not covered by the GLT theory due to the intrinsic non- Hermitian nature of the underlying matrix sequences. Additionally, estimates of the number of outliers and of the asymptotic behavior of the outliers in the preconditioned matrix sequences would have precise practical impact in estimating a priori the number of needed iterations of the proposed preconditioned GMRES procedures for reaching a preassigned accuracy.

In Chapter 9, we addressed a fundamental open question concerning the spectral distribution of geometric means of Hermitian positive definite GLT matrix sequences. We proved that when the GLT symbols commute, the invertibility condition on the symbols could be completely removed, resolving a long-standing conjecture. This result was established both in the scalar setting for any dimension and in the<tbc>

general block setting under the assumption that the symbols commute. We further demonstrated that the result is maximal: when the symbols do not commute and are simultaneously degenerate, the classical relation may fail and the geometric mean sequence may not coincide with the classical geometric mean of the symbols. Numerical experiments revealed new spectral phenomena explained by the theory of momentary GLT symbols, including secondary eigenvalue distributions and extremal spectral behavior connected to the order of vanishing of the associated GLT symbol. The numerical evidences open the door to further theoretical studies. Finally, the study of the spectral distribution when we consider the geometric mean of more than two matrix sequences is completely open and requires normwise error estimates for using the relevant tools.

## Future research directions

The same theoretical apparatus, including GLT theory, approximating classes of sequences, and non-Hermitian perturbations of Hermitian matrix sequences, could be applied to even more complex cases. For instance, high-order finite element approximations in _d_ spatial dimensions lead to _d_-level Toeplitz matrices with matrix- valued generating functions, corresponding to the GLT symbol [14]. Using similar approaches, we could also consider discontinuous Galerkin methods or isogeometric analysis. These cases lead to matrix-valued symbols in 2_d_ independent variables, as in the general GLT theory already available [8, 10, 11, 41, 42]. Finally, as a future task in this research direction, we will consider the design of optimized code in order to match the theoretical complexity derived in the present work for the preconditioning strategies proposed in the research chapters. The implementation of efficient algorithms that fully exploit the structure of the preconditioners, combined with careful optimization and parallelization, would further enhance the practical applicability of our approach.
